articles.title: Europe’s Russia Sanctions Reach China, but the Costs Return Home - China-US Focus
articles.summary: Europe’s Russia Sanctions Reach China, but the Costs Return Home  China-US Focus
articles.full_text:
Economic warfare in Europe has stranded Russia in the global market, but has yet to produce a reduction in its ambitions. Yet the EU is seeking to expand penalties with no clear outcome in hand. 
EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said he and China’s commerce secretary Wang Wentao had made a “crucial first step” towards rebalancing EU-China trade relations after their talks in Beijing on Oct 9, 2026.
Sanctions imposed in response to a war ultimately face one decisive test: whether they help end it. After four years and twenty-one packages against Russia over Ukraine, Europe can point to mounting economic costs without being able to demonstrate a corresponding change in Moscow’s conduct.
On 23 July, the EU added fourteen entities based in mainland China and Hong Kong to restrictions targeting alleged support for Russia’s military-industrial complex. Beijing answered within a day by placing fourteen European entities under export controls, prohibiting Chinese exporters—and foreign actors handling Chinese-origin goods—from supplying them with controlled dual-use items.
The identical number of targets conceal an asymmetry. A Chinese company denied European dual-use goods may be able to find substitutes elsewhere; a European manufacturer dependent on Chinese-controlled inputs may have fewer alternatives.
Indeed, European firms caught by Beijing’s Announcement No. 30 were soon asking whether they could still obtain the materials their production depended on and whether suppliers further down the chain could continue selling to them at all.
That episode exposes a larger difficulty. The EU’s turn toward Chinese firms is evidence that Brussels is reaching the limits of the targets it can hurt without generating opposition among its own member states. The fallback creates a new exposure: retaliation that can return the costs of Russia sanctions directly to European companies and, through them, to the governments whose unanimous support every subsequent package requires.
Sanctions have raised Russia’s procurement and transport costs, restricted access to Western technology, forced it to sell oil at a discount and damaged its longer-term economic prospects. What they’ve not done is compel Moscow to end or reduce the war, nor moved Beijing’s policy toward Russia by a single inch.
Demertzis and Brookings reach the same weakness by different routes: measures have arrived in stages, allowing Moscow time to adapt, while enforcement gaps, energy exemptions, third-country rerouting and a shadow fleet operating around the oil-price cap have diluted the effect each successive package was intended to produce.
Twenty-one packages in, costs to the EU states continue to scale while leverage does not. Still, Brussels is now preparing to scale again: 1,600 additional individuals and entities allegedly linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex could be proposed, increasing the existing list by about a third. The size makes the question sharper: will another tranche generate leverage that more than twenty previous packages did not, or simply extend a campaign whose marginal returns are becoming harder to identify?
This is where China enters.
The fourteen mainland Chinese and Hong Kong companies were among fifty-one entities added to a list subject to tighter restrictions because of purported support for Russia’s war economy or circumvention of existing controls. Their coercive effect therefore depends on whether the targeted firms need European-origin inputs that cannot readily be replaced.
The political attraction of such listings is easier to see. Chinese companies are often simpler for 27 governments to agree on than targets with powerful constituencies inside Europe. No member state has a national champion behind the Chinese company; fewer domestic lobbies are waiting outside ministries; and the listing can still be presented as action against a declared “systemic rival.” The July measures themselves were calibrated: major Chinese actors were omitted because member states feared retaliation.
That is what sanctions saturation begins to look like. As politically easier targets become scarcer, pressure shifts toward the names nobody around the Council table feels compelled to defend. Sanctions are moving toward the targets political agreement can still reach.
The mismatch runs deeper. Europe built much of its external influence through market access, regulation and standards. That model is strongest when access to the single market is the prize and substitution is costly. It is less suited to a contest in which power can run through control of individual technologies, minerals and components embedded inside another economy’s production chains.
China’s retaliation reverses the direction of European regulatory power. Brussels restricts access to European technology; Beijing asks which European firms depend on Chinese inputs and restricts those instead. Aggregate market size becomes less important than control of the component the other side cannot easily replace.
Washington adds another layer of coercive power that Brussels cannot reproduce. The U.S. can combine tech controls with the reach of the dollar system and secondary sanctions. Europe retains some leverage through its own market and technologies, but not the same financial reach. Against Chinese intermediaries that can replace European suppliers, EU restrictions can therefore impose compliance and commercial costs without producing the behavioural effect Brussels wants.
Beijing’s July response demonstrated the difference in another form: speed. While an EU sanctions package requires unanimous agreement among all 27 member states through extended negotiations, a Chinese export-control listing can be issued through a rapid executive decision. China responded in less than 24 hours; Beijing gave EU officials only about one hour’s warning before announcing its retaliation.
Combined with control over critical inputs, that institutional asymmetry produces escalation dominance. Beijing can identify exposed European entities, prepare its response and activate it before Brussels has begun negotiating its next collective move. The damage can then be concentrated on companies with the least room to adjust.
The exceptional-authorisation clause in Announcement No. 30 adds another lever. An exporter can apply to MOFCOM for permission to proceed in individual cases. That discretion allows Beijing to present the restrictions as calibrated rather than indiscriminate while encouraging affected firms to seek relief through national governments. A retaliatory list can therefore become a wedge between companies and Brussels, and between member states and the institutions that placed those companies in China’s crosshairs.
The political effect is more consequential than the numerical symmetry. The costs Beijing imposes land on member states, each dispute activates domestic lobbies, and each government has to explain the damage to voters—who never approved the exposure in the first place.
The ultimate vulnerability is unanimity itself. Every EU sanction package depends on all governments agreeing. Once retaliation becomes predictable, capitals can look ahead to which of their companies, universities or suppliers might appear on Beijing’s next list. Each exposed constituency creates an argument for an exemption, a narrower designation, a delay or a veto before the next package even reaches agreement.
In other words, China’s answer to the twenty-first package does not have to block the twenty-second to matter. It only has to raise the domestic price of voting for it.
A retaliation doctrine, if Brussels had one, would price that exposure before every vote: which targets carry real coercive weight; which European industries would absorb the response; which components have no reliable second supplier; and which companies would turn to national governments once the bill arrived.
Brussels has never produced a package-by-package account of what these measures achieve. Such scrutiny could expose an uncomfortable reality: the listings may impose greater costs on European firms than the coercive pressure they generate against Russia, while sanctioning a Chinese company can serve political leaders by parading resolve through another package, even when the coercive objective is vague or the expected leverage negligible.
Twenty-one packages in, Brussels is preparing another major expansion while the war continues and retaliation is beginning to travel back through Europe’s own dependencies. The danger is no longer confined to the companies caught in the exchange: once Beijing can turn supply-chain exposure into pressure on the unanimity behind EU sanctions, retaliation begins to erode Europe’s ability to agree to the next package.

articles.title: CBAM and EUDR: why European buyers now demand carbon footprints from African exporters - Capmad
articles.summary: CBAM and EUDR: why European buyers now demand carbon footprints from African exporters  Capmad
articles.full_text:
On 1 January 2026, the operational phase of the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) will start to apply to imports of cement, steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen, with importers required to open a CBAM account once they exceed a threshold of 50 tonnes of goods per year. The European Commission clarified in 2024 that importers or their customs representatives will need a CBAM account number if they cross this threshold as from 1 January 2026. For South African steelmakers, already warned that around 6% of their steel and aluminium exports to the EU, worth some EUR 1.2 billion a year, are directly exposed, this date has become a strategic milestone rather than a mere regulatory constraint. Workshops held with European officials established that the share of South African steel and aluminium exports concerned by CBAM represents about 6% of volumes to the EU, for a value close to EUR 1.2 billion per year.
Beyond carbon‑intensive industries, the new EU rules on deforestation‑free products are making carbon accounting and traceability unavoidable for African exporters of agricultural commodities. As from 30 December 2024, any company placing agricultural commodities such as cocoa from Côte d’Ivoire on the EU market will have to demonstrate that its supplies are legal and deforestation‑free in order to comply with the EU Regulation on deforestation‑free products. For European buyers, this obligation is already flowing through into the technical specifications they impose on African exporters, who must now provide detailed emissions data and forest‑footprint information for each shipment.
Why requirements are shifting toward carbon footprints
The growing demand for detailed carbon footprints does not stem from a generic CSR trend, but from the way Brussels has designed its climate‑related trade instruments. The CBAM regulation, adopted in 2023, creates a carbon tariff on imports of emissions‑intensive products to curb carbon leakage and align non‑EU producers with EU climate standards. To calculate this levy, the European importer needs credible data on the embedded emissions of the imported products; without such data from its African supplier, it risks being charged on the basis of default emission factors that are significantly more punitive.
On the agricultural side, the dynamic is similar but operates through deforestation rather than an explicit tax. EU Regulation 2023/1115 on deforestation‑free supply chains requires that palm oil, coffee, cocoa, rubber, soy, timber and certain derived products be placed on the EU market only after strict due diligence based on traceability data down to the plantation level. In practice, this means that European buyers now expect African exporters to deliver data sets comparable to a carbon footprint: GPS coordinates of plots, land‑use histories and, increasingly, emissions inventories linked to deforestation and processing.
West African cocoa and coffee in the spotlight
In cocoa and coffee value chains, this shift is translating into very specific demands from European roasters, chocolate makers and traders. Research on the Ivorian cocoa sector already shows large variations in traceability across cooperatives and underlines that by late 2024, companies trading these products in the EU will have to prove the legality and deforestation‑free status of their supplies, which implies fine‑grained plot monitoring and information systems aligned with the EUDR.
The reconfiguration does not concern certified chains only. Sector analyses on the EUDR’s impact on African coffee and cocoa trade show that exporters are now being pushed to deploy digital traceability platforms capable of registering plots with GPS data, tracking deforestation with satellite imagery and generating structured due‑diligence documentation for European clients. In practice, the carbon footprint is no longer just a high‑level corporate exercise, but a lot‑by‑lot management tool required upstream by buyers.
How European buyers are rewriting their specifications
Faced with the regulatory calendar, European buyers are translating CBAM and EUDR obligations into very concrete contractual clauses. In the cocoa chain, for instance, cooperatives that have been certified for several years under standards such as Rainforest Alliance or Fairtrade are identified as better positioned to meet these demands, because they already operate farm‑monitoring and data‑collection systems that European buyers seek to rely on. African exporters unable to supply such information risk, in the short term, being pushed toward less demanding markets or losing EU market share altogether.
The requirements tend to cluster around three information blocks that buyers see as inseparable:
- exhaustive mapping of suppliers and subcontractors, down to smallholder level;
- an emissions inventory covering at least energy use, transport and land‑use change;
- the ability to update the carbon footprint annually, in line with the climate‑reporting obligations of large European companies.
In heavy industry, the logic is similar: without verified, auditable emissions factors provided by African companies, European buyers cannot optimise their exposure to CBAM. South African industry players exporting to the EU have been explicitly urged to familiarise themselves with CBAM and prepare to demonstrate that their steel and aluminium exports comply with the emissions standards required in the EU.
African responses still taking shape
Regional initiatives are starting to structure a response, but remain in a ramp‑up phase. The African Organisation for Standardisation (ARSO) has developed a regional cocoa sustainability standard (ARS‑1000) designed to provide traceability and data frameworks compatible with the EU deforestation regulation, in order to help African producers and exporters stay eligible for the EU market. This largely voluntary approach shows that the issue is no longer whether European clients will require detailed carbon footprints, but how African exporters can share the costs of compliance.
In several countries, the supervisory authorities of export crops are gradually aligning with this data‑driven logic. Technical discussions between the European Commission and cocoa authorities in Ghana, Côte d’Ivoire and Cameroon in 2023 focused on traceability systems and on implementing a joint roadmap for the EUDR, with Ghana’s Cocoa Board explicitly seeking support to build traceability capacity and meet the forthcoming due‑diligence requirements. In this context, the carbon footprint is increasingly becoming a shared language between African regulators and European buyers.
The countdown to EU deadlines
In the near term, the dates are known and leave little room for manoeuvre. In the cocoa sector, the 30 December 2024 deadline for the effective application of the deforestation‑free products regulation is forcing a rapid acceleration of plantation mapping and database consolidation for buyers. For industrial sectors covered by CBAM, the transitional period also ends around 2026, when CBAM certificates will become payable and directly linked to reported emissions. Recent Commission communications stress that as from 1 January 2026, CBAM reporting will determine certificate payments and market access for importers exceeding the 50‑tonne threshold for relevant goods.
For African exporters, the immediate question is therefore less about debating the legitimacy of these instruments than about deciding at which level – company, value chain or region – they organise the production and consolidation of carbon data that their European partners now treat as a contractual prerequisite.

articles.title: France, Germany Agree on Softer EU Car Emissions and UK Status - Global Banking & Finance Review
articles.summary: France, Germany Agree on Softer EU Car Emissions and UK Status  Global Banking & Finance Review
articles.full_text:
France, Germany Reach Deal on EU Car Emissions and UK Special Status
Franco-German Agreement on EU Automotive Emissions and Market Access
By Philip Blenkinsop
Background and Proposed Emissions Rules
BRUSSELS, Oct 16 (Reuters) - France and Germany struck a deal on Friday to soften proposed EU car emissions rules and open the door for Britain to be treated as a trusted partner under the bloc's "Made in EU" rules.
The European Commission proposed last year that automakers cut CO2 emissions by 90% from 2021 levels in 2035, with the remaining 10% offset through measures such as the use of low-carbon steel and alternative fuels.
Franco-German Plan Details
Under the Franco-German plan, the 2035 target would be set at 90%, but without the need for additional compensatory measures. The approach is broadly in line with the wishes of German automakers.
European automotive stocks gained after the deal was announced, lifting the STOXX 600 Automobile and Parts Index nearly 2%.
Local-Content and Market Access Provisions
The joint plan also addresses an EU proposal introducing local-content and low-carbon requirements for products bought through public procurement, public auctions or subsidy schemes.
France has pushed for these products to be limited to those manufactured in the European Union. Other EU members, including Germany, argue that countries closely linked to EU automotive supply chains and free-trade-agreement partners should also be included.
Inclusion of the UK and Other Partners
The Franco-German plan says that for the automotive sector, "Made in EU" should cover the EU's 27 countries and other European partners that were part of the EU internal market on January 1, 2020.
That would include Britain, which left the EU single market at the end of 2020.
UK Response and Conditions
An official at British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's Downing Street office said inclusion in the "Made in EU" scheme would be good news for Britain's automotive sector. However, he said the Franco-German proposal would need wider European backing and that details had yet to be seen.
The Franco-German plan also says that inclusion should be subject to an agreement on full reciprocity, along with "dynamic alignment with EU conditions for investment from third countries and with EU trade protection measures".
That could mean Britain adopting measures the EU has taken to restrict imports of Chinese-built hybrid and battery-electric vehicles.
Reactions and Controversy
Industry and Political Responses
A GOOD DAY FOR JOBS OR A 'HISTORIC MISTAKE'?
The Franco-German paper also proposed compliance periods spanning multiple years for CO2 emission targets, no revision before 2030 of the utility factor for hybrid vehicles, which measures the share of driving done electrically, and recognition of cars powered by renewable and low-carbon fuels as zero-emission vehicles.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called the deal "a good day for motorists and for jobs in Germany, France and Europe".
The deal will not please all automakers. Toyota's European division, which sells cars in Europe from plants in the EU, Britain, Turkey and Japan, said on Thursday that including trusted partners such as Britain, Canada, Japan, South Korea and Turkey would give the EU the scale needed to compete with China.
Turkey's trade minister said this week on a trip to Brussels that trusted partners such as Turkey should not be excluded.
Environmental and Green Group Criticism
Green and environmental groups criticised the emissions proposals.
German Greens lawmaker Swantje Michaelsen said the German government was holding back the automotive industry, with high fuel prices already accelerating demand for EVs.
Anna Krajinska of transport and environment campaign group T&E called the deal a "historic mistake" that would reduce the incentive for industry to invest in EVs.
"German and French political leaders claim they are acting to save jobs, but this may well be the deal that buries Europe’s auto industry," she said.
Next Steps and Outlook
France and Germany still need to convince other EU members and the European Parliament for their plans to enter into force. They are unlikely to reach a final common text before early next year, after an EU-UK summit planned for November 20.
(Reporting by Philip Blenkinsop and Makini Brice. Additional reporting by Alistair Smout, Nick Carey, Rachel More and Kirsti Knolle. Writing by Charlotte Van Campenhout and Philip Blenkinsop. Editing by Xevi Fontdegloria and Mark Potter)

articles.title: UK to ‘act in lockstep’ with EU over China car tariffs, says minister - The Telegraph
articles.summary: UK to ‘act in lockstep’ with EU over China car tariffs, says minister  The TelegraphFrance drops opposition to UK being included in ‘Made in Europe’ legislation  The GuardianUK is prepared to align with EU tariffs on Chinese EVs, minister indicates  POLITICO.euFrance and Germany to allow UK to join EU car policy if it aligns on China tariffs  Financial TimesTariffing Chinese cars risks solving the wrong problem: Executive View  AM-online
articles.full_text:
Britain could accept the EU’s demand for tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles, Anas Sarwar, the trade minister, has suggested.
Mr Sarwar told Politico that Britain and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to combat the flood of Chinese imports of electric vehicles (EVs).
His comments were at odds with those of Jonathan Reynolds, the Business Secretary, who just a day earlier, reiterated his concern that Beijing could retaliate against British car exports to China.
However, the Financial Times reported on Thursday that France and Germany would now insist that the UK increase tariffs on Chinese cars, meaning manufacturers, such as BYD, Geely and Chery, face levies of up to 45pc.
In return, France would drop its opposition to the UK’s car industry joining the EU’s proposed “Made in Europe” scheme. Under the scheme, an EV would qualify for subsidies and public tenders only if at least 70pc of its parts are made within the bloc.
Paris’s previous hard line had left British manufacturers of cars and components fearing they would be frozen out of the Continent, putting up to €80bn (£68bn) of trade at risk.
Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister, has turned the UK’s inclusion in “Made in Europe” into a key goal for his summit with the EU on Nov 20.
The Financial Times said that if Britain agreed to the tariffs, the “Made in Europe” scheme would be extended to countries that “were part of the EU internal market on Jan 1 2020”.
That would include Britain, but not other countries hoping to join the scheme, such as Japan, Korea and Turkey.
A No 10 official on Thursday welcomed the EU’s apparent willingness to include the UK in the scheme, but did not commit Britain to introducing the tariffs.
“We’ll of course wait to see the detail, and there’s a process still to run in Europe,” he said.
This suggests Britain still sees an opening to continue negotiating.
“The UK and Europe share deep economic and strategic ties,” the official said. “And where we find common cause and approach challenges in a spirit of cooperation, we can create opportunities for businesses and workers on both sides.”
Mr Reynolds had said on Wednesday: “When we make any trade decision in terms of trade defence tariffs in relation to the EU, that’s based on the UK interest – it’s not based on any other country asking for that.”
But on the sidelines of a German-British business summit in London on Thursday, Mr Sarwar said Brussels and London had to “grapple with the challenge that comes from rapid expansion in China”.
“The more that the UK and the EU work together and act in lockstep, the better it is for both the UK and the European Union,” he said.

articles.title: France and Germany agree to ease EU car emissions rules in new deal - France 24
articles.summary: France and Germany agree to ease EU car emissions rules in new deal  France 24
articles.full_text:
Paris and Berlin on Friday confirmed their deal aimed at protecting Europe's struggling automotive sector, having reached agreements on the flashpoint issues of EU car emissions and "made in Europe" components. A draft deal reviewed Thursday showed the two countries backing looser EU emissions rules for carmakers.
France and Germany said in a joint statement they agreed on a common approach to secure the future of the European automotive industry, aiming to cut CO2 emissions while ensuring next-generation electric vehicles are developed and built in Europe.
The plan sets out a European decarbonisation pathway with regulatory flexibility and incentives for investment, research, production and resilient supply chains, the statement said.
"Our shared ambition is clear: to successfully transform our automotive industry while maintaining our climate ambition and ensuring that the cars of the future are produced in Europe," the two countries said.
Diplomatic sources confirmed to AFP Thursday that Paris and Berlin had backed a further scaling down of EU emission rules for cars as part of the long-negotiated deal.
Europe's two economic powerhouses also agreed to include Britain in the definition of what vehicles would count as "made in Europe" under EU measures aiming to bolster the bloc's industries, according to a draft document outlining the pact.
Watch more2026 Paris Motor Show: Western carmakers face steep competition from Chinese rivals
Paris and Berlin had long been at loggerheads on the course Europe should take as it seeks to revive its struggling auto industry and the accord is likely to shape the continent's policy going forward.
Germany wanted less stringent carbon emission targets for carmakers and a broad interpretation of "made in Europe" to include key non-EU trade partners.
France on the other hand had pushed to preserve the bloc's climate ambitions and to keep the "made in Europe" public procurement scheme the purview of EU nations.
Berlin won the first argument while Paris carried the day on the latter, the draft showed.

The European Commission had proposed that the bloc's ban on sales of new petrol and diesel vehicles in 2035 be scrapped in favour of a requirement for manufacturers to cut new vehicle exhaust emissions by 90 percent.
The remaining 10 percent would have had to be compensated for through various credits obtained among other things by using low-carbon steel.
The Franco-German deal scraps the latter requirement, according to the draft, stating that residual emissions should not have to be compensated by manufacturers.
It also opens the door for cars running on renewable fuels to count as "zero-emission" and makes it much easier for automakers to reach CO2 targets.
So-called "super credits" the commission had suggested carmakers would benefit from for small "affordable" electric cars are extended to all vehicles "irrespective of their size or length".

'Good news' for Britain
The agreement on "made in Europe" restricts its application regarding cars to the EU's 27 countries, with an opt-in for a handful of others, notably Britain and Norway under certain conditions.
That is a narrower definition than the one proposed by the commission in March.
London hailed the move. If confirmed, it "would be good news for the British automotive industry and the jobs and investment it supports across the UK", the office of Prime Minister Andy Burnham said.
The EU executive had unveiled plans to tie companies' access to public money to minimum thresholds for EU-made parts in their products – to ensure that public and foreign investments support manufacturing inside the bloc.
But under Brussels' proposal, dozens of partner countries that have deals with the EU allowing European companies to access public money on a par with local firms could have been brought into the fold.
European carmakers had asked for Britain to be included, citing deeply integrated supply chains.
The pact will need backing from other EU states and the European Parliament to become law, but carries weight given the economic heft of the two signatories.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

articles.title: Inconclusive sparring at EU summit puts budget timeline into question - Euronews
articles.summary: Inconclusive sparring at EU summit puts budget timeline into question  EuronewsGermany pours cold water on Irish-drafted EU budget proposals  Irish IndependentFrance's Macron warns EU leaders they need budget deal before year-end, say diplomats  ReutersShorten EU budget to 3 or 4 years, Cyprus president tells POLITICO  POLITICO.euCzech Prime Minister Babis rails against EU budget support for Ukraine  The Kyiv Independent
articles.full_text:
EU leaders stuck to their red lines on the next long-term budget at Thursday's summit, with several now rejecting the presumed December deadline. Council President António Costa is now expected to take over the negotiations, with a new compromise due in a few weeks.
EU leaders have refused to budge on the bloc’s next long-term budget and openly cast doubt on whether a deal can be sealed by the end of the year, a slippage that would mean significant delays and a collision with a string of national elections.
Until now, capitals were committed to reaching a final agreement by December 2026. But at Thursday’s summit in Brussels, where talks dragged longer than expected, a growing number of governments are asking whether that is really necessary.
"We are not reaching an agreement this month. Not next month. I don’t know even if it’s possible to reach an agreement before the end of the year," said caretaker Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. "I think we are not in a hurry."
For months, European Council President António Costa has repeated that leaders must unanimously agree the next seven-year budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), by December at the very latest.
If talks spill into 2027, he warns, there will not be enough time to complete the complex legislative work needed to get the budget up and running by 1 January 2028.
Following the inconclusive summit, where the Irish presidency’s compromise proposal to cut the overall volume by €141 billion was largely rejected, Costa will take over the negotiations, which was largely expected.
The European Council President is due to present a new negotiating proposal in a few weeks, which is bound to follow a completely different logic from the Irish one. EU leaders have been called in for a special summit on 26 November.
In particular, Costa's proposal is due to keep the national contributions low, a new package of EU-wide taxes to finance the budget, and maintain sufficient flexibility for unforeseen expenses, a budget line the Irish proposal significantly cut down.
Already before the summit, the draft joint conclusions were watered down concerning the deadline, softening language that explicitly set out “the aim of reaching a final agreement by the end of the year.”
By contrast, the final language says that "an agreement before the end of 2026 would allow for the adoption of legislative acts in 2027, which is necessary to ensure that EU funding reaches beneficiaries without interruption in January 2028."
Speaking before the summit, several leaders made clear that they do not feel bound by an end-of-year timeline, as it would be extremely difficult to explain to their domestic audiences that they accepted a bad deal because of an artificial deadline.
"The date cannot become more important than the content," Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni told the Senate on Wednesday.
"We will not sign an agreement that is not advantageous to us just to meet a deadline. We will sign an agreement only when it is right for Italy."
There is, however, no consensus on what a “good deal” looks like. Every government wants to take as much as possible from the EU budget while paying in as little as possible.
The main battle line runs between two camps: the so-called “frugals,” a German-led coalition of six net contributors pushing for steep cuts to the overall volume, and the Friends of Cohesion, a 17-strong bloc of southern and eastern countries fighting to preserve traditional funding programmes for the poorest regions.
But the camps are not monolithic. Some Friends of Cohesion, like Spain and Italy, have a vested interest in agricultural funds. Others, like the Baltic states, want to boost defence spending due to their proximity to Russia.
Among the frugals, Germany and Sweden are seen as the most radical, while Finland is keen on farming subsidies. France, the bloc’s second-largest economy, has yet to pick a side, trapped between its European ambitions and a runaway budget deficit.
Belgium and Luxembourg are somewhere dithering between the factions.
"In the end, we need a good Multiannual Financial Framework. So, of course, everyone wants to make speed. But it’s more important to have a good deal than a bad deal," Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said.
In other words, the red lines are so entrenched, and the room for compromise so slim, that a landing zone currently looks like a mirage.
In Brussels circles, deals on sensitive topics are only struck under intense time pressure, because neither side feels compelled to make concessions until the last minute. Signalling that one does not feel bound by a timeline may therefore be a negotiating tactic to stand one’s ground.
For EU officials, even more worrying than the potential delay to funding programmes are the string of elections due in 2027 in France, Italy, Poland, Finland, Estonia, Slovakia and Greece. Some fear that if no deal is reached by the end of this year, it could slip to autumn 2027.
Paris is a particular concern. Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is currently the favourite to win the presidential race, and she has promised to cap France’s contribution at €5 billion a year, a sharp cut from the current level of around €8 billion.
Meanwhile, elections in Spain, where voters go to the polls on 29 November, and Sweden, which voted in September, "are likely to create some issues", said Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides.
Christodoulides reiterated the need to reach an agreement by the end of the year. He is one of the few EU leaders still saying so.

articles.title: Europe’s debt map flips: Belgium borrows like Greece as France pays more than Italy - AOL.co.uk
articles.summary: Europe’s debt map flips: Belgium borrows like Greece as France pays more than Italy  AOL.co.uk
articles.full_text:
Imagine an investor who fell asleep in the summer of 2012, at the height of the euro crisis, and woke up this morning. He would remember a simple map. In the north, a core of countries that borrowed cheaply, with Germany at the centre. In the south, a periphery of debtors – Greece, Portugal, Spain, Italy, Ireland – that paid dearly for the privilege of staying in the single currency. Fourteen years later, that map no longer describes the eurozone.
Belgium, home to the European Union institutions, now borrows for ten years at 4.29%. Greece, bailed out three times, pays 4.35%, almost the same rate. Portugal, rescued in 2011, pays less than Spain. Ireland, rescued in 2010, pays almost the same as the Netherlands. And France, which he remembered as part of the core, pays more than Italy.
The old periphery has moved north. That is the backdrop against which eurozone governments are about to ask investors for more money than ever before.
What moved the border
Bond yields are the interest rates a government pays to borrow. They rise when investors think a country will need more money than it can comfortably repay, and they fall when it proves the opposite. Greece has spent a decade proving the opposite.
In 2025, Athens ran a budget surplus of 1.7% of gross domestic product (GDP), and its debt, though still the highest in Europe, fell by more than nine percentage points of GDP in a single year.
“For years, when markets talked about sovereign risk in Europe, the focus was usually on the periphery,” Ken Egan, head of European sovereign credit at the rating agency KBRA, told Euronews.
Over the past decade, he said, those countries have followed more prudent fiscal policy, improved their primary balances, extended debt maturities, collected taxes better through digitalisation and rebuilt their banks.
“That has helped smooth refinancing risks and put debt on a much firmer path than 10 or 15 years ago.”
Belgium went the other way. Its deficit widened to 5.2% of GDP last year, larger than France’s 5.1% in the same year, and its debt rose above 109% of GDP in the first quarter of 2026, and investors noticed.
“The traditional core has changed as well, but in a different direction,” Egan said.
“In some cases there is less clarity around the policy path, more political uncertainty, rising structural spending pressures and much higher refinancing costs than governments had become used to during the low-rate period.”
France’s position on the map is defined by one figure above all: the state spends 57.2% of everything the economy produces, the highest share in the G20. Debt has reached €3.6 trillion, or 119% of GDP, up from 98.2% before the pandemic.
The bill due in 2027
On 29 September, the French Treasury set out how much it will need to borrow next year: €340 billion in medium- and long-term bonds, a record, equal to about 11% of GDP and up from €310 billion this year.
Much of it is not new spending but old debt coming back for refinancing, as bonds issued during the pandemic and the energy crisis mature.
Every euro of that debt is being renewed at a higher price.
France has paid an average interest rate of 3.55% on medium- and long-term bonds issued so far this year, up from 3.14% last year. Its annual interest bill is forecast to rise from €62.6 billion in 2026 to €72.9 billion in 2027, roughly a fifth of what the state collected in revenue last year.
That last number is the one investors now read first.
“Markets are looking much more closely at the fiscal story, and not just at how much governments are borrowing, but what they are borrowing for,” Egan said.
“Borrowing that supports investment and future growth is one thing; borrowing mainly to cover a rising interest bill is viewed quite differently.”
Germany is issuing a record €512 billion of securities this year, but to pay for defence and infrastructure, which is the kind of borrowing markets forgive.
Italy and Spain will each refinance several hundred billion.
And the IMF, in its latest World Economic Outlook, pointed to a detail that makes every government more exposed: in the G7 and Spain, nearly 30% of public debt now matures within a year, so a change in interest rates reaches the budget within months rather than decades.
Why sovereign yields keep rising
Between February and September, the average 10-year yield across the G7 rose by more than a full percentage point to its highest level in nearly two decades, the IMF’s fiscal chief Rodrigo Valdés and his deputy Era Dabla-Norris wrote this week.
The oil shock, persistent inflation and the money pouring into artificial intelligence all played a part. But at the centre, they wrote, are fiscal fundamentals: investors demand more to lend for ten years to governments that keep spending more than they collect.
The European Central Bank (ECB) has added to the cost, raising its deposit rate twice this year to 2.50% to contain inflation.
The German 10-year yield, the floor for the whole eurozone, has climbed from 2.64% in February to 3.45%. France’s has risen twice as fast and briefly touched 5% in early October, the widest gap with Germany since 2012.
The danger, Egan said, is that the market itself becomes part of the problem.
“A political headline or weak budget can push the curve higher, refinancing becomes more expensive, fiscal space narrows, and the market then has another reason to demand a higher premium.”
That loop turns faster than it used to, because the buyers have changed.
For a decade the ECB bought government bonds with newly created money; now it lets them run off.
“There is less natural long-duration demand in the market, with central banks stepping back, pension demand changing and more of the marginal buying coming from price-sensitive investors,” Egan said. Higher energy prices, he added, make it worse by “weakening growth while keeping inflation and rates higher”.
The IMF describes the result in one sentence: in a growing number of countries, the interest rate on new debt is now higher than the growth rate of the economy.
When that happens, debt rises on its own unless the government runs a surplus before interest.
Most of Europe does not. “The more countries wait, the more painful the adjustment becomes,” the Fund wrote.
Is this 2012 again?
Not yet, says Lombard Odier. The Swiss bank’s investment office argues that markets are “pricing uncertainty rather than the conditions for a new sovereign debt crisis”. France’s interest payments remain affordable, at slightly above 2% of GDP, half Italy’s.
Its current account deficit is small, and it does not depend on foreign money the way Portugal, Spain and Greece did in 2012, when they imported capital worth 7% to 12% of their economies every year.
The bank’s forecast is dull rather than dramatic: French spreads stay wide until a credible budget passes parliament, probably not before the May 2027 presidential election, and the euro drifts lower, to $1.09.
Clara Raposo, vice-governor of the Banco de Portugal, offered a different warning this month.
Sovereign bond markets, she said, have become more sensitive to inflation, fiscal doubts and geopolitics, and shocks now spread faster from one country to another, amplified by funds that sell first and ask questions later.
“Trust may be intangible, but its economic consequences are real,” Raposo said.
Your debt, my inflation
The transmission is not only financial.
A randomised experiment with German firms in the Bundesbank’s panel, which surveys roughly 7,000 firms, published by the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) earlier this year, found that half of them think the ECB will hold back on rate rises to protect weaker treasuries.
When researchers showed them a pessimistic forecast for the average debt-to-GDP ratio of France, Italy and Spain, the firms raised their expectations for German inflation three years ahead by 1.4 percentage points among those who distrust the ECB.
Fiscal stress in one member state, in other words, can raise inflation expectations in another, and the channel is trust.
In 2012, the question was whether the periphery could pay. In 2027, the question is who, exactly, the periphery is.

articles.title: France and Germany strike deal to boost Europe's struggling car industry - Modern Ghana
articles.summary: France and Germany strike deal to boost Europe's struggling car industry  Modern Ghana
articles.full_text:
The deal between Europe's two economic powerhouses aims to cut carbon emissions and support the development and manufacture of electric cars in Europe, the two countries said in a joint statement published on Friday.
"Our shared amibition is clear: to successfully transform our automotive industry while maintaining our climate ambition and ensuring that the cars of the future are produced in Europe," it said.
The deal also provides "concrete incentives for investment, research and development, European production and resilient supply chains".
The agreement still needs the backing of other EU states and the European Parliament to become law, but is expected to shape the continent's future policy.
European car manufacturers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts, which have been increasingly targeting Europe as they face barriers to selling in the United States and weaker demand at home.
Chinese electric vehicles and hybrids accounted for 10.7 percent of the European market in the second quarter of 2026, up from 5.7 percent a year earlier, Schmidt Automotive Research said.
Franco-German dynamic
Paris and Berlin had long been at loggerheads on the course Europe should take as it seeks to revive its struggling auto industry.
Germany wanted less stringent carbon emission targets for carmakers and a broad interpretation of "made in Europe" to include key non-EU trade partners, such as Norway and the UK.
France, on the other hand, had pushed to preserve the bloc's climate ambitions and to keep the "made in Europe" public procurement scheme within the scope of EU member states.
Both countries' leaders welcomed the deal.
French President Emmanuel Macron said it showed a "clear ambition to successfully transform" the European automotive industry while upholding Europe's climate goals.
"We hope that this Franco-German dynamic will lead to a swift agreement with our partners, for the sake of our jobs and our industry," he wrote in a post on social media platform X.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz described the deal as a "good day for car drivers and for jobs in Germany, France and Europe".
"This sends a pro-investment signal to the industry," he wrote, also on X.
Softened emissions targets
The European Commission proposed last year that CO2 emissions from cars should drop by 90 percent from 2021 levels in 2035, and that carmakers would have to close the gap to 100 percent by using low-carbon steel and alternative fuels.
However, under the Franco-German deal, the target would be set at 90 percent without the need for any other compensatory measures.
The softened target is broadly in line with the wishes of German car manufacturers.
The deal also opens the door for cars running on renewable fuels to count as "zero-emission" and makes it much easier for automakers to reach CO2 targets.
'Good news' for the UK
The provisional Franco-German plan says that, for the automotive sector, the "Made in EU" label should cover the EU's 27 member states and other European partners that were part of the EU internal market on 1 January, 2020.
That would include the UK, which officially left the EU single market on 31 January, 2020.
An official at UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's office said it would be good news for the UK's automotive sector if it was included in the "Made in EU" scheme. He added, however, that the Franco-German proposal would need European consensus and that details were yet to be seen.
The Franco-German plan also says this inclusion should be subject to an agreement on full reciprocity, along with "dynamic alignment with EU conditions for investment from third countries and with EU trade protection measures".
That could mean the UK having to adopt the measures the EU has taken to limit imports of Chinese-built hybrid and battery electric vehicles.
(with newswires)

articles.title: Germany and France want own ‘Made in Europe’ rules for cars, outside EU industrial policy - EUobserver
articles.summary: Germany and France want own ‘Made in Europe’ rules for cars, outside EU industrial policy  EUobserver
articles.full_text:
France and Germany want more detailed “Made in Europe” rules for electric cars, and want them split off from the rest of the EU’s flagship industrial law.
The Franco-German deal, agreed after months of haggling on the margins of the EU summit in Brussels late on Thursday (15 October), says both files should then be adopted “as fast as possible and simultaneously”.
That would split the most fought-over part from the rest of the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), which also sets “Made in EU” and low-carbon requirements for steel, cement, aluminium and clean-tech products such as batteries and solar panels.
Paris hopes the new car definition will serve as a benchmark for the rest of the IAA, which sets “Made in Europe” rules for steel, cement, aluminium and clean energy technologies.
But this still has to be negotiated with other member states, people familiar with the talks said.
[ Ready for a smarter inbox? Get EUobserver’s free daily update - delivered every morning at 7:30 sharp. .]
“We are driven by a clear ambition: to successfully transform our automotive industry while upholding our climate goals and our production in Europe,” said French president Emmanuel Macron on social media, announcing the deal.
“This is an investment signal to industry,” said German chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Made in Europe
The paper comes as Ireland, which holds the EU's rotating six-month presidency, is wrapping up a third compromise text on the industrial plan, which Irish officials hope will reach final agreement by mid November.
Publicly, Paris and Berlin said on Friday that their car deal will not affect climate targets and that their course “remains unchanged”.
But the paper behind the deal shows the trade-off that’s been made. Berlin accepted France’s demand for stricter “Made in Europe” rules that apply to fewer countries, while Paris agreed to looser emission rules for carmakers, as Germany had wanted.
To count as “Made in Europe”, a car would have to clear thresholds that tighten over time, and only cars meeting these rules could be bought, leased or rented with public subsidies, or bought by public authorities.
From 2028, the car must be assembled in Europe, with at least 70 percent of total value creation in components - excluding the battery.

articles.title: Budget, Ukraine, migration: Five takeaways from the EU leaders’ summit - Euronews
articles.summary: Budget, Ukraine, migration: Five takeaways from the EU leaders’ summit  EuronewsEU resists bid to weaken emissions rules as leaders spar over energy costs  Financial TimesCosta angers EU leaders as splits mar summit  POLITICO.euStatement by the President: EUCO of 16 October 2026  European CommissionEU member states struggle to reach an agreement to lower energy prices  Le Monde.fr
articles.full_text:
EU leaders ended their Brussels summit with no deal on the budget, a new €70bn Ukraine funding gap, open clashes over energy and migration, but fresh resolve to create new trade defence tools to battle China.
EU leaders gathered in Brussels on Thursday and Friday with a packed agenda, from the long-term budget and financial support for Ukraine to migration, energy and China.
The summit alternated between entrenched positions on the bloc’s budget, a warm welcome for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and clashes over energy and migration policies.
Here are the five highlights.
Rallying behind Ukraine
The bitter row between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump dominated the second day of the summit.
Leaders closed ranks behind Zelenskyy and promised to keep sanctions in place for as long as Russia pursues its full-scale invasion. They also condemned the diesel deal struck by Trump with Russian President Vladimir Putin, although the Bulgarian prime minister broke ranks to support it.
The reception gave Zelenskyy a moment of diplomatic relief as Trump doubled down, claiming Zelenskyy was “more difficult” to deal with than Putin and demanding new elections in Ukraine. Trump also called Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries, its main leverage, a “disgrace”.
“I defend the interests of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people exclusively,” Zelenskyy said in a defiant tone. “We were attacked, occupied, and our people were killed. It is only logical that we have the right to defend ourselves.”
“We will keep living, fighting, and most importantly, living with dignity,” he added.
In his address, Zelenskyy asked leaders for an additional €70bn in financial and military support next year to counter Russia’s escalation.
The request upends the bloc’s plans, which assumed last year's €90bn loan would cover both 2026 and 2027. EU leaders tasked the Commission to come up with a proposal on how to address Kyiv's financial needs.
Filling the gap will be anything but easy. Soaring borrowing costs make joint debt unpalatable. The immobilised Russian assets, which Zelenskyy raised again, remain politically divisive. And bilateral contributions risk leaving the burden on a handful of wealthy countries.
EU budget
On Thursday, leaders debated the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) at length but, as expected, made little headway, as the “frugal” net contributors and the southern and eastern “Friends of Cohesion” dug in.
One thing is clear: the negotiating box tabled by the Irish presidency just days ago, which proposed slashing €141bn from the overall budget to appease the frugal, is now officially dead.
European Council President António Costa will take over the talks. He is due to present a new compromise in the coming weeks, which many expect to come before the special summit he has called for 26 November, just days before the Spanish elections.
Costa is expected to pursue three main lines: keep national contributions as low as possible, rework the package of EU-wide taxes, including by drawing on European Parliament proposals, and restore the flexibility instruments the Irish presidency ruthlessly cut.
That Costa would sooner or later step in was always on the cards. More worrying is that leaders on both sides now openly say they feel no pressure to close the deal by the end of the year.
Seasoned negotiators know that deadlines force concessions. Member states may be playing with fire: a no-deal in December would raise the prospect of talks slipping until after an electoral season that could reshape Europe’s political landscape.
Migration
Migration proved once again among the most contentious issues, after the last discussion, in June, descended into a shouting match between Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on one side and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni and Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen on the other.
This time, Rome unexpectedly extended a hand to Madrid just before the dossier reached the table on Friday. Italy and Spain reached what appears to be a first step towards ending their border dispute, after a string of tit-for-tat checks introduced in the wake of the Ceuta crisis.
Italy’s temporary border controls were due to expire on Thursday evening. They were extended by a week to align with Spain’s, which expire on 22 October. The two interior ministers are due to agree on replacement measures by then.
But while Meloni opened the summit in a conciliatory tone, Sánchez’s other main European nemesis, Frederiksen, did not spare her fellow social democrat over his plan to regularise the status of 600,000 migrants.
“I have asked the European Commission to examine what happens when a country does almost the exact opposite of what the rest of us are doing,” Frederiksen said, referring to Spain in all but name.
Meloni, Frederiksen and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten hosted an informal breakfast before the discussion with 17 other EU leaders to explore “innovative solutions” on migration. Support is growing for emergency measures allowing asylum applications to be suspended during crises.
Tensions between the migration hard-liners and Spain and France came to the fore as the Italian, Danish and Polish governments pushed to rewrite the conclusions to call for avoiding “measures that could create incentives for illegal migration.”
By contrast, the final text merely urges the Commission to coordinate with the member states "on all types of instrumentalisation."
China
On “macroeconomic imbalances”, EU jargon for avoiding naming China, leaders held their course despite the deal between the European Commission and Beijing to curb hybrid car imports.
Over lunch on Thursday, they pressed the Commission to prepare a toolbox of new trade defence instruments, including safeguards with quotas and tariffs, to shield the chemicals and machinery industries from Chinese competition.
China loomed large as the bloc faces a trade deficit of about €360bn with Beijing. Chemicals and machinery, among the sectors hardest hit by cheap Chinese imports, were singled out as the next industries needing urgent protection after the hybrid car quotas.
While the car quotas were negotiated with Beijing, leaders called on Thursday for unilateral safeguards to be introduced “without delay”, according to officials.
The Commission presented last week’s deal as the first phase of negotiations launched in June. But time is running out: the EU’s trade deficit with China keeps widening month after month, and Chinese customs data show Chinese exports to the EU up 25% over the past year.
The EU’s strategy is to keep talking as long as dialogue delivers concrete results, while strengthening its trade defences. France and Germany last week urged the Commission to develop a new instrument to respond swiftly to market disruptions caused by China, which has been accused of unfair trade practices.
“The competition must be fair. We will create instruments against leveraging capacities, against high subsidies, against undervalued currencies. And there will be a toolbox for that. The toolbox will be bigger. It will also be applied as necessary,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said.
Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told leaders her institution would begin work on such a tool, though it remains unclear whether it will be ready before the end of the year.
Other instruments are in the pipeline, including a diversification tool to encourage EU companies to diversify their suppliers of strategic products such as critical raw materials, and a solidarity mechanism to help member states hit by possible Chinese countermeasures.
Energy
On Thursday, leaders were dragged into an interminable discussion on energy. The Visegrád Group (V4) and Italy asked to amend the summit conclusions to call on the Commission to propose new measures to curb short-term swings in electricity prices and to reassess the proposed Emissions Trading System (ETS).
The V4, Italy and, to a lesser extent, Greece led the push because they face some of Europe’s highest energy costs, a concern largely shared by other member states, which ultimately called for a coordinated European response to the ongoing energy crisis.
The attempt to reopen the ETS, however, triggered an ideological backlash from Finland, Denmark and Sweden. The system makes companies pay for their emissions and encourages investment in sustainability.
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš, by contrast, lashed out at the carbon tax, accusing it of wrecking Europe’s competitiveness by fuelling soaring energy costs for the benefit of market speculators.
“We’ve been engaged in a drafting exercise all day at the leaders’ level about something technical,” an EU official vented at the margins of the summit. “It’s not resulting in any new measures or new policies that actually help EU member states in their problems.”
Rome and the V4 know they lack the qualified majority to reopen the EU’s carbon market rules. The aim was rather to signal to domestic audiences that they are doing what they can to contain the surge in energy prices.

articles.title: EU AI Act Deadlines Moved: Credential Press Reissues 16 Exam and AI Act Books - The National Law Review

articles.full_text:
Press Release Date 10-16-2026
New editions follow the Digital Omnibus dates, the AIGP Body of Knowledge 2.1 and PECB's multiple-choice ISO exams, for candidates and compliance teams.
LONDON, ENGLAND, UNITED KINGDOM, October 16, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Exam prep publisher Credential Press has reissued 16 of its certification guides, practice books and EU AI Act titles, each rebuilt against the current version of the exam or the law it covers. The biggest change is in its AI governance titles: the EU AI Act's deadlines for high-risk AI systems have moved, and a book written before the change gives its reader the wrong dates.
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, entered into force on 27 July 2026. It moved the EU AI Act's high-risk rules to 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. The Regulation itself began applying generally on 2 August 2026.
The dates matter outside the EU too. The Act's scope does not follow corporate geography: a provider outside the EU can be fully in scope when it places an AI system on the EU market, and so can a provider or deployer outside the EU whose system's output is used in the Union.
"We would rather reissue our books than leave one candidate studying for an exam that no longer exists," said Sotiris Spyrou, founder of Credential Press. "Every edition prints the version it follows on its copyright page. If the version on the board's own site is different, the book is out of date, and a reader can check that in a minute."
What the new editions follow:
 - AIGP Exam Guide and AIGP Practice Questions, for candidates sitting the IAPP's AI governance exam: Body of Knowledge and Exam Blueprint version 2.1, effective 2 February 2026, with the EU AI Act dates as the Omnibus set them.
- AI Governance Framework and AI Governance Worked Scenarios, for compliance, legal and risk teams preparing for the new deadlines: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as amended by the Omnibus. The handbook works through the Regulation in the order it creates obligations; the companion decides 24 situations against the Articles.
- ISO 42001 Lead Implementer Exam Guide and Practice Questions: PECB's Candidate Handbook version 1.5. The exam is 80 multiple-choice questions with three options each, and 48 of the 80 measure evaluation rather than recall.
- ISO 27001 Lead Implementer Exam Guide, Lead Implementer Practice Exams and Lead Auditor Exam Guide: PECB's English exam, now multiple choice instead of essays. The practice book holds three full papers of 80 questions, 240 in all.
Seven more titles were reissued alongside them, for the CISSP, CISM, CCSP, FRM Part I and ISO 45001 Lead Auditor exams.
On PECB's multiple-choice ISO exams, ISO 42001 and ISO 27001 included, the pass mark really is a percentage: 70% passes, which is 56 of 80 questions. ISC2, ISACA and the IAPP report scaled scores instead, and GARP publishes no pass mark at all. The board-by-board table of published pass marks, with the source and review date for every figure, is at credentialpress.com/pass-marks.
Credential Press has 42 titles on sale, covering credentials from five boards: the IAPP, ISACA, ISC2, PECB and GARP. Each exam guide is paired with a practice book that tests the blueprint in the exam's own format. The books are sold on Amazon and listed at credentialpress.com/books.
About Credential Press
Credential Press publishes exam guides and practice books for professional certifications in privacy, information security, audit, risk, AI governance and quality management. Every title is written from the exam board's own published documents, scoped to the published blueprint, and dated to the edition it covers. Credential Press is an imprint of Verity AI Ltd (verityai.co) and is independent of the IAPP, ISACA, ISC2, PECB, GARP, ISO and the European Commission.

[SMM Steel] European HRC: CBAM Compliance Risks Disrupt Import Trade as Mills Push Q1 Forward Prices
[Europe] Obligations under the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) returned to the market spotlight today. Trading activity stalled as third-country suppliers struggle to obtain verified carbon emissions data—particularly for precursor raw materials like slabs and pig iron. Lacking primary documentation subjects shipments to punitive default benchmark values, sparking concerns over potential cancellations of Q1 import contracts by risk-averse buyers and traders. In pricing, the Northwest European HRC ex-works price held flat at 740 EUR/tonne EXW (831 USD/tonne), while the Italian domestic price edged up to 742 EUR/tonne EXW (833 USD/tonne). The combination of CBAM compliance challenges and tariff rate quota (TRQ) risks has severely constrained foreign steel inflows. Traders quoting Q1 and Q2 arrivals on DDP terms are offering prices above European domestic baselines at 780–800 EUR/tonne DDP. Specific offers today placed Japanese and Egyptian origins at 800 EUR/tonne DDP, Taiwanese material for March arrival at 790 EUR/tonne DDP, and Indian origin at 740–750 USD/tonne CFR. Turkish mills, despite nominal CFR price advantages, saw buying interest dampened by certification gaps and quota expiration risks. While mills remain cautious regarding broad Q1 volume allocations, selective forward pricing for 2027 delivery has already begun circulating among key accounts.

articles.title: "Annual limit of 350,000 units" China concedes hybrid vehicle exports under EU trade pressure; prospects of difficulties in securing alternative markets and local production - https://economy.ac/
articles.summary: "Annual limit of 350,000 units" China concedes hybrid vehicle exports under EU trade pressure; prospects of difficulties in securing alternative markets and local production  https://economy.ac/
articles.full_text:
Authored On
Modified
Discussion expected on China trade imbalance and industry damage response at EU summit
China maintains optimism despite hybrid vehicle export limits, but market skepticism persists
Expansion of local production by Chinese automakers in Europe faces burdens from production costs and local procurement regulations
There are forecasts that trade relations with China will emerge as a key agenda at the European Union (EU) summit. As trade imbalances deepen and conflicts between the two sides intensify, international attention is focused on the EU’s further response measures. Recently, China has made some concessions, such as agreeing to limit hybrid vehicle export volumes amid tense trade relations, but considering sluggish domestic demand and high entry barriers in alternative export markets, it appears difficult to reduce dependence on Europe in the short term.
EU struggles with trade deficit against China
According to Reuters on the 14th (local time), leaders of the 27 EU member states will hold a summit on the 15th-16th in Brussels, Belgium, to discuss damage to regional industries and trade response measures caused by a surge in imports of Chinese automobiles and manufactured goods. The EU's trade deficit in goods with China reached 360 billion euros (about US$419 billion) last year, and hit 200 billion euros (about US$233 billion) in the first half of this year. This deficit is occurring not only in automobiles, which have been the main source of conflict between the two sides, but also across manufactured goods including machinery, textiles, basic metals, and chemicals, raising growing concerns over weakening competitiveness and employment declines among regional companies.
Meanwhile, the policy direction of the EU Commission is shifting toward curbing the influx of Chinese products into the region. A representative example is the imposition of high tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). Since 2023, the Commission has conducted an anti-subsidy investigation on Chinese EVs for about a year, and in July 2024, it imposed provisional countervailing duties on Chinese EVs, judging that Chinese government subsidies distorted competition in the regional market. This was the first large-scale trade sanction against Chinese EVs. In October of the same year, the EU finalized, with member states' approval, additional tariffs up to 35.3% on Chinese EVs per company. These tariffs are added to the existing 10% tariff on vehicle imports and will be applied from October 30, 2024, for five years.
China limits hybrid vehicle import volumes
Amid this trade pressure, China recently made some concessions in negotiations with the EU, easing tensions. On the 12th, the Financial Times reported that the Commission is pushing a plan to limit annual import volumes of Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to 350,000 units. This agreement was reached during trade talks between Maroš Šefčovič, EU Commissioner for Trade, and Wang Wentao, China's Minister of Commerce, held in Beijing on the 8th-9th. The import limit will be implemented in December this year, setting an annual import cap at 350,000 units in 2027, with a 6% annual increase starting in 2028, through 2030.
The restriction applies to hybrid vehicles produced in China and exported to the EU, including vehicles manufactured by European automakers in their Chinese plants. However, vehicles of Chinese brands produced within the EU are exempt from the import quota. The EU estimates China's hybrid vehicle exports to the EU will reach about 800,000 units this year. This agreement aims to reduce the import volume of Chinese hybrid vehicles by more than half and lower their market share from the current approximately 6% to around 3% within the regional market.
"Exports will rather expand," China's confidence
On the other hand, China claims that this agreement creates opportunities for expanding exports of its enterprises. On the 12th, China's Ministry of Commerce released an official statement noting, "According to EU statistics, EU imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles were 107,000 units in 2024 and rose to 302,000 units in 2025," adding that "both sides agreed to expand imports based on 2025 volumes, ensuring export capacity and stable growth for Chinese companies." While the EU emphasizes the reduction effect based on expected imports this year, China highlights that the agreement allows increasing export volumes based on last year's actual import figure of 302,000 units.
Additionally, China’s Ministry of Commerce explained that the hybrid vehicle trade agreement is based on three principles: respect for facts, non-discrimination, and compliance with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules. Regarding the non-discrimination principle, it stated, "No measures should target only Chinese products or discriminate against Chinese companies," and added, "The import quota allocated to China will not be less than that allocated to any other import source country in the EU." On WTO compliance, it affirmed, "China retains all rights within the WTO framework, including initiating dispute settlement procedures and requesting trade remedies."
Table 1. Chinese Hybrid Vehicle Import Restriction Plan and Positions of Both Sides
| Category | Main content | 
|---|---|
| Import Restriction Plan | Set an annual import limit of 350,000 Chinese hybrid vehicles in 2027, with a 6% annual increase from 2028 through 2030 | 
| EU Position | Measure to reduce Chinese hybrid vehicle inflow by more than half compared to this year's expected imports and lower market share | 
| China's Position | Quota increases compared to last year's actual imports, making the agreement favorable for export expansion and stable growth | 
Difficulty in seeking alternative markets
However, skepticism remains about China's optimism in the market. There are concerns that China will face difficulties absorbing its existing European export volumes in other markets. First, the Chinese domestic automobile market is sluggish due to weakened consumer sentiment and reduced purchase subsidies. According to the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA), domestic passenger car sales in China were about 1.63 million units in September, a 28.1% year-on-year decline, marking the 12th consecutive month of decrease. Entry barriers in alternative export markets are also rising. The U.S. has imposed a 100% additional tariff on Chinese EVs and tightened regulations on Chinese connected car software and hardware, effectively blocking market entry. Mexico approved a bill last December imposing tariffs up to 50% on about 1,400 items, including automobiles imported from non-FTA countries such as China, while Brazil raised tariffs on imported electric and hybrid vehicles to 35% starting July.
Absorption capacity in existing major export markets is also limited. According to a March report by global accounting firm PwC, Chinese exports of passenger and light commercial vehicles to Russia fell sharply by 46% to about 556,000 units last year due to factors such as increased import taxes by the Russian government and weakening domestic vehicle demand. Southeast Asia, targeted by China as a new export hub, is relatively small in scale. PwC data shows that automobile sales in six major ASEAN countries—Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Philippines, Vietnam, and Singapore—totaled about 3.5 million units last year, with Chinese automakers holding only 11% market share.
Uncertain effectiveness of local production strategies
Under these circumstances, Chinese companies are striving to establish local production and supply chains in Europe to open new paths. On the 12th, Stella Li, BYD’s Senior Vice Chairman, told French economic broadcaster BFM Business in an interview that the company plans to secure two additional production hubs in Europe, with France being a strong candidate. BYD already built its first complete car production plant in Europe in Hungary, which is scheduled to begin full operation in the fourth quarter this year. Additionally, XPeng continues contract manufacturing through Magna International’s factory in Austria and is considering partnering with local manufacturers to build new factories or utilize existing ones. Changan Automobile also aims to expand its European production capacity to 180,000 units annually by 2028 and 350,000 units by 2030.
The problem is that expanding local production in Europe may not directly enhance the competitiveness of Chinese companies. They have to bear higher labor and energy costs in Europe compared to China and incur additional expenses while establishing new local parts supply chains. Furthermore, the direction of the EU’s industrial regulations remains unsettled. The Commission is currently promoting stricter local production and parts procurement requirements for EVs under the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), with ongoing debates among member states and industries over the scope of products recognized as European. Controversies persist over whether vehicles and parts produced in non-EU countries such as Turkey, the UK, and Morocco should be recognized as European. Chinese automakers risk additional burdens of adjusting their parts procurement and production systems depending on the regulations finalized in the future.
