articles.title: Exclusive: Musk approached Trump to slow down Starlink in Ukraine - The Telegraph
articles.summary: Exclusive: Musk approached Trump to slow down Starlink in Ukraine  The TelegraphStarlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy  The GuardianEXCLUSIVE: Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say  ReutersEurope's answer to Starlink: Who is building IRIS² and what is Germany's role  EuronewsTrump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network  BBC
articles.full_text:
The speed cap imposed on Ukraine limited drones using the Starshield system to around 160kmph, making it virtually impossible to intercept Russia’s barrages of jet-powered drones and missiles, which travel double the speed.
On Friday, Mr Zelensky said signals were being restored. He said: “Our defence ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities. Have they returned to the previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.”
It is not the first time Mr Musk has been accused of limiting the use of his Starlink platform to the detriment of Ukraine.
In 2023, he confirmed he had rebutted requests by Kyiv to use the system in drone attacks on Crimea, the peninsula illegally annexed by Russia, to avoid being complicit in a “major act of war”.
However, Mr Musk was lauded by Ukrainians earlier this year for his direct role in blocking illegal access to Starlink by Russian soldiers fighting in Ukraine.
‘We are watching you’
A source told The Telegraph that Poland had been leading warnings against Europe becoming too reliant on Mr Musk or his SpaceX company.
Writing on social media, Radek Sikorski, Poland’s foreign minister, warned the tech billionaire: “As your European customers, we are watching you.”
The EU is planning to have its Iris2, a Starlink replacement, operational by 2030. Mr Zelensky arrived in Brussels bruised and seeking more support from his European allies after his war of words with Mr Trump.
Diplomats said leaders had advised the Ukrainian president to tone down his criticism of his US counterpart amid fears Washington could further withdraw its support for Kyiv.
Mr Trump has been highly critical of Ukraine’s strikes on Russia’s oil refineries, blaming them for soaring energy prices before the midterm elections next month.

articles.title: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role - BBC
articles.summary: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role  BBCUkraine advances in occupied Donetsk as Trump hands Putin diesel deal  Al JazeeraOperation Vivaldi: success of Ukraine’s counteroffensive shows it has learned to manoeuvre on a drone-filled battlefield  The ConversationUkraine says it frees more territory in Donetsk region counteroffensive  ReutersUkraine reports more battlefield gains as Putin’s invasion loses momentum&n...
articles.full_text:
- Published
A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.
Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.
This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months.
The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.
While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September – and suffered few casualties in return.
The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".
Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.
He is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.
This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.
Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.
Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability.
Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.
Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.
Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.
The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.
An infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."
He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.
Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous".
"The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."
Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.
In Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation.
"As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed."
"I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".
That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present.
"The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained.
"This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvres… each of these actions is a building block towards victory."
All this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.
This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin.
Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause.
But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war.
The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front.
I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end."
Additional reporting by Kostas Kallergis and Anastasiia Levchenko

articles.title: The case of EUDR in Ethiopia: how to secure climate, trade and development goals, and overcome risks of market exclusion - ODI: Think change
articles.summary: The case of EUDR in Ethiopia: how to secure climate, trade and development goals, and overcome risks of market exclusion  ODI: Think change
articles.full_text:
Trade-related climate measures (TrCMs) are fundamentally reshaping global soft commodity markets. While the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) pursues the legitimate goal of reducing global forest degradation, its heavy reliance on punitive due diligence – enforced primarily through the loss of market access – poses severe, unintended development risks for smallholder-dominated economies.
In Ethiopia, the historical birthplace of coffee, over 90% of production relies on smallholders farming small plots under native forest canopies. While these traditional systems are inherently biodiversity-rich and ecologically sustainable, complying with rigid digital plot geolocation and complex proof-of-legality requirements presents an acute structural challenge.
Despite regulatory postponements moving large-operator enforcement to late 2026, progress across decentralized value chains remains uneven. Without coordinated interventions, compliance hurdles risk triggering widespread "green squeeze" market exclusion, threatening rural livelihoods, foreign exchange reserves, and national macroeconomic stability.
Priority policy recommendations
- Support first-mile aggregators: Partner directly with informal collectors and primary washing stations to transition toward transparent, traceable aggregation, while expanding seasonal liquidity for local cooperatives.
- Pursue tailored EU regulatory dialogue: Engage EU authorities to establish country-specific guidelines and pragmatic standards of proof for legality, prioritizing institutional adjustments over cost-prohibitive certification models.
- Introduce environmental incentives and carbon finance: Complement mandatory due diligence with positive incentive schemes – such as carbon credits, ecosystem service payments, and guaranteed sustainability premiums – that reward existing agroforestry shade canopy systems.

articles.title: Euro Advances vs CAD as Inflation Data Offsets French Jitters - TradingPedia
articles.summary: Euro Advances vs CAD as Inflation Data Offsets French Jitters  TradingPedia
articles.full_text:
Key Moments
- EUR/CAD traded around 1.5920 on Friday, extending gains for a second straight session.
- Stronger-than-expected Eurozone inflation data supported the Euro even as French political risk lingered.
- WTI crude oil prices remained on track for a weekly rise of over 5%, underpinning the commodity-linked Canadian Dollar.
Euro Climbs Despite French Political Concerns
EUR/CAD extended its upward move for a second consecutive day, with the pair trading near 1.5920 during Friday’s session. The advance in the Euro came even as ongoing political uncertainty in Europe – especially in France – threatened to cap further gains for the single currency.
Investor sentiment toward the Euro was supported by stronger-than-expected inflation readings across several Eurozone economies, which bolstered demand for euro-denominated assets. However, concerns around the political backdrop in France remained a potential headwind.
ECB Signals on Policy and French Debt
European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde underscored the need for France to tackle its national debt issues through fiscal consolidation. Her comments tempered market expectations that the ECB could step in to purchase French government bonds as a way to restrain rising yields.
Lagarde also indicated that energy-related price pressures had not yet broadened across the wider euro-area economy, a point that supported a cautious policy stance. At the same time, ECB policymaker Gediminas Šimkus kept a tightening bias on the table, stating that a rate increase this month remains possible if conditions warrant it. Market pricing continued to reflect expectations for an additional ECB rate hike in December.
Oil Strength Supports Canadian Dollar
On the Canadian side, the commodity-linked Canadian Dollar (CAD) stood to benefit from firm crude prices. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) oil remained on course for a weekly advance of more than 5%, as worries over supply disruptions in the Middle East intensified.
The US Central Command confirmed that a Singapore-flagged container vessel that sank in the Strait of Hormuz earlier in the week had been hit by an Iranian projectile. The incident heightened uncertainty over the restoration of physical oil flows and pushed tanker freight rates to record highs.
Data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA) showed that US crude oil inventories fell by 8.6 million barrels last week, the sharpest weekly drawdown since February. WTI was also positioned to outperform Brent for the week, supported by comparatively lower shipping costs for US crude that helped stimulate broader demand for American barrels.
Geopolitical Flashpoints Add to Market Tensions
Beyond the Strait of Hormuz, geopolitical risks extended to Yemen. According to a BBC report on Thursday, Yemen’s Houthis carried out a deadly missile and drone strike on the presidential palace in Aden, the interim capital of the Yemeni government. The attack killed five people – including two members of Prime Minister Shaya Al-Zindani’s security team – and injured 16 others.
Key Drivers of the Canadian Dollar
The Canadian Dollar (CAD) is influenced by a combination of monetary policy, commodity markets, and macroeconomic trends. The Bank of Canada (BoC) plays a central role through its interest rate decisions, which affect borrowing costs across the economy and shape capital flows into Canadian assets.
Oil prices are a particularly important driver, as petroleum is Canada’s largest export. Rising oil prices typically support the CAD by lifting export revenues and improving the trade balance, while declining prices tend to weigh on the currency.
| Key CAD Driver | Mechanism | Typical Impact on CAD | 
|---|---|---|
| Bank of Canada interest rates | Changes in policy rates influence overall interest rate levels and capital inflows | Higher rates are generally CAD-positive; lower rates are CAD-negative | 
| Oil price | Affects export revenues and trade balance, given oil is Canada’s largest export | Rising oil prices tend to support CAD; falling prices tend to pressure CAD | 
| Inflation | Higher inflation can lead to expectations of tighter BoC policy | Higher inflation is often CAD-positive via higher expected interest rates | 
| Macroeconomic data | Indicators such as GDP, PMIs, employment, and sentiment gauge economic health | Stronger data generally boosts CAD; weaker data usually weighs on CAD | 
| Trade balance | Difference between export and import values reflects external demand | A stronger trade balance is typically supportive of CAD | 
| Market risk sentiment | Global appetite for risk assets versus safe-havens | Risk-on sentiment tends to benefit CAD; risk-off sentiment can hurt CAD |

articles.title: ICE, EV, FCEV and now... VEEF? Toyota wants a new category for cars running on renewable fuel - Autocar
articles.summary: ICE, EV, FCEV and now... VEEF? Toyota wants a new category for cars running on renewable fuel  AutocarJapan calls for trusted partner status to support Europe’s reindustrialisation and strengthen their economic partnership  The Parliament MagazineToyota urges EU to include UK and Turkey in automotive legislation  CompleteCar.ieToyota Is Scared Of The “Made With Europe” Initiative  AUTOJOSHToyota calls for UK’s 2030 ZEV target to be cut to 50%  AM...
articles.full_text:
Toyota has proposed a new 'VEEF' category for cars which run on renewable fuels and said such models should be treated in the same way as electric cars in Europe.
Sanding for 'Vehicles running Exclusively on Eligible Fuels', VEEF would accord renewable fuel-powered ICE cars the same incentives as battery-electric alternatives, in recognition that they can achieve a similar recution in CO2 on a well-to-wheel basis.
Toyota said renewable fuels should be officially recognised as a zero-emission solution by the EU, and that regulatory support for the new category would enable Europe to dramatically cut emissions from the 300 million ICE vehicles already on the regions' roads today, accelerating decarbonisation efforts in parallel with wider adoption of electric alternatives.
Toyota has long been a vocal advocate of renewable fuel, using them in various motorsport applications and partnering a number of other automotive firms to evaluate it for real-world use.
Over the past six months, it has collaborated with BMW, Bosch and energy company Repsol on a trial in Spain, where some 20 production-spec cars were operated using 100% renewable fuel over six months to prove the viability of the technology.
The fuel, made from residual biomass, is said to have no impact on a car's performance and requires no modifications to its mechanicals.
Toyota said the trial proved that such fuels work in real-world situations and that they can be supplied using existing fuelling infrastructure - whereas BEVs and hydrogen FCEVs need their own networks of expensive bespoke chargers and pumps.
Bosch's contribution to the trial was in ensuring the traceability of the fuel used – crucial to determining its environmental credentials – and ensuring that any cars involved only used the renewable fuel.
Any ICE car designated as a VEEF under the proposals would have to be blocked from running on conventional petrol - likely using technology to determine the type of fuel nozzle used at a fill-up.
Toyota acknowledged that production of renewable fuels is currently far too low to power vehicles on any meaningful scale but said the creation of a new regulatory framework for VEEFs would lay the foundations for the industry to scale up.
The specific fuel posited by Toyota as an alternative to batteries or hydrogen is second-generation biofuel, made using waste residue from organic products - much cheaper to produce than the fully synthetic e-fuel being produced by Porsche, for example.
Toyota estimates that at current levels, there's enough biomass in Europe to sustain the region's ICE vehicle fleet through to 2040.
"If we are serious about reducing carbon emissions as much and as fast as possible, renewable fuels have a big role to play," said Toyota Europe's chief technical office, Shinichi Yasui.
R&D boss Thiebault Paquet concurred and said that compared with BEVs and FCEVs, they "do not require much investment on the vehicle side, because they're 'drop-in' fuels - they can be used and we don't have to change anything.
"It's not like 100% ethanol where you have to have a different injector, the valve seats need to be protected etc."

articles.title: Berliner Zeitung: Germany is being sacrificed for the sake of multiculturalism, Ukraine and the USA - EADaily
articles.summary: Berliner Zeitung: Germany is being sacrificed for the sake of multiculturalism, Ukraine and the USA  EADaily
articles.full_text:
Germany is bleeding — both financially and because of its ideological course. This is because politicians pursue goals that do not meet the interests of the country, publicist and entrepreneur Thomas Fasbender, who has lived in Moscow for more than 20 years, writes in the Berliner Zeitung.
Military operation on Ukraine, which has been going on for almost five years, is costing Russia very dearly. This year, 14.9 trillion rubles are spent on military operations and other defense expenditures of the country, which in terms of about 158 billion euros. This figure is calculated on the basis of a fairly broad approach of peace researchers from the Swedish Institute SIPRI and corresponds to 34% of the country's budget.
And how are things in Germany? We have 80 years of peace behind us; the Cold War, which ended without bloodshed 36 years ago, brought us "peace dividends"; only a few temporary foreign missions affected the budget. If only! According to the definition close to the SIPRI approach, the planned military expenditures of the Federal Republic of Germany next year will amount to 151.3 billion euros, which is about 26% of the federal budget for 2027.
This amount includes more than 11 billion euros of military assistance to Ukraine; SIPRI also takes into account military assistance to other countries. This explains the difference compared to the widespread figure of 140 billion euros (regular budget plus special fund).
Note: the military spending of a huge Russia, whose area is 50 times the area of Germany, whose external border is five times longer, whose population is 70% larger and which has been fighting for almost five years, in 2026 will be only 7 billion euros higher than Germany's spending in the coming year. If it doesn't make you think, then nothing will help.
Amazing proportionality
Attention is attracted not only by data comparison, but also by growth dynamics. In the last year before the military operation, Russia's military expenditures amounted to 55.7 billion euros at the exchange rate of that time. They jumped to 99.1 billion euros in 2022, peaked at 168 billion in 2025, and declined slightly in 2026.
Germany's military spending, with some delay, is showing an amazing dynamic: from 47.8 billion euros in 2021 to just over 100 billion euros in 2025 and up to 151 billion planned for next year (all figures are given in accordance with the SIPRI classification).
In fact and Russia and Germany have tripled their military spending in five years, although only one of these two countries is involved in a bloody conflict. Military assistance to Ukraine cannot explain the dynamics of German military spending. Last year it amounted to 8.5 billion euros, and earlier it was significantly less.
Germany's military expenditures of 151 billion euros planned for 2027 are formed from three sources: the departmental budget of the 14th Federal Ministry of Defense provides for 109.7 billion euros, the special fund of the Bundeswehr is 29.9 billion euros. In addition, the departmental budget 60 provides for 11.6 billion euros for "strengthening States that have been attacked in violation of international law in the areas of security, defense and stabilization," that is, for Ukraine.
To the detriment of future generations
76% of this amount — including spending on intelligence services, civil protection and protection of the population, as well as on IT security - is financed by loans, which are covered by new borrowings in the amount of 115.4 billion euros. The savings target for civil departments is "only" four billion euros.
Thus, the federal government relies on the decision taken at the beginning of 2025 to abolish the "debt limit" for security-related expenditure items. The increase in military spending planned by politicians will not come at the expense of reducing spending on social assistance, basic income or development assistance — it will come at the expense of future generations, including those who have not yet been born. In the face of a shrinking population, it is easy to understand what this means.
The key concept remains political will. The political center has put forward as an alternative premise that in the coming years Russia will strike at the North Atlantic Alliance. Another prerequisite, which is identical in its consequences to the first and also does not allow for alternatives, was the need to satisfy the US requirement for military spending in the amount of at least 5% of GDP. Together, these two factors form an economic stimulus program — small for some German companies, but large-scale for many American ones.
Anyone who asks questions or even expresses disagreement is pushed to the political periphery, marginalized and stigmatized. This also explains why parties such as the Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the Sarah Wagenknecht Union (SSV) are attractive to voters who ask these questions and express disagreement. Guided by common sense, they refuse to accept the idea that in the coming decades hordes of Russians will cross the Oder and move west.
Our politicians, who are not guided by common sense, react with a loud "Stop!". In the XXI century, as we are taught, we are talking about cyber wars, hybrid wars, drone wars, sabotage wars and information wars. What does the wise German Michael answer (an analogue of the Russian hero of Ivanushka's fairy tales-the fool. — Approx. EADaily)? There is no need to allocate 151 billion euros a year for defense in such conditions.
No, these billions do not serve to protect Germany from sabotage and disinformation. They serve the large Western and global project "free world". Only in this context does the financial scale make sense. Where is the "free world" most protected? In the Hindu Kush — well, not quite now. It used to be like that. In the Taiwan and Malacca Straits, in the Persian Gulf and on The Red Sea. In the Arctic and in the western Pacific, in Europe from Finland to the Black Sea.
The "liberal Empire" will not give up its dominance, for example, in the western Pacific, without a fight. Germany is expected to support it. The report of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, adopted in 2025, states: "If China uses force against Taiwan, the United States will probably be forced to simultaneously respond to threats from Beijing and Moscow. European NATO allies will have to take on more responsibility for containing Russia."
The word "will have to" describes a chain reaction that will lead to a war for hegemony in the 21st century. Germany's support for the hegemon — the United States — has already been incorporated into the calculations. This goal is served by 151 billion in the coming year, as well as 5%. But not the defense of the motherland.
Protection of freedom
Thus, military expenditures in the state budget are simultaneously reoriented in ideological terms: "free world" instead of "protecting Germany." The question of whether this is permissible from the point of view of constitutional law remains open. Anyway, the state task of overcoming such practical limitations as defense is being transformed into an ideological project.
We find a similar example of ideological reassessment in a completely different sphere. Germany provides non-citizens, including those who will not bring any benefit to the country in the foreseeable future, with generous opportunities for entry and stay. The instruments of this policy are, for example, the right to asylum, relocation of family members, protection status for refugees, and the like.
This generosity and the costs associated with it cause a heated discussion. In addition, these costs, as a rule, are almost impossible to accurately determine, including because of statistical - politically motivated? — inaccuracies. What expenses do we know about?
Expenses that cannot be attributed to a specific category
Let's start with social expenses for persons who do not have German citizenship (with the exception of persons with dual citizenship). There is no official data on this issue. Only in the case of civil benefits and payments to asylum seekers, expenses can be calculated relatively reliably. In the case of civil benefits, we are talking about an amount of about 22 billion euros, and in the case of payments to asylum seekers — a little less than 6.2 billion.
This also includes social assistance and accommodation assistance, basic care for the elderly and people with disabilities, as well as expensive care assistance. All these costs are not distributed depending on citizenship. The same applies to housing benefit (in 2025 — a total of 4.9 billion euros). Administrative expenses of employment centers — 6.8 billion euros last year — are also not distributed depending on the nationality of the persons who are being assisted.
As for the basic provision of citizens of other countries in old age, in The media still cites an estimated amount of 2.2 billion euros. There are also data on child benefits. Last year, the amount of child benefits paid by the Family Welfare Fund amounted to 55.7 billion euros for 17.6 million children. Of these, 23% or 12.7 billion euros were paid to persons who did not have a German passport.
The total amount, including social assistance and housing allowance, cannot be determined either from official publications or from authoritative journalistic materials, as well as data on financial assistance from the state or total expenditures on education, public administration, infrastructure, security or health care in connection with the stay of persons who are not German citizens.
What we know: at the end of last year, this group of people numbered 12.4 million people, or 14.9% of the total population. What are the costs associated with this? What income compensates them? The fragmentary budget items mentioned here amount to well over 40 billion euros per year. Is this the whole iceberg or just its tip?

articles.title: Euro Currency Value Plummets Against Dollar and Pound - GreekReporter.com
articles.summary: Euro Currency Value Plummets Against Dollar and Pound  GreekReporter.com
articles.full_text:
The sharp currency slide completely wipes out the euro’s entire summer value recovery, following a toxic sell-off that exploding energy costs, a severe French sovereign bond crisis, and a roaring American dollar triggered. This market retreat accelerates despite the European Central Bank (ECB) delivering two successive interest rate hikes this year.
Under standard macroeconomic conditions, tightening monetary policy provides a strong shield for a fiat currency. However, escalating geopolitical headwinds and fiscal instability are currently overpowering the central bank’s defensive interventions.
Rising U.S. inflation powers a dollar super-cycle
The euro plunged to a multi-month low of $1.111 on Wednesday before staging a minor correction to $1.121 during early trading on Thursday.
The shared currency has depreciated by over 5 percent since late August. This decline reflects an aggressive global surge in the greenback. The U.S. Dollar Index hit an 18-month high after American inflation unexpectedly jumped to 3.7 percent in September.
This hotter-than-forecast reading prompted global investors to double their bets on an upcoming Federal Reserve interest rate hike on October 28. The Fed’s benchmark interest rate currently hovers between 3.75% and 4.0%, leaving the ECB’s conservative 2.5% rate far behind.
The ECB increased its deposit rate by a quarter-point to 2.5% on September 10 to combat an aggressive energy shock. The military conflict in Iran has heavily exposed Eurozone economies, which import the vast majority of their crude oil.
Consequently, Eurozone inflation accelerated to a three-year high of 3.8 percent. Despite this pressure, financial markets expect the ECB to pause its tightening cycle at its upcoming October 29 meeting. Central bankers remain deeply divided on the next step. Belgian Central Bank Governor Pierre Wunsch expects further hikes, while Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel urges patience until wage growth stabilizes. Meanwhile, robust economic data out of the United Kingdom is boosting bets for an immediate Bank of England rate hike, supercharging the British pound.
The French fiscal crisis rattles bond markets
Deep-seated panic over France’s crumbling public finances is severely compounding the euro’s downward spiral.
The spread between French and German 10-year government bonds recently blasted past 150 basis points. This critical indicator of financial market anxiety marks the highest risk premium since the Eurozone debt crisis of 2011.
According to data from the national statistics agency INSEE, France’s total public debt hit a record 119% of national GDP. This staggering shortfall equates to roughly €3.59 trillion (~$4.02 trillion). This mountain of sovereign debt doubles the European Union’s official fiscal stability ceiling of 60%.
The French government’s draft 2027 budget aims to slash the deficit to 5.0% through €54 billion (~$60.5 billion) in austerity savings. However, the spending plan faces a brutal path through a fractured parliament. Violent student protests are currently paralyzing Paris as demonstrators demand extra public funding for the national education system.
ECB President Christine Lagarde swiftly crushed any hopes of an emergency central bank intervention to rescue French bonds. Speaking from the IMF-World Bank summit in Bangkok, Lagarde stated that France must solve its own structural problems through domestic fiscal policy. Adding to the regional market chaos, Spain is also heading to a snap general election on November 29, fueling further political instability across the Eurozone.

articles.title: Russia's war reaches Bulgaria's shores, putting Radev's Moscow-friendly stance to the test - The Kyiv Independent
articles.summary: Russia's war reaches Bulgaria's shores, putting Radev's Moscow-friendly stance to the test  The Kyiv IndependentPutin brings war into Nato’s waters  The TelegraphDrone strikes in the Black Sea raise fears of Russian escalation to test NATO’s response  AP NewsBulgarian PM summons Russian ambassador after ship sinks in Black Sea drone attack  BBCBulgaria seeks NATO anti-drone systems, says defence minister  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev in Sofia, Bulgaria, on Oct. 6, 2026. (Nikolay Doychinov / AFP via Getty Images)
The balancing act of Bulgaria's Moscow-friendly leader stands on shaky ground.
Since taking office in May, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has taken a harsh line on Ukraine while adopting steps his critics say are accommodating to Moscow.
Radev's course has now come under scrutiny as Bulgaria, a southeastern NATO member state, feels first-hand the spillover of Russia's war against Ukraine.
Four merchant vessels were hit by drones near Bulgaria's Black Sea coast in October. Two of the vessels sank and several sailors are reported dead or missing.
Under fire from opposition, Radev, a former military officer and Bulgaria's ex-president, only cautiously hints at Moscow's complicity — stopping short of a direct accusation.
"Radev’s balancing act between the West and Moscow would eventually catch up with him."
With Russian drone incursions and Moscow-backed hybrid operations on NATO territory growing ever more brazen and frequent, Bulgaria has no guarantee that the strikes in its waters will come to an end.
Radev's room to maneuver between Bulgaria's NATO membership and a thaw in ties with Moscow is shrinking, observers say.
"I have argued for some time that Radev's balancing act between the West and Moscow would eventually catch up with him," Dimitar Keranov, an analyst at the German Marshall Fund's European Resilience program, told the Kyiv Independent.
"It now has."
Russia's war reaches Bulgarian waters
Two Turkish-managed ships were hit by naval and aerial drones about 70 nautical miles (130 kilometers) east of the Bulgarian town of Byala on Oct. 6, inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
The Alfa Watan, flying a Togo flag, sank, with 10 crew members — including nine Syrian nationals — presumed dead.
Two more vessels were hit by drones near the Bulgarian Black Sea coast on Oct. 13, including the Ukrainian-owned, Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, hit east of Byala. Its crew, including seven Ukrainians, was rescued.
The second ship, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity, was hit by drones east of the Bulgarian village of Krapets and sank, with 11 sailors reported missing.
The attacks came amid escalating hostilities in the Black Sea, with Moscow attempting to impose a blockade on Ukrainian trade by attacking ports and merchant ships.
Several commercial ships were also hit in and around Romanian waters over the past weeks.
While Ukraine has blamed Russia, Radev was initially hesitant to name the origin of the drones, saying only "they were clearly either Russian or Ukrainian."
Both Russian and Ukrainian drone incursions have been recorded along NATO's eastern flank over the past months, with the latter being a result of Russian jamming diverting Ukrainian unmanned vehicles.
But Radev's hesitation has provided an opening to the country's opposition.
On Oct. 6, lawmakers from the GERB–SDS, a center-right opposition coalition, blasted Radev for failing to properly identify the culprit.
The coalition's junior partner, the SDS (Union of Democratic Forces), even called the attack "an act of aggression by the Russian Federation in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone."
Finally, after the second attack, Radev acknowledged that Russia was the one to benefit from the attacks, and Sofia summoned the Russian envoy.
Nevertheless, Radev has not formally accused Moscow, citing a lack of decisive evidence.
Keranov summarizes this position as a "convenient deflection."
"Formal attribution takes time, but once a government concludes that the logic points to Moscow, it does not need a final forensic report to act on that assessment."
But Ruslan Stefanov, a program director and chief economist at the Center for the Study of Democracy, a Sofia-based European public policy institute, says waiting for proof is reasonable.
On the other hand, "continued failure to identify Russia as the main driver of instability and unsafe navigation in the Black Sea does not reflect operational reality and is widely seen as part of a broader pattern of unnecessary and harmful caution toward Moscow," he said.
"Moscow is testing Bulgaria because it sees it as the weak link on NATO’s southern flank."
The maritime attacks are not the only security-related incidents hitting Bulgaria in recent weeks and months.
Earlier in October, two masked men were said to have set fire to 11 out of 17 Starlink antennas at a facility near Sofia.
Ivaylo Mirchev, one of the leaders of the opposition Democratic Bulgaria (DB), hinted at connections to "Russian-style sabotage."
Yet Radev has remained tight-lipped about who was behind the arson, even though Poland blamed Moscow for a similar attack against a Starlink station on Polish territory in September.
Ukraine widely uses Starlink network services, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, for both civilian purposes and to support military operations.
And in August and September, explosions hit two arms facilities of the EMCO company, which supplies weapons to Ukraine.
The company called the September incident sabotage, while the Bulgarian Interior Ministry did not rule out either foreign interference or company neglect.
NATO's 'weak link'
As Bulgaria's president, Radev was ranked among the most Ukraine-skeptical voices in the EU — often compared to former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
Since assuming the premier office, he has pulled Bulgaria out of the U.K.- and French-led Coalition of the Willing and halted arms supplies to Ukraine from Bulgarian army stocks.
He has also lambasted Western military aid for Kyiv, claiming it prolongs the war, and instead urged a diplomatic resolution.
At the EU level, Radev's government has blocked the inclusion of Moscow Patriarch Kirill in the 21st sanctions package and pushed to water down the EU's language on Ukraine's accession.
In light of these steps, drone strikes off the Bulgarian coast put Radev in an "uncomfortable position," Stefanov said.
"He built his campaign on the claim that there can be no military victory over Russia and that Bulgaria's interest lies in de-escalation," the expert noted.
"Those choices now raise the obvious question of why Bulgaria has not been spared."
Keranov believes that "Moscow is testing Bulgaria because it sees it as the weak link on NATO's southern flank."
Most NATO members along the alliance's frontier — from Romania to the Baltics — have already toughened their response to Russian provocations, with allied jets repeatedly downing invading drones.
Their leadership is also less reluctant to openly blame Moscow for the incursions.
While Radev's hesitation has provided ammunition to his domestic opponents, the prime minister's political position remains strong, Keranov said, adding that his popularity at home is not the real question.
"It is whether Bulgaria acts like a strong NATO member or keeps signaling indecision."

articles.title: EU’s support to Ukraine matters more than ever, von der Leyen says, as US relationship sours – as it happened - The Guardian
articles.summary: EU’s support to Ukraine matters more than ever, von der Leyen says, as US relationship sours – as it happened  The GuardianZelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace'  BBCZelensky praises ‘real leaders’ in Europe as his relationship with Trump deteriorates  CNNEU eyes more financial support for Ukraine after US pivot  Financial TimesEU rallies in support of Ukraine amid Trump standoff  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
She says the EU’s support “matters more than ever.”
She says the bloc “is doing a long, but the reality is simple: as long as this war continues, Ukraine’s financing needs will keep growing.”
“Right now, the European Union and its member states account for 80% of external aid to Ukraine, and we will continue to lead. But we urgently need also other partners to step in.”
She ends:
“As throughout these five years of war, no one wants more peace than the people of Ukraine, and it is our duty to support them, to be in the position to find a just and sustainable peace for Ukraine.”
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.
Earlier,
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy has asked the leaders for another €70bn next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia as he joined a key EU summit in Brussels (10:10, 13:44, 15:13, 15:26, 16:00).
EU’s Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa confirmed the bloc will look at the request (19:01, 19:14, 19:20), as they said the EU’s support to Ukraine “matters more than ever” given growing pressures from Russia.
During a press conference in Brussels, Zelenskyy responded to US president Donald Trump’s criticism of his actions (13:51, 13:56, 14:04), and confirmed that Starlink satellite systems were back up, but with speeds not completely restored to previous levels (13:42).
Zelenskyy smiled but offered no response to a suggestion he was being used as a “scapegoat” for Donald Trump’s domestic problems ahead of next month’s midterm elections (14:06).
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said there was a “broad consensus” on the EU’s need to keep supporting Ukraine throughout this coming winter, acknowledging Kyiv’s request for further financial assistance (16:45), and appearing to back retaliatory strikes against Russian communication and energy supply systems (16:49, 16:54).
Several other EU leaders offered their backing for Ukraine, (10:10, 10:21, 10:25, 10:36, 11:09, 11:23), with top EU figures saying the bloc would not lift any sanctions on Russia unless it stops the war (10:10), and criticising Trump’s diesel deal with Russia (10:10, 19:32).
Zelenskyy declined to say if Ukraine will be targeting Russian refineries (13:47).
EU’s Costa insisted the new EU budget needed to be agreed by the end of the year, despite calls to delay its adoption considering a number of big elections in the EU (19:27).
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, insisted the bloc needed a bigger budget with “flexibilities” to respond to various crises (19:12).
Germany’s Merz conceded there were still “significant differences” between EU capitals on the budget, with talks expected to continue until the end of the year (16:43, 16:54, 16:59).
Separately,
Pope Leo spoke with the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, this afternoon, expressing his grave concern for the humanitarian situation in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky (17:36).
The Kremlin said Putin expressed his support for Leo’s ideas, but blamed Ukraine for the situation in the city (18:22).
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
Speaking at the same time, France’s Emmanuel Macron told reporters that he did not consider a diesel deal struck by Trump with Russia as useful.
“This decision is not good for anyone. It sends a negative signal. It a an element of division and doubt,” Macron said after an EU summit in Brussels, Reuters reported.
After some concluding comments on the bloc’s response to the growing sales of Chinese electric cars in Europe, von der Leyen and Costa wrap up their press conference.
Costa gets asked if he is more confident that a deal can be found by the end of the year.
And there is also a question about Marine Le Pen’s suggestions that the budget should not be decided this early given so many key elections in Europe next year that are likely to reshape the political landscape of the continent.
Costa repeats Merz’s point from earlier that it usually takes about a year to implement a budget (16:59), and anything that would threaten to delay its entry into force from January 2028 puts it a risk altogether.
“This has nothing [to do] with elections,” he says, and adds if that was a consideration, there would never be a good moment as there are always elections somewhere.
“But unfortunately, the life is not only elections. We are talking about our farmers, our companies, our students, our researchers, our universities – and they are waiting for new European funds.”
On migration, von der Leyen says all leaders recognise “enormous progress” made on this issue in recent years, but more needs to be done.
He says the number of illegal crossings has gone down by over 56% in the last two years, and down by 34% in the first nine months of this year.
Asylum applications are also falling, she says.
“These trends need to continue to remain successful.”
She says there is a “new phenomenon” of state and non-state actors trying to “engineer sudden mass movements of people … to overwhelm the authorities.”
It will come as news to the likes of Poland and Lithuania that it’s anything new given the pressure from Belarus for years.
She says the EU’s support “matters more than ever.”
She says the bloc “is doing a long, but the reality is simple: as long as this war continues, Ukraine’s financing needs will keep growing.”
“Right now, the European Union and its member states account for 80% of external aid to Ukraine, and we will continue to lead. But we urgently need also other partners to step in.”
She ends:
“As throughout these five years of war, no one wants more peace than the people of Ukraine, and it is our duty to support them, to be in the position to find a just and sustainable peace for Ukraine.”
Von der Leyen also mounts a defence of the commission’s proposal on the next EU budget, effectively saying that as leaders keep coming to the EU asking it to fix things, it’s understandable that it’ll need more resources.
“If there’s one lesson we have painfully learned over the last seven years, that is the lesson that we are in a very fast changing and volatile world and that there will be more crises. We just don’t know what is going to be happening. … I could only act in these crisis because of the flexibilities in the budget … andin each crisis, everybody was calling for Europe to step in.”
He says the new proposals have “even less flexibilities,” and so the commission is not happy with them.
“The question before us is not which priorities we should abandon, but how to finance these priorities.”
She points out to high energy price increases since the start of Trump’s war against Iran.
“This is the reality we have to deal with today, and we discussed this intensively with the member states. Because of the fact that the member states have very different energy mixes, we know there is no silver bullet as a solution.”
She says the G7-agreed release of oil and diesel, the EU’s extension of temporary state aid framework, and some other technical changes should provide some relief.
“For the mid term, it is important that as long as Europe depends on imported oil and gas and our prosperity remains exposed to the events beyond our control, it is important for us to stay the course of the transition; that is a transition towards affordable, clean and homegrown energy sources, … nuclear and renewables.”
She talks about the need to “modernise and improve our grid network” in Europe.
She also briefly discusses proposed changes to the ETS system and the EU’s trade with China, saying there was a “remarkable unity” on the latter point to reduce the “unsustainable” bilateral trade deficit.
Finally, on migration, Costa says the system is “working but … must still be improved.”
“Migration remains a very political issue where there are different political visions which are known to all of you. The European Council will continue to work on this issue,” he says.
'Ukraine remains a central priority for Europe,' EU's Costa says
On the next EU budget, Costa says the negotiations will need to conclude by the end of the year, and there was some progress made.
But with lots of diplospeak, he admits that there are still some differences between different countries, and so he needs to “accelerate” the work on this issue.
On Ukraine, he says “Ukraine remains a central priority for Europe.”
“Our resolve to stand by Ukraine and its people is as strong as ever. At the same time, every genuine step towards peace matters and we support all genuine efforts towards it. Unfortunately, Russia’s action point the other way.”
He calls for “more pressure on the aggression, not less,” and for more financial support for Ukraine, with a request to the commission to propose new funding.
He warns:
“Supporting Ukraine has never been more relevant as Moscow is intensifying its hybrid campaigns across Europe. We see acts of sabotage and repeated violations of member states airspace in territorial waters.”
He talks about good discussions on cutting red tape and competitiveness of the bloc, and confirms what Merz said earlier about a special meeting on this issue in February next year (16:43).
On energy, he says that “current volatility on energy prices [is] putting intense pressure on households and businesses.”
“This crisis is triggered by events far beyond our borders, but we are also paying the price of our dependency on fossil fuels and the lack of a single market for energy. Given the urgency of the situation, there cannot be business as usual.”
He says there will be a united EU response to this issue.
He also talks about discussions on trade policy, with “total unity among the member states” on supporting the bloc’s efforts to diversify trade routes. Again, he references Merz’s proposals for a new trade instrument.

articles.title: EUDR Compliance Readiness in 2026 – Key Lessons for Forest Products Companies - ResourceWise
articles.summary: EUDR Compliance Readiness in 2026 – Key Lessons for Forest Products Companies  ResourceWise
articles.full_text:
With the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) nearing implementation, forest products companies must ask whether their compliance processes can provide the evidence needed to demonstrate due diligence.
In 2026, ResourceWise hosted a four-part EUDR Readiness Briefing Series to help industry professionals track regulatory developments, address operational challenges, and assess supply chain traceability.
A key takeaway: readiness requires more than collecting supplier information. Companies must verify material origins, link them to products and shipments, and maintain defensible documentation.
Companies with existing EUDR solutions or internal processes should identify gaps before they affect compliance reporting or EU market access.
A recurring theme was the distinction between established responsible-sourcing practices and the specific evidence EUDR requires.
Forest products companies have long used certification, chain-of-custody systems, legality assessments, and supplier documentation to support sustainable sourcing. These programs offer a valuable foundation but do not, on their own, prove EUDR compliance. Companies must demonstrate that covered products meet the regulation’s deforestation-free and legality requirements, supported by due diligence information.
This means evaluating whether existing programs can provide geolocation evidence, risk assessments, and links between production areas and products sold in the EU. Companies may not need to rebuild their sustainability programs, but must ensure they provide EUDR’s specific, verifiable evidence.
Geolocation was a major operational challenge discussed in the webinars. Collecting coordinates is a starting point, but does not establish the full production area or verify accuracy.
Under EUDR, companies must provide geolocation for relevant production plots. Depending on plot size and type, this may require polygons rather than a single point. For forest-product companies with extensive supplier networks, obtaining accurate polygons can create significant administrative work—especially when suppliers have varying technical capabilities or information must be gathered across many harvest sites.
Webinar discussions emphasized moving beyond data collection to processes that:
Having geolocation data is not the same as reliably verifying it. For companies assessing EUDR readiness, existing systems may collect coordinates but lack efficient ways to validate them or use them in downstream reporting.
Unlike supply chains with products traceable to a single production site, forest products pass through multiple stages before reaching their destination. Wood may be harvested, transported to a sawmill, turned into chips or residuals, sent to a pulp mill, and made into paper or packaging. Materials from different origins may be mixed during storage, processing, and manufacturing, making it difficult to link products or shipments to their source areas.
ResourceWise experts emphasized that effective traceability must reflect how wood and fiber move through the supply chain, linking harvest origins, supplier transactions, manufacturing facilities, and finished-product shipments. Sawmill and harvest residuals are especially important: they make up a substantial share of many supply chains, but movement through intermediaries can complicate origin reporting.
EUDR traceability must reflect real production and sourcing practices, not assume a simple path from raw materials to finished products. Companies with existing compliance systems should ask: Can they track mixed fiber, residuals, and multiple sourcing locations without significant manual work?
EUDR readiness depends on supplier participation across the forest products value chain. Even companies with established compliance systems may struggle if suppliers cannot provide consistent, usable information.
ResourceWise's implementation experience shows supplier data availability improving as companies prepare and origin requests become more common. But collecting data is only part of the process: companies also need reliable ways to transmit, validate, organize, and update records.
In the third briefing, Barry Parrish, ResourceWise’s Director of Sustainability, highlighted the value of supplier communication, training, and structured project management. Based on ResourceWise’s experience, communicating requirements, training suppliers to submit data, and collecting geolocation information can take about two months.
Companies should assess not just whether they have the required data, but how efficiently they can obtain missing information and maintain complete records. Those managing extensive supplier networks should ask:
These operational factors determine whether compliance remains manageable as reporting volumes grow.
A final theme was the need to move beyond collecting compliance data and integrate it into daily operations. Accurate harvest-area data, risk assessments, and supplier records must support EUDR-regulated products and shipments by linking origin details to production and shipment records and due diligence documents.
The webinars also discussed the EU's TRACES-based EUDR Information System for submitting due diligence statements. Companies must make these reporting processes operational before commercial shipments require them, including for materials produced before the regulation applies but placed on the EU market afterward. Compliance should therefore inform inventory and shipment planning, not just production.
Overall, EUDR readiness must cover the entire workflow, from supplier data collection to final compliance documentation.
The four-part series reinforced an important distinction between having an EUDR compliance strategy from having a process that reliably supports implementation.
Companies with compliance systems should assess how they perform across real supply chains: Can geolocation be verified? Do origins remain traceable through processing and mixing? Can evidence be linked to shipments and reporting requirements?
They should also evaluate maintenance demands. Workflows reliant on manual data collection, spreadsheets, or repeated supplier requests may be hard to scale.
Rather than simply asking whether a solution exists, forest products companies should ask whether it produces accurate, defensible information efficiently and consistently.
ResourceWise developed Forest Trackt to address the specific traceability and geolocation challenges found throughout forest products supply chains.
The platform helps companies collect supplier information, generate harvest-area polygons through geospatial change detection, connect origin data to downstream products and shipments, and prepare compliance-ready reporting.
These capabilities are particularly relevant for companies managing extensive supplier networks, sawmill residuals, and complex fiber flows.
For organizations reviewing existing EUDR processes, Forest Trackt offers an opportunity to evaluate where greater automation, traceability, and data verification could strengthen readiness.

articles.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy is asking Europe for an additional €70 billion to support Ukraine in its war with Russia  Informat.ro
articles.full_text:
Context: The EU approved a loan for Ukraine, but funding for 2027 remains a problem
Before the request from Brussels, Ukrainian leaders indicated that financial and military support for the following year was only partially covered, while negotiations on funding for 2027 had reached an impasse. In this context, Volodymyr Zelenskyy called for increased pressure on Russia and strengthened support for defense during meetings with European and NATO leaders.
At the same time, Ukraine presented assessments of the costs of the war and the funding shortfall for the following year, while the authorities in Kyiv submitted requests for additional funds to the European Union. In parallel, the Ukrainian government adopted the 2027 budget, with record allocations for defense and security, noting the need for external financing.
On the European side, the Commission announced installments from the support loan for Ukraine, including for the purchase of military equipment. However, discussions remained focused on covering the shortfall for 2027 and on how the installments could be used for Kyiv’s defense needs.

articles.title: UK Government Issues Final Compliance Guidance Ahead of 2027 Carbon Tax Rollout - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: UK Government Issues Final Compliance Guidance Ahead of 2027 Carbon Tax Rollout  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) has published comprehensive technical guidance detailing how overseas manufacturers, UK importers, and independent verifiers must monitor and report emissions ahead of the United Kingdom’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) launch on January 1, 2027.
The extensive regulatory framework, released on October 16, 2026, marks the final administrative push to prepare supply chains for a new tax regime designed to equalise the carbon costs borne by domestic and international producers.
The UK CBAM will place a carbon price on imports of highly emissions-intensive goods—specifically iron, steel, aluminium, fertiliser, hydrogen, and cement. The policy aims to ensure that overseas products face a financial carbon burden comparable to goods manufactured domestically under the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS).
Preparing for the 2027 Deadline
The primary objective is to prevent "carbon leakage," an economic phenomenon where domestic production shifts to jurisdictions with weaker climate regulations to avoid carbon costs, which undermines global emissions reductions and disadvantages local industries.
The newly published guidance establishes three critical pillars of compliance. First, it outlines the strict methodologies overseas installations must use to monitor and calculate both direct and indirect embedded carbon emissions during the production of CBAM goods.
Second, the documents define the rigorous verification processes required before this data can be submitted to UK tax authorities. Finally, the government detailed the specific responsibilities of official accreditation bodies, which will be tasked with approving and auditing the independent verifiers assessing the emissions reports.
To assist businesses in financial planning, HMRC also published illustrative CBAM rates and a series of worked examples demonstrating how the sector-level tax will be calculated using the official rate methodology.
Shifting the Compliance Burden
The mechanism fundamentally alters the compliance burden for UK importers. While the overseas manufacturer generates the emissions, the UK entity importing the goods is legally responsible for ensuring that the CBAM requirements are met and the associated carbon tax is paid.
If importers fail to provide accurate, verified emissions data, their goods could face significant delays at customs, or they could incur severe financial penalties. The government has stressed that proper preparation over the next two months is essential to avoid supply chain disruptions.
The UK system mirrors the European Union’s own Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, which entered its transitional phase earlier, but the two regimes maintain distinct administrative boundaries and calculation metrics.
Notably, the UK guidance confirms that goods originating from or traded through Northern Ireland remain outside the scope of the UK CBAM, reflecting the region's unique customs status. Furthermore, the regulations include provisions for carbon price relief, ensuring that importers can deduct any carbon taxes or fees already paid in the goods' country of origin.
The SME Data Challenge
Industry groups and trade representatives have broadly supported the policy's environmental goals but continue to warn about the profound administrative complexity involved in calculating embedded emissions.
For major multinational corporations with dedicated compliance departments, gathering data from global supply chains is a manageable, albeit resource-intensive, task. However, for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which often lack direct leverage over their overseas suppliers, securing verified primary emissions data presents a formidable challenge.
SMEs have expressed concern that some international suppliers may simply refuse to comply with the burdensome data requests, forcing UK buyers to either switch suppliers or rely on default emission values, which typically result in a higher tax liability.
The publication of the illustrative rates is intended to help these businesses model their potential costs and evaluate whether their current supply chains remain economically viable under the new regime.
The regulatory architecture supporting the tax is grounded in the Finance Act 2026, with the operational details governed by secondary legislation. The government has indicated that while the core policy framework is now firmly established, minor technical updates to the guidance may still occur as authorities finalise the digital reporting platforms.
With the January 2027 enforcement date rapidly approaching, the publication of the verification and monitoring rules effectively starts the clock for UK industry. Importers are now urged to immediately engage with their overseas manufacturing partners, establish secure data-sharing protocols, and secure the services of accredited verifiers before the new carbon border tax takes full effect.

articles.title: Indonesia readies contingency measures against EU and UK steel tariffs - ANTARA News
articles.summary: Indonesia readies contingency measures against EU and UK steel tariffs  ANTARA News
articles.full_text:
Director of World Trade Organization (WTO) Negotiations at Indonesia's Trade Ministry Dina Kurniasari speaks at a seminar on changes to steel tariffs in the European Union and the United Kingdom, in Tangerang, Banten, on Friday (October 16, 2026). (ANTARA/A. Muzdaffar Fauzan)
The ministry’s Director of World Trade Organization (WTO) Negotiations, Dina Kurniasari, said shifting trade policies among partner countries—including tariff changes, quota systems, and decarbonization requirements—pose direct risks to Indonesia’s export performance.
“These tariff changes certainly have implications for market access and the competitiveness of Indonesian steel products,” Dina said in Tangerang on Friday.
She noted that Indonesia’s trading partners have increasingly adopted trade remedy measures to protect domestic industries, address global production overcapacity, and meet climate commitments.
While the WTO framework allows member states to modify their bound tariffs, Dina stressed that such adjustments must comply with multilateral trade rules and respect the rights of trading partners.
An analysis by the ministry’s Trade Policy Agency (BKPerdag) identified three main risks facing Indonesia’s steel industry.
The most immediate concern is reduced price competitiveness for Indonesian steel products in EU and UK markets as tariffs drive up prices.
Market access could also be constrained by strict import quotas and increasingly stringent climate policies, including the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).
Together, these pricing and regulatory challenges are increasing uncertainty in global trade, underscoring the need for Indonesian steel producers to adopt risk-mitigation strategies.
Dina emphasized that Indonesia remains committed to promoting transparent and non-discriminatory international trade rules through diplomatic channels. At the same time, she said, the ministry is preparing for worst-case scenarios to protect the domestic industry.
The tariff increases come as Indonesia continues to expand its domestic steel production capacity.
Indonesian Iron and Steel Industry Association (IISIA) Vice Chairman Ismail Mandry said the association’s 189 member companies have a combined annual production capacity of 18 million tons.
Meanwhile, national steel imports for the 2024–2025 period are projected to reach approximately 8 million tons annually, with imports totaling 7 million tons as of August.
