articles.title: Europe risks retreating on Ukraine just as Russia weakens - The Parliament Magazine
articles.summary: Europe risks retreating on Ukraine just as Russia weakens  The Parliament Magazine
articles.full_text:
Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine is well into its fifth year with no sign of abating. If anything, Moscow is becoming more brazen and dangerous, while European support for Kyiv risks crumbling.
The irony is that European Union leaders, meeting in Brussels for the second day of the European Council summit, could weaken Ukraine's negotiating position at the very moment Russia's own capacity to keep fighting is under increasing strain.
The explanation for Russian President Vladimir Putin's growing appetite for risk is relatively straightforward: his government is running out of cheap and politically painless ways to finance the war.
The Kremlin's narrowing financial options
Russia has failed to make full use of high oil prices this year. Moscow has already overshot its original 2026 budget, which envisaged a deficit of 1.6% of gross domestic product. The shortfall is now expected to reach about 3.2% of GDP.
Much of the extra spending has been war-related. Russia's finance minister has warned that the military requires another 2 trillion rubles before the end of the year, largely to cover the mounting costs of recruitment and casualties.
The draft 2027 budget offers little relief. Its target of cutting the deficit to 2.2% of GDP rests on optimistic growth and inflation forecasts. It also assumes that defense spending will stay nearly flat in real terms, which has not happened in any year since the full-scale invasion.
While the deficit is modest by international standards, foreign capital markets are closed to Russia. Therefore, it can fund any gaps only by borrowing from domestic banks, raising taxes or lowering investment in infrastructure and public services.
None of these can be scaled indefinitely. Russia's remaining fiscal buffers are finite. Additional borrowing is becoming more expensive. Government spending can only be squeezed so far without further shrinking the civilian economy.
Putin's all-in is a bluff
If Russia's position is likely to become more difficult in 2027, Putin has every incentive to improve it before those constraints tighten.
In Ukraine, Russia is intensifying attacks on cities and critical infrastructure as winter approaches. Moscow's objective is not simply military attrition but the gradual exhaustion of Ukrainian society.
Russia is also escalating its hybrid campaign against NATO members. Cyberattacks, sabotage, arson, disinformation and targeted violence are gaining importance as instruments of its posture towards the West.
Incidents across Germany, Poland, Bulgaria, Romania, the Czech Republic and the Baltic states suggest that Europe faces a prolonged and deepening confrontation.
Targets will range from critical infrastructure and IT networks to military installations, defense manufacturers and public opinion itself.
Thankfully, a direct Russian armed attack on NATO territory or the use of tactical nuclear weapons remains unlikely.
A conventional strike against NATO might fit Moscow's narrative of conflict with the West, but it would do little to improve Russia's immediate prospects in Ukraine. The Kremlin lacks the spare troops to sustain a second front, while any such attack would risk triggering an Article 5 response with consequences Putin could not control.
The military value of tactical nuclear weapons is similarly questionable. Ukrainian forces are dispersed and entrenched, offering no obvious target whose destruction would decisively shift the balance on the battlefield.
The political costs would also almost certainly outweigh any operational gains: a nuclear strike could galvanize Western unity, strengthen European resolve, possibly remove what ambiguity is left in US policy and prompt China and India, Putin's key backers, to press him to step back.
The trouble for Russia is that its escalation options are limited and none can resolve its core problems in Ukraine on a timeline that matters for this year's fighting.
Moscow aims to capture Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, the largest remaining Ukrainian-held cities in the Donbas region, and thereby trigger a political crisis capable of weakening President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and ultimately removing him from office. That seems unlikely.
Meanwhile, the Russian population is increasingly paying the price of the war through inflation, high borrowing costs and precarious incomes for anyone not employed in the rapidly expanding defense sector, as well as the loss of everyday conveniences, from cheap imported goods to reliable mobile internet.
French and Italian tests for Ukraine
None of this, however, should provide much comfort to Kyiv.
US President Donald Trump's recent diesel deal with Putin, accompanied by a fresh verbal attack on Zelenskyy, has reinforced Ukrainian and European fears about Washington's reliability.
More troubling still is the possibility that Europe itself will become less dependable.
The EU heads into a crowded electoral cycle in 2027, with national votes threatening to expose the widening gap between its rhetorical commitment to Ukraine and its willingness to bear the financial and political burden.
Two contests deserve particular attention: France and Italy.
Next April and May, France will hold arguably its most consequential presidential election since World War II.
Marine Le Pen leads the polls, although she still faces a formidable second-round challenge. To win the May 2 runoff, she must expand her support beyond a projected first-round score of roughly 35% without alienating the working-class voters central to her coalition or frightening wealthier and middle-class voters concerned about economic stability.
Much will depend on whether France's fragmented political center can unite behind a credible alternative. The main rivals are Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, both former prime ministers under President Emmanuel Macron.
A recent poll for Le Figaro put Philippe second with 21%, 12 points behind Le Pen. But his campaign has been cautious and unexciting.
This is why much of France, and Europe, is bracing for a Le Pen win. Her victory would have profound implications for Ukraine, although not necessarily in the ways many assume.
The National Rally, or RN, has moderated several elements of its Ukraine policy. Senior party officials say a Le Pen presidency would continue training Ukrainian troops, participate in the coalition of the willing and potentially deploy French forces to Ukraine following a ceasefire.
They insist Kyiv alone should determine the terms of any peace settlement and reject pressuring Ukraine to recognize Russian territorial gains. Nor, they argue, would Le Pen seek to withdraw France from NATO's integrated military command while the war continues.
The greater danger is not that Le Pen would abandon Ukraine militarily, but that she would undermine the funding on which its war defense depends.
The RN remains opposed to expanding bilateral financial assistance to Kyiv and is deeply skeptical of the EU budget. As one senior party official asked: "How can we explain to voters we need to cut everything domestically, yet the only thing increasing is aid to Ukraine?"
The European Commission's proposal for the next long-term budget includes a reserve fund of up to €100 billion for Ukraine. Even if EU leaders reach an agreement later this year or in early 2027, Le Pen could torpedo it before it takes effect. The RN is also against using Russia’s immobilized assets in Euroclear.
Despite the €90 billion loan agreed last year, Ukraine already faces a funding gap of €70 billion next year, according to Eurasia Group estimates. These policies would therefore inevitably weaken Kyiv's bargaining power.
So too would the party's opposition to Ukraine's accession, although most member states oppose privately resist Ukrainian membership despite their public support.
Italy presents a different but equally revealing risk.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni remains the favorite to win next year's election. But Roberto Vannacci, a former paratrooper general and veteran of Iraq and Afghanistan, is seeking to exploit political space to her right with his new nationalist party, National Future.
Its populist agenda, wary of both NATO and Ukraine, threatens to pull Italian politics toward a more confrontational stance on migration, national sovereignty and foreign policy.
Even if Meloni retains power, these electoral pressures could complicate her efforts to maintain the strongly pro-Ukraine position that has distinguished her first term.
Inside or outside the EU
More broadly, European capitals have a long list of reservations about Ukraine's accession.
Member states oppose granting Ukraine immediate free movement of labor or goods, given immigration pressures and fears that Ukrainian agriculture would undercut EU farmers. The backlash from French and Polish farm lobbies against the Mercosur trade deal shows how difficult this issue will be.
EU capitals also worry about corruption and the rule of law, especially because Brussels has struggled to address these problems in member states such as Hungary.
Ukraine has made substantial progress since the Euromaidan revolution, including the creation of genuinely effective and independent anti-corruption agencies. But the war has understandably slowed reform, and the recent scandals show that significant gaps remain.
The so-called Mindichgate affair, an alleged $100 million embezzlement scheme exposed last November, was followed by smaller revelations of graft, vote-buying in parliament and other unethical conduct among Ukraine's political elite.
A complicated path to Brussels
Ukraine has also moved slowly on accession-related reforms.
The Verkhovna Rada, Ukraine's parliament, has stalled contentious, unpopular bills on taxation and banking, along with other measures required by the International Monetary Fund and the EU.
Part of the problem is procedural: seven years have passed since the last parliamentary election and many lawmakers have resigned, but voting thresh

articles.title: Ukrainian drones force closure of all four Moscow airports overnight, cancelling dozens of flights - Euronews
articles.summary: Ukrainian drones force closure of all four Moscow airports overnight, cancelling dozens of flights  EuronewsZelenskyy has yet to authorize more aggressive phase of Ukraine's M&M's drone operation - The Atlantic  HromadskeUkrainian Drones Launch Massive Attack on Russia, Suspending Operations in All Moscow Airports  МілітарнийSky closed over Moscow multiple nights in row as Ukraine resumes refinery strikes  The Kyiv IndependentUkraine Plans More Powerfu...
articles.full_text:
Moscow’s airports were closed for 101 hours in the first 14 days of October, more than double the total for all of September.
Ukrainian drones forced all four of Moscow's main airports to close overnight, with Vnukovo, Domodedovo, Zhukovsky and Sheremetyevo suspended for up to seven hours and more than 160 flights cancelled.
Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 94 drones heading towards the capital had been shot down.
Pulkovo airport in St Petersburg was twice forced to halt operations during the same night. Governor of Leningrad region Alexander Drozdenko said four drones were destroyed over the region.
Euronews could not independently verify the claims.
According to Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo, Moscow's four airports were closed for a total of 101 hours in the first 14 days of October, compared with 46 hours across the whole of September.
On Tuesday, Ukraine carried out one of its largest drone operations against the Russian capital, deploying close to 500 drones.
On 9 October, according to multiple reports, the presidential aircraft carrying Vladimir Putin — returning from a summit in Turkmenistan — was unable to land in Moscow due to a drone attack and was diverted to St Petersburg. Putin's plane was not reported to have been a direct target.
Russian officials have neither confirmed nor denied the reports.
Ukraine has not officially confirmed any organised campaign to shut down Russian airports, in what media outlets have dubbed "Operation M&Ms".
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not yet authorised the military to proceed with an original, more aggressive plan for such a campaign, according to reports.
In September, Zelenskyy said Russian skies "are becoming unsafe" and that "drones will appear in the skies over Russia, and that will have to be taken into account", urging international airlines to stop flying to Russian airports.
Kyiv has targeted Russia's military, energy and commercial facilities in a bid to defund Moscow's war machine, as its all-out war in Ukraine continued well into its fifth year.
Yet US President Donald Trump reiterated criticism of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries in an interview, calling them "a disgrace" after his shock announcement of a deal to purchase diesel from the Kremlin.
"There are many targets that can be hit. But when you shell oil refineries that produce, you know, diesel fuel, and we and the whole world need that, (Zelenskyy) is not doing the world a favour," Trump said.

articles.title: EU and China reportedly discussed sanctions relief tied to ASML supplier - NeoTeo
articles.summary: EU and China reportedly discussed sanctions relief tied to ASML supplier  NeoTeo
articles.full_text:
The European Union and China were reportedly discussing a reciprocal sanctions delisting involving Sindlhauser Materials GmbH, a German company in ASML’s supply chain. Tom’s Hardware reported the talks on October 15, citing Bloomberg’s October 14 report.
Under the reported proposal, China would ease export controls affecting Sindlhauser, while the EU would lift restrictions on an unnamed Chinese firm. Tom’s Hardware described that firm as accused of aiding Russia’s war against Ukraine. The discussions reportedly took place during a Beijing visit by Maroš Šefčovič, the EU Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security.
Why Sindlhauser matters to ASML’s supply chain
Tom’s Hardware describes Sindlhauser as a German precision-manufacturing and advanced-coatings company that relies almost entirely on Chinese rare earths and critical minerals. The company is part of ASML’s supply chain.
The report says China’s controls restrict Chinese exporters from selling dual-use items—goods with both civilian and military applications—to Sindlhauser. They also restrict third parties from transferring China-origin dual-use items to the company. Tom’s Hardware reported that Sindlhauser could face a risk of closure in the coming months if the restrictions remained.
German federal and Bavarian authorities reportedly helped the company explore alternative suppliers and ways to recycle existing materials.
The reported EU approval threshold
China placed Sindlhauser and 13 other European companies on its export-control list in July 2026, according to Tom’s Hardware. The report said an EU delisting would require unanimous support from member states. It also said the two sides had agreed to share more information and provide advance warning of future export restrictions.

articles.title: The European Union Deforestation Regulation’s Uneven Impact: Who is exposed and what are the costs? - International Institute for Sustainable Development
articles.summary: The European Union Deforestation Regulation’s Uneven Impact: Who is exposed and what are the costs?  International Institute for Sustainable Development
articles.full_text:
The European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) applies from December 30, 2026, but its impact varies depending on the perspective taken. Seen from the EU perspective, the regulation covers around 4.3% of its imports from outside the bloc, a modest share overall but concentrated in a small number of commodities and suppliers. From the perspective of exporting countries, however, exposure can be much greater, accounting for more than a quarter of total export value in some cases. Successive simplifications are estimated to reduce annual compliance costs by around 75%, although the remaining costs are spread unevenly along the value chain.
For decades, agricultural expansion has driven deforestation worldwide. According to the EUDR's preamble, the European Union imported and consumed a third of the globally traded agricultural products associated with deforestation between 1990 and 2008, and its consumption was responsible for 10% of worldwide deforestation associated with the production of goods or services over that period. In response, the bloc adopted the EUDR to reduce its contribution to global deforestation and forest degradation. The law covers seven commodities: cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya, and wood, along with a list of derived products. To be placed on or exported from the EU market, these goods must be (i) deforestation-free, (ii) legally produced, and (iii) covered by a due diligence statement.
Although the EUDR targets EU consumption, its effects will be felt well beyond the bloc’s borders. Who is actually exposed? And who will bear the cost of compliance? Understanding what the EUDR will change means looking at several factors together: countries’ exports to the European Union, the bloc’s own import patterns, how deforestation risk is assessed, and what the regulation requires of different actors along the value chain.
The EUDR’s Evolving Rules and Risk Classification
The EUDR has evolved significantly since its adoption. Its timing, product scope, and obligations have changed repeatedly since adoption, and each change affects which goods are covered, who must carry out due diligence, and how much compliance costs. The country risk classification, which determines how closely imports from each country are checked, is also subject to periodic review.
The regulation entered into force in June 2023, but its application date has been postponed twice, most recently to December 30, 2026 (June 30, 2027, for most micro and small operators). A December 2025 amendment simplified the rules, shifting the due diligence obligation to the first operator placing a product on the EU market and introducing a simplified regime for micro and small primary operators. Most recently, the European Commission adopted Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/2102 in July 2026, amending the list of covered products to remove certain products, such as cattle hides, skins, and leather, and to add products such as soluble coffee and certain palm oil derivatives. The regulation will apply to these products from December 30, 2027. The European Commission also published updated guidance in July 2026 to reflect the December 2025 amendments, clarifying the obligations of downstream operators and of micro and small primary operators. In its May 2026 simplification review, the European Commission stated that it does not consider it appropriate to propose further amendments to the regulation itself, although the country classification will be reviewed periodically and guidance may continue to be updated. This analysis reflects the rules as they stand at the time of writing.
Three Perspectives on the EUDR’s Impact
Exporters: Which countries are most economically exposed?
| The countries that supply the European Union with the largest volumes of EUDR-covered goods are not necessarily the ones most economically exposed to the regulation. Two measures show the difference: | 
By size, Brazil and China are the European Union’s two largest suppliers, accounting for 14.7% and 14.4% of EUDR-covered imports respectively (see figure below). Brazil’s exports span soya, coffee, wood, and cattle, while China's are mainly wood and rubber products. These two economies are most exposed in terms of the actual volumes of trade of covered goods.
Measured by dependence, however, the picture reverses. Both Brazil and China export large volumes of other goods, so EUDR-covered sales to the European Union account for only a small part of their total exports: about 5% for Brazil and even less for China, which does not appear among the 10 most-exposed countries (see figure below). For a group of smaller exporters, the share is far higher. EUDR-covered goods sold to the European Union account for half of São Tomé and Príncipe’s total exports, mostly cocoa and palm oil. Burundi, Côte d'Ivoire, and Cameroon each rely on EUDR-covered goods sold to the European Union for at least a quarter of their total export value. Across the most exposed countries, dependence is usually concentrated in a single commodity: coffee in Burundi, Ethiopia, Rwanda, and Uganda, and cocoa in Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon, Ghana, and Sierra Leone.
For these countries, a high share shows that much of their export value depends on EU buyers being able to document that products are deforestation-free and legally produced. If a supply chain cannot provide that information, EU buyers may drop it, or the trade may be redirected to other markets. The measure is therefore an indicator of exposure, not an estimate of losses.
The European Union: How much of the bloc’s trade is affected?
| EUDR products represent a relatively small share of EU imports from outside the EU, but there is substantial concentration in particular commodities and origins. | 
EUDR-covered commodities accounted for around 4.3% of the European Union’s imports in 2024, but this share is not evenly dispersed. Wood alone makes up a third (35%) of those imports, while rubber, cocoa, coffee, and soya contribute roughly 13%–14%, oil palm 8%, and cattle only 2%.
That concentration deepens at the country level. For several commodities, a single country supplies over a third of the European Union’s total imports, including cocoa from Côte d’Ivoire and coffee from Brazil. Indonesia supplies around 40% of the European Union’s oil palm products’ imports, and Brazil close to half of its soya imports (see figure below).
From the European Union’s point of view, the regulation covers a manageable share of total trade, concentrated in a few product lines. But that concentration also creates vulnerability. Because the supply of commodities like cocoa and soya depends heavily on a small number of countries, a compliance problem in just one of them could affect a large share of the European Union’s supply of that commodity, even though the commodity itself represents only a small share of total EU trade.
Operators: What does EUDR compliance cost, and who will pay?
| Even if aggregate compliance costs have fallen following simplification, those costs and adjustment pressures may be unevenly distributed across operators, exporters, and producers. | 
The compliance burden of the EUDR depends heavily on two things: the country risk classification and what the regulation requires of actors along the value chain. Under Article 29, the European Commission assigns every country one of three tiers: low, standard, or high risk. This classification reflects the European Union’s assessment of deforestation risk under its own criteria. The figure below shows the current classification.
The classification rests primarily on quantitative criteria: the rate of net forest area loss, drawn from the United Nations (UN) Food and Agriculture Organization’s Forest Resource Assessment (FAO FRA), and the rate of expansion of agricultural land or production for the seven regulated commodities, from FAOSTAT. A country qualifies as low risk if it meets any one of three conditions: it recorded no net forest loss between 2015 and 2020, its average annual forest area loss stayed below set relative and absolute thresholds, or it showed no expansion of cropland, livestock production, or overall agricultural land linked to the regulated commodities. Countries close to these thresholds undergo a second, more qualitative review that considers factors such as the strength of a country’s forest governance and its cooperation with the European Union. The regulation requires the list to be reviewed as often as necessary in light of new evidence, and the European Commission has said it envisages a first review in 2026, following the publication of updated FAO FRA data.
The risk tier determines whether operators can use simplified due diligence. It also sets, under Article 16, the minimum share of operators that competent authorities must check: at least 1% for products from low-risk countries, 3% for standard-risk countries, and 9% for high-risk countries. Half of the 20 most exposed countries are officially rated low risk under Article 29, including São Tomé and Príncipe, Burundi, Ghana, and Rwanda. Products from these countries are eligible for simplified due diligence, although their high dependence on the European Union market means that the regulation still applies to a large share of their export value. However, several highly dependent countries are rated standard risk, including Côte d’Ivoire and Cameroon, where EUDR-covered sales to the EU account for around a quarter of total exports, as well as Ethiopia, Uganda, Sierra Leone, Honduras, and Liberia. Operators sourcing from these countries must carry out full due diligence, so these countries combine high dependence on the EU market with the full set of information requirements. None of the 20 most exposed countries are rated high risk.

articles.title: Euro extends recovery as US rate hike bets fade - Economies.com
articles.summary: Euro extends recovery as US rate hike bets fade  Economies.com
articles.full_text:
The euro rose against a basket of global currencies in European trading on Friday, extending its recovery against the US dollar for a second consecutive day as investors continued buying the currency following its decline to a 17-month low. The euro is on track for its first weekly gain since August.
European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde said this week that the bank stands ready to act if rising energy prices intensify inflationary pressures. Investors are now awaiting further economic data from the eurozone, which will play an important role in shaping the central bank's policy outlook and interest rate decision at its October meeting.
The euro's advance comes as expectations for a US interest rate hike in October continue to weaken, particularly following less hawkish comments from several Federal Reserve officials suggesting there is no urgency to tighten monetary policy further.
Price overview
• EUR/USD today: The euro rose 0.2% against the US dollar to $1.1241, compared with today's opening level of $1.1219. The pair recorded a session low of $1.1208.
• The euro ended Thursday's trading up 0.55% against the dollar, recording its second gain in three sessions as it continued recovering from a 17-month low of $1.1113.
• In addition to buying activity at lower levels, the euro benefited from declining US Treasury yields and a weaker US dollar.
Weekly performance
So far this week, which officially concludes with today's settlement, the euro has gained approximately 0.5% against the US dollar, putting it on track for its first weekly advance since the final week of August.
Christine Lagarde
ECB President Christine Lagarde said this week that the central bank is closely monitoring the risk that higher energy prices, driven by geopolitical developments, could feed through into wages and the prices of goods and services, potentially keeping inflationary pressures elevated for longer.
Lagarde added that the ECB is monitoring wage developments and workers' pay demands for signs of additional pressures that could influence the inflation outlook, emphasizing the bank's readiness to act if inflationary risks emerge.
She also said that the primary solution to France's debt problems lies within France itself, through its fiscal policies, rather than relying on ECB intervention to support the bond market.
European interest rates
• ECB Chief Economist Philip Lane said he has not yet seen strong evidence that higher energy prices are generating second-round inflationary effects, noting that the economic impact of energy prices remains uncertain.
• Money markets currently price in approximately a 50% probability of a 25-basis-point ECB interest rate hike in October.
• Investors are awaiting further eurozone economic data on growth, inflation, unemployment and wages to reassess those expectations.
US dollar
The US Dollar Index fell 0.2% on Friday, extending its losses for a second consecutive session and moving further away from an 18-month high, reflecting continued weakness in the US currency against a basket of global currencies.
Alongside accelerating profit-taking, the dollar has come under pressure after less hawkish remarks from several Federal Reserve officials reduced expectations for a 25-basis-point interest rate hike this October.
US 10-year Treasury yields are currently trading near their lowest levels in three weeks, heading for a second consecutive weekly decline and their largest weekly loss since February, adding further downward pressure on the US dollar.
Federal Reserve Governor Michelle Bowman said the central bank has sufficient time to wait and assess developments in financial markets and the economy following September's interest rate increase before deciding whether further action is necessary.
San Francisco Federal Reserve President Mary Daly said another interest rate hike would likely be needed, but not urgently. She noted that the central bank could afford to wait until the outlook becomes clearer.
Following those comments, according to the CME Group's FedWatch Tool, the probability of the Federal Reserve leaving interest rates unchanged at its October meeting rose from 46% to 73%, while the probability of a 25-basis-point increase fell from 54% to 27%.
Euro outlook
US dollar weakness alone is not enough to guarantee a sustained recovery in the euro, as the single currency's performance remains closely tied to economic developments and monetary policy expectations in Europe.
If Europe's economic outlook improves while US Treasury yields continue to decline, the euro could find additional support for further gains. However, persistent energy price pressures and fiscal risks in Europe, or renewed expectations of tighter US monetary policy, could limit the euro's recovery and restore momentum to the US dollar.

articles.title: Andrew Bailey: Businesses are cutting costs to cope with Iran war energy shock - The Telegraph
articles.summary: Andrew Bailey: Businesses are cutting costs to cope with Iran war energy shock  The Telegraph‘Early days’ to see full effect of energy prices on inflation, BoE’s Bailey says  Financial TimesBank of England's Breeden says cost-cutting by firms helping central bank  ReutersRising energy costs hitting UK firms, warns Bailey  The TimesBank of England Governor Says Too Early to Make Call on Second-Round Inflation  WSJ
articles.full_text:
Businesses hit by the Iran war are choosing to cut costs rather than pass on price rises to struggling households, Andrew Bailey has said.
The Governor of the Bank of England suggested inflation in Britain had been kept in check by bosses opting to squeeze profits to combat higher energy bills caused by the conflict.
However, he warned that companies would find this “harder” the longer the war in the Middle East dragged on.
Speaking at the Institute of International Finance’s annual meeting in Bangkok, Mr Bailey said: “Talking to businesses, there is a very, very big focus on cost cutting and a very big focus on the difficulty of passing through.
“Firms are clearly squeezing margins as well as cost cutting, using margins. The longer the energy situation goes on, the harder that gets.”
Mr Bailey also noted that soaring mortgage rates had kept inflation under control by reducing homeowners’ disposable income and limiting their ability to spend.
He added: “Our mortgage rates have gone up, they’re pretty much the top end of the G7, in terms of increases in mortgage rates.”
Mr Bailey’s comments suggest that he may be willing to wait longer to assess the impact of a prolonged conflict before considering an increase in interest rates.
However, investors are still pricing in a 93pc chance of an interest rate rise next month.
The Governor cautioned that it was “too early” to draw firm conclusions about the impact, with the Bank’s next interest rate decision published just days after John Healey’s maiden Budget on Oct 28.
But Mr Bailey insisted he was not complacent, noting that the economy had been more “resilient” to the oil price shock than initially expected.
The Bank kept interest rates on hold at 3.75pc in September, although three members of its Monetary Policy Committee voted for a rate rise to 4pc, including the Bank’s chief economist.
Mr Bailey said he had been surprised by how the economy had been able to weather the oil price shock, even as diesel prices hit £2 a litre.
The economy grew by 0.1pc in August, defying analysts’ expectations. However, Mr Bailey noted that growth remained weak by historical standards.
“It’s not as strong a growth as frankly we need. It’s not as strong a growth as we’ve had in the past. But there are signs,” said Mr Bailey.
He added that investment remained a source of support, while consumers were able to “smooth consumption” by dipping into what analysts have estimated is a £1tn savings reserve built up during the pandemic.
Figures from Moneyfacts show that the average interest rate on a new five-year fixed mortgage deal has hit 6pc for the first time in three years, adding hundreds of pounds to monthly payments for some borrowers.
The Bank previously said 1.3 million UK homeowners may face higher mortgage payments by the end of 2028 as a result of the war in the Middle East.
Kevin Warsh, the chairman of the US Federal Reserve, also said he was surprised at the resilience of the global economy.
“Almost everywhere in the global economy is showing resilience that I’m not sure I would have predicted five or six months ago, given what’s happening in geopolitics and hotspots around the world,” he said.
However, Mr Warsh said he would not “pre-judge” future decisions before the Federal Reserve’s next meeting later this month.
The central banker repeated that he was an optimist on AI but warned that the transition would be a “very bumpy one”.
Speaking on a separate panel in Bangkok, he said: “It’s going to change the real economy. We don’t know in the next 12 or 18 months its effect on employment [but] we will have more wealth, then that has to be a very good thing.
“But the path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one. Bumpy in our understanding of the technology. Bumpy because we really don’t know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies.”

articles.title: Le Pen ready to 'debate' Zelenskyy after vow to end French aid - Euronews
articles.summary: Le Pen ready to 'debate' Zelenskyy after vow to end French aid  EuronewsFrance’s Marine Le Pen vows ‘trial of strength’ with EU  Financial TimesMacron tells Le Pen to 'stay humble' ahead of French vote  Le Monde.frMarine Le Pen’s EU dream is a nightmare for Brussels  POLITICO.euMarine Le Pen vows to massively cut France’s funding to the EU if elected president  connexionfrance
articles.full_text:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the National Rally's presidential candidate of ignoring key details of military cooperation between Paris and Kyiv.
French aid to Ukraine has become an issue in the 2027 presidential campaign. Marine Le Pen, who says she will end it if she reaches the Élysée Palace, has said she is ready to debate the question directly with Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Speaking on CNews on Thursday, Marine Le Pen said she was prepared to travel to Ukraine to discuss the issue with the Ukrainian president: "We could perfectly well debate this issue whenever he wishes," she said. "
If Mr Zelenskyy would like us to talk, I will gladly come to Ukraine. But what I want to tell him is that we no longer have the financial means to provide assistance," she added.
"I have nothing, personally, against Zelenskyy," she added.
Earlier, on Wednesday, speaking to Flemish television VRT News, the far-right candidate condemned the cost of French support for Ukraine, which she puts at €6 billion a year.
That figure roughly corresponds to the average annual level of French aid to Ukraine since February 2022, including bilateral support and contributions to European mechanisms.
"From my election, for six months we will maintain the aid...so as not to force anyone's hand. But afterwards we will stop financial assistance to Ukraine because we no longer have the means to do so," she said.
The Ukrainian president responded to her comments, saying that "Madame Le Pen does not fully grasp certain details" of Franco-Ukrainian military cooperation.
Zelenskyy: Ukraine also contributes to France's defence
In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Zelenskyy defended the benefits of military cooperation between France and Ukraine, particularly in the field of weapons technology.
France "can only gain" from this partnership, he insisted. "We give something back," he stressed.
Zelenskyy notably pointed out that the experience gained by his army on the battlefield allows France to test and improve its equipment in real combat conditions.
He cited the Franco-Italian SAMP/T air-defence systems, which have been modified several times to adapt to realities on the ground, as well as the Franco-British Scalp/Storm Shadow missiles. A "win-win" partnership, according to the Ukrainian leader.
Emmanuel Macron reiterates France's support
Incumbent President Emmanuel Macron reiterated France's support for Ukraine on Thursday, after talks with Zelenskyy in Brussels.
In the face of intensifying Russian attacks, the French president said it was "vital" to provide Kyiv with "all the means necessary" to defend itself and protect its population and infrastructure, stressing that "France will continue to shoulder its responsibilities".
French foreign minister Jean-Noël Barrot also responded to Marine Le Pen's statements, arguing that ending French aid to Ukraine would be "the surest way of bringing the war closer to our borders."
Outcry from Marine Le Pen's opponents
Gabriel Attal, the Renaissance candidate for the presidency, also criticised Le Pen's position on Franceinfo, accusing her of wanting to "let Ukrainians be butchered."
"Supporting Ukraine is not a humanitarian operation to make ourselves feel good, it is our own defence," the former prime minister insisted.
MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, winner of the social-democratic primary, likewise denounced a "capitulation" and "submission" to Vladimir Putin.
"If we cut aid to Ukraine, that means subjecting the whole of Europe to Vladimir Putin," the centre-left presidential candidate said on France 5, arguing that Le Pen should "absolutely not take power."
Horizons candidate Édouard Philippe described Marine Le Pen's comments as a "betrayal" in a message on X.
"To say that France will stop helping Ukraine at the end of 2027 is to weaken it even further at a time when, more than ever, we need to close ranks around it," he wrote.
Marine Le Pen's comments have also stirred reactions beyond her rivals in the race for the Élysée.
Liberal lawyer Charles Consigny, a commentator on RMC's Les Grandes Gueules and former Les Républicains candidate in the 2022 legislative elections, believes Le Pen's position serves Vladimir Putin's interests.
"Putin is eagerly awaiting Marine Le Pen's victory," he argued in a post on X.
Within the National Rally camp, MP Laure Lavalette has defended ending French financial support for Kyiv.
"We can no longer help Ukraine. The coffers are empty," she said on RMC, before admitting that she did not know the amount of France's contribution.
Germany, Europe's leading contributor to aid for Ukraine
According to figures from the German research centre, the Kiel Institute, France has committed a total of €27 billion to supporting Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion, including €7.9 billion in bilateral aid and €19 billion via European mechanisms.
In absolute terms, Germany remains Europe's biggest contributor to aid for Ukraine, with more than €50 billion pledged since February 2022, ahead of France, Italy and the Netherlands.
Relative to GDP, however, bilateral aid is highest in Denmark and Estonia.

articles.title: Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries ‘a disgrace’ - The Guardian
articles.summary: Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries ‘a disgrace’  The GuardianTrump: Zelensky is destroying Ukraine  The Telegraph"He doesn't want to settle": Trump says he does not want to deal with Zelenskyy  Українська правдаAs Obstacles to Peace Go, Zelenskyy Ranks Below Trump  Bloomberg.comThe Rupturing Trump-Zelensky Relationship Stands to Hurt Ukraine and Its European Allies  The New York Times
articles.full_text:
Donald Trump has called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised Volodymyr Zelenskyy after an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.
Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries after Zelenskyy said Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire unilaterally declared by Trump on Sunday, having briefly halted its attacks to demonstrate its readiness for peace talks. Russia had continued its strikes on Ukrainian power plants.
In an interview with Newsmax aired on Thursday, the US president said: “All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that’s a disgrace.
“There are a lot of targets you can hit, but when you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, diesel oil, and we need that, and the world needs that, then he’s not doing a good service for the world.”
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since Trump announced an easing sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel on to global markets.
Zelenskyy criticised the agreement, which was widely interpreted as an attempt to curb high fuel prices before the US midterm elections, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than four and a half years ago. US efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.
Trump repeated to Newsmax his views of the two leaders involved in the conflict. “I’m not a big fan of Zelenskyy,” Trump said. “I think they actually both would like to see it end, but I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than Putin.”
Arriving in Brussels to meet EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy did not comment on Trump’s latest remarks. He said he was “so thankful that we have such huge support from the EU” and its leaders, whom he described as “real leaders”.
He went on to say that Ukraine wanted to end the war as quickly as possible, but “we don’t see now signals from [the] Russian side that they are ready for this”.
Kyiv’s relationship with Washington was strained further this week when Ukraine said Starlink services had been restricted, in effect hobbling Ukrainian drone strike missions and crucial air defences with a flick of the switch.
During a visit to London this week, the Ukrainian president said the sudden restriction of Starlink had left him feeling personally betrayed by Trump and lamented losing a partner.
The British defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said on Thursday that his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, had assured him in a face-to-face meeting that the vital satellite communications system had been restored. In an interview with the BBC, he said it was unclear what had caused the disruption, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.”
Amid growing doubts about long-term US commitment to Ukraine, European leaders declared their support for Zelenskyy.
Standing alongside the Ukrainian leader in Brussels, the European Council president, António Costa, said Ukraine could “count on us not only to support you in war” but also in the path to negotiating EU membership.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU had supported Trump’s energy ceasefire, “but we have seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute” and instead had escalated its attacks. She said the EU intended to increase pressure on Russia, promising a 22nd round of sanctions, adding: “We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war.”
The promise of further European sanctions against Russia comes weeks after the EU lifted sanctions against two prominent Russian oligarchs at the request of France and Luxembourg.
After meeting Zelenskyy, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said it was “crucial” that Ukraine received “all the means necessary to protect itself”.
The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, posted online: “I can reassure you, dear Ukrainian friends and President Zelenskyy: YOU ARE NOT ALONE.”
As Zelenskyy met Macron in Brussels, he said that the Kremlin had “launched yet another vile drone strike on Ukrainian energy infrastructure” in the city of Lutsk, which caused blackouts.
The Kremlin, meanwhile, accused Ukraine of derailing US peace efforts by resuming its strikes on refineries.

articles.title: ‘We’re done,’ Zelensky says, as Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian oil refineries. The Kremlin claims the attacks never stopped. - Meduza
articles.summary: ‘We’re done,’ Zelensky says, as Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian oil refineries. The Kremlin claims the attacks never stopped.  MeduzaRussia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume  BBCZelenskyy defies Trump as Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian refineries  Financial TimesRussia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses  The GuardianPutin Admits Moscow Failed to Anticipate Ukrainian Strikes on...
articles.full_text:
Ukraine is resuming strikes on Russian oil refineries, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced.
Zelensky said Ukraine had held off on striking Russian oil refineries for three days at the request of U.S. President Donald Trump.
Russia, meanwhile, had not honored the so-called energy ceasefire, Zelensky said, continuing to strike Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and killing about 100 civilians over the past week.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” the Ukrainian president said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday morning, October 15.
The first strike by Ukraine’s military after the pause appears to have hit the Ryazan oil refinery. The plant, owned by Rosneft, is one of the key fuel suppliers for Moscow and the Moscow region.
Ryazan Governor Pavel Malkov announced the morning of October 15 that classes had been canceled in 14 schools and 25 kindergartens in Ryazan because of “a mass drone attack on the region.” The Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ published a photo early that morning showing a flare over the Ryazan oil refinery, suggesting it was linked to the drone attack.
Authorities in the Ryazan region confirmed the strikes, saying a fire had broken out at the refinery. Malkov also said that “a warehouse and vehicles on the grounds of another enterprise in Ryazan” had been damaged. He declined to give further details, adding that the damage was being assessed.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said Ukraine’s military attacked the Ryazan oil refinery with 69 drones and four Flamingo cruise missiles. The Russian military said it had shot down the drones and missiles, but added that “a fire broke out at the refinery as a result of falling drone debris.”
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Wednesday afternoon, October 14, that Ukrainian forces had struck two oil refineries, one in the Saratov region and one in the Ryazan region. “We see that the Ukrainian side is not showing any movement toward an energy ceasefire,” he said. At the time, authorities in the Ryazan region and eyewitnesses had not reported any strike on the refinery there, and Novak’s claim about a strike on an oil refinery in the Saratov region remains unconfirmed.
Russian presidential press secretary Dmitry Peskov, commenting on Zelensky’s remarks about resuming strikes, referred to Novak’s statement. According to Peskov, there had been no moratorium on Ukraine’s part, and strikes on Russian oil refineries and energy facilities had continued throughout this period. “There is nothing new here,” Peskov said, once again accusing Ukrainian authorities and Zelensky personally of “not wanting to make peace.”
War in photos. Aftermath of a Russian strike on Kyiv.
Russian forces struck Kyiv with drones and missiles overnight on October 14, killing three people and injuring about 20. A nine-story apartment building caught fire in the Desnianskyi District as a result of the strike.

The understanding reached between China and the European Union on hybrid vehicle trade is reciprocal and mutually beneficial, showing that rules-based consultations can resolve trade differences, the Ministry of Commerce said on Thursday.

articles.title: Nightmare for Putin as officer defects and helps kill hundreds of Russians - AOL.com
articles.summary: Nightmare for Putin as officer defects and helps kill hundreds of Russians  AOL.comThe Defector: A Russian Officer Turned Against His Country and Helped Ukraine Kill Hundreds  WSJA Russian Officer Helped Ukraine Kill 300 Soldiers, Then Escaped To Kyiv: Report  NDTVRussian officer helped Ukraine kill over 300 troops by leaking military secrets: Report  The Times of IndiaDefection in the Russian army. Officer changing sides  Defence24.com
articles.full_text:
A Russian army officer has helped Ukraine kill over 300 of Vladimir Putin's soldiers after becoming disillusioned with his country's military. Lieutenant Lev Stupnikov, 26, shared the location of infrantrymen, medics, officers and officials in one attack Ukraine carried out with his help. He had shared information about the group which was gathered near the city of Vuhledar preparing for an offensive. Stupnikov provided the Ukrainians with the exact location and secretly took a photo he sent to Ukrainian intelligence.
His contact told him in a message to "walk away", then in another text said, "I'm waiting for a message that you've left", before sending a third which read: "LEAVE". Stupnikov told the Wall Street Journal he pretended to need the loo and disappeared among some trees, crouching down as if to relieve himself.
Seconds later he was knocked over by the force of an explosion as Ukraine fired missiles at the group. Asked by the Ukrainians in the immediate aftermath to send a photo, Stupnikov texted back: "There's just meat."
In that attack, the lieutenant reported 68 killed and 60 wounded, including 10 officers among the dead. A top target for Ukraine, Colonel Gusein Musayev, who was commander of the 36th Motorised Rifle Brigade, was a top target also killed in the attack.
Stupnikov is one of thousands of Russians who have deserted since Russia launched its illegal war against Ukraine. A UN report published in September last year said 50,000 had done so, representing almost 10% of the Russian troops deployed to Ukraine.
Some 16,000 were prosecuted for offences connected to desertion. The report said people who refuse to fight are tortured, with "beatings, starvation and death threats".
Stupnikov's mother, Tatiana, who was opposed to Putin's rule, helped to enable his betrayal as well as his disenchantment with the army, including the state of some of the Soviet-era vehicles used during training. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Stupnikov was appalled at how innocent civilians were being targeted with bombs.
When Tatiana found out her son was being sent to war, she encouraged him to leave Russia, but he didn't. In February 2024, she wrote to Dmytro Karpenko, who was working with Ukraine's military intelligence, asking for him to help her son desert.
Stupnikov agreed to work with Karpenko, leading to a series of acts of sabotage against Russia. He told the Wall Street Journal "it was constant, endless tension".
Eventually, Stupnikov made a daring escape to Ukraine across the frontline. He was later joined by his mum and 16-year-old sister.
Reflecting on what he did, Stupnikov said: "Did I betray my oath? I pledged to defend freedom, independence and the constitutional order. But Putin destroyed all three."

articles.title: Russian Firms Stand to Gain Most From Trump’s Diesel Deal, Analysts Say - The Moscow Times
articles.summary: Russian Firms Stand to Gain Most From Trump’s Diesel Deal, Analysts Say  The Moscow TimesZelenskiy blasts Trump's diesel deal and calls Russian peace moves a 'parody'  ReutersTrump offered Ukraine enhanced security guarantees before diesel deal with Putin  The TelegraphOpinion | Trump’s Democracy-for-Diesel Deal Shames Us All  The New York Times‘No logic’: Finland slams Trump for siding with Putin against Ukraine  POLITICO.eu
articles.full_text:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Moscow could do more for Russian oil companies than for the American consumers he wants to help, analysts say.
While Russian firms stand to benefit from looser export restrictions, the promised shipments may do little to bring down U.S. fuel prices.
The agreement has drawn scathing criticism from Ukraine and its European allies, as well as scrutiny from lawmakers at home. But does it make economic sense?
What does Trump want?
Trump announced that Russia would “immediately” supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and global markets, followed by another 500,000 metric tons in November and 1 million metric tons thereafter.
The deal comes as U.S. diesel prices have risen to $6.179 per gallon, up nearly 70% year-on-year, amid the turmoil that has gripped the global oil market since the start of the Iran war in late February.
Reduced refinery output has sharply cut global diesel exports, which totaled about 172.2 million metric tons in the first nine months of 2026, down 10% from the same period last year.
Higher prices are hurting Americans, including the truckers and farmers who are part of Trump’s traditional support base. With just a month to go before the midterm congressional elections, 73% said they disapprove of his handling of the cost of living, according to poll aggregator Silver Bulletin.
Additional Russian supplies are not intended to directly ease a U.S. diesel shortage because the country already produces roughly a quarter more diesel than it consumes. But U.S. fuel prices are shaped by global markets. The more other countries are willing to pay for diesel, the more domestic consumers must pay in turn.
More Russian diesel on the global market could therefore help lower American prices by narrowing the gap between supply and demand, regardless of whether it is shipped directly to the U.S.
Encouraging Russia and Middle Eastern producers to increase fuel supplies is the most straightforward way for Washington to bring prices down.
That’s because U.S. refineries are already operating at close to full capacity, while restricting exports to force domestic fuel prices lower could create other problems, including storage constraints.
Can Russia help?
Like the U.S., Russia is a net exporter of diesel, meaning it produces more than it consumes and sells the surplus abroad.
That has not changed despite Ukraine’s drone campaign against Russian refineries in recent months. While the attacks have caused sporadic gasoline shortages, Russia’s pre-war diesel output was more than double domestic demand, compared with a surplus of just 15-20% for gasoline.
Russia has therefore continued to export diesel, though in smaller volumes. Shipments totaled about 427,000 metric tons in September, compared with roughly 3 million metric tons a month before Ukraine intensified its strikes, Reuters reported.
These figures only cover shipments to the limited number of countries, mostly in Central Asia, exempted from restrictions Russia imposed in July to keep its domestic market supplied.
Other estimates are higher. Kpler put September shipments at 584,000 metric tons.
Energy analyst and former Gazprom Neft executive Sergei Vakulenko, citing shipping data, said Russia exported at least 1.6 million metric tons of diesel by sea between July and September, despite a broad export ban that exempted supplies to Mongolia and Central Asia.
Vakulenko, now based in Germany with the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, said Russian authorities had made little effort to stop these “grey” shipments because the country lacked the storage capacity to hold the surplus.
This means that Russia could supply the 500,000 metric tons Trump requested for November without causing domestic shortages simply by legalizing existing grey exports, he said.
Moscow partially lifted its diesel export ban from Oct. 10 following the agreement with Trump.
Supplying 1 million metric tons of diesel a month during the winter is also realistic, especially as domestic demand falls after the autumn harvest season, Vakulenko added.
U.S.-based energy analyst Tatiana Mitrova also said the volumes Trump requested from Russia “would have gone to the global market anyway without any additional effort.”
So what’s the catch?
The volumes Trump announced may be realistic, but they could be too small to bring prices down significantly.
For example, 500,000 metric tons of Russian diesel equals roughly 4% of monthly U.S. consumption or 0.4% of monthly global consumption. It would cover about 13% of the estimated monthly global diesel shortfall of 4 million metric tons.
Russian supplies could have a greater impact if exports returned to levels seen before Ukraine intensified its attacks. But Kyiv has yet to agree to halt its strikes, and Moscow would need to repair its damaged refineries and restore lost capacity.
“The volumes under discussion are too small, all else being equal, to noticeably affect global prices, especially before the midterm elections,” Vakulenko said.
Without an effective energy truce, the diesel deal will largely amount to “appearances rather than a real increase in Russian diesel supplies to the global market,” he said.
The deal could provide “temporary relief to a global market facing a significant diesel deficit,” but Russia’s constrained refinery capacity limits how much additional supply it can deliver, analytics firm Kpler said in a note.
Shipping Russian oil products through the Baltic and Black seas poses another challenge, as Ukrainian drone attacks also disrupt those routes, Kpler added.
Moscow-based analyst Kirill Rodionov said Russian companies stand to reap the most benefits from the deal, as it would allow them to officially export more diesel at higher prices.
Those exports would do little to lower U.S. fuel prices, but would allow the Trump administration to claim at least a partial foreign policy success, he said.

articles.title: Pope urges humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky in call with Russian President - Vatican News
articles.summary: Pope urges humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky in call with Russian President  Vatican NewsPope Leo speaks with Putin from hospital, just days after lung cancer surgery  CNNPope calls Russian president Vladimir Putin urging Ukraine truce days after lung cancer surgery  Sky NewsPutin agrees to cooperate with Pope Leo's plea for aid for Ukrainian town  ReutersPope speaks to Putin from hospital, voices concern over Ukraine  The Washington Post
articles.full_text:
Vatican News
The Holy See Press Office released a statement on Friday afternoon, saying that Pope Leo XIV spoke by telephone with Vladimir Putin, President of the Russian Federation.
"During the conversation, the Holy Father expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, and called for a ceasefire to allow the delivery of food and medical assistance, and the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population," said the statement.
"Finally, the Holy Father reaffirmed the Holy See’s commitment to promoting dialogue and peace," it concluded.
Pope Leo has been in Gemelli Hospital since Tuesday when he underwent an operation which removed the lower lobe of his right lung.
He previously spoke by phone with President Putin on June 4, 2025. The city of Oleshky lies along the frontline of the Russian-occupied Kherson region, on the banks of the Dnieper River.
Cardinal Parolin: Pope took initiative on behalf of besieged city
Afterwards, on the sidelines of a conference at the Catholic University of the Sacred Heart, Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Parolin said, “It was the Holy Father who took the initiative to plead the case of this besieged city, where some 2,000 civilians need humanitarian routes through which they can leave.”
“The Pope called for a ceasefire to allow humanitarian aid, especially food, to reach the city and to enable those who wish to leave to be evacuated," he said.
“I hope that, in response to the Holy Father’s request, President Putin will agree to do what the Pope has asked,” Cardinal Parolin added. “The fact that he accepted the call and spoke with the Pope may, I hope, be a sign that the Pope’s request will indeed be carried out.”

articles.title: Chinese automakers make tech-led pitch for Europe's premium car market - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: Chinese automakers make tech-led pitch for Europe's premium car market  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
Chinese automakers, including BYD, Changan’s Avatr and Geely’s Zeekr, are targeting Europe’s premium car market with technology-led luxury vehicles featuring advanced driver-assistance systems, rapid charging and enhanced comfort.
Having rapidly gained share in Europe's mainstream car market with affordable models and the latest tech, Chinese carmakers now have their sights on a bigger prize: the continent's highly lucrative premium segment.
At this week's Paris car show, Chinese brands showcased premium vehicles packed with advanced driver-assistance systems, rapid charging and comfort features, hoping to persuade buyers to choose unfamiliar Chinese badges over established luxury names.
"You need to be in this market long enough to build up your presence and credibility," said Zheng Yeqing, a vice president at Chinese electric vehicle maker Xpeng, which launched in Europe in 2020 and saw its sales there more than double to more than 29,000 cars in the first eight months of 2026. "It takes persistence."
Europe's premium segment is dominated by Germany's BMW , Mercedes-Benz and Volkswagen's Audi, whose decades of brand heritage carry far more weight with European buyers than they do in China, where consumers place greater emphasis on technology features.
With domestic vehicle sales in China falling 20 per cent in the first half of 2026 and competition intensifying, Chinese automakers increasingly need the margins that premium vehicles can deliver.
Europe is the obvious battleground. Chinese brands are effectively shut out of the US, the world's most lucrative car market, while BMW, Mercedes, Audi and Porsche sold almost 2 million vehicles in Europe in the first nine months of this year alone.
Chinese brands such as Geely's Zeekr have already gained share from German premium rivals in China with lower-priced models packed with technology features.
Avatr unveiled an electric premium sedan and SUV in Paris that will start at around €60,000 ($67,400) and feature rapid charging and comfort extras including a massager in every seat.
Justin Li, who heads the all-electric brand's overseas expansion, said Avatr estimates that Europe represents 72 per cent of sales of cars priced above $50,000 outside the US market.
"If we want to be a premium brand, if we don't enter Europe ... we don't really win," Li said.
Redefining luxury?
Typically, a German premium car launch includes images celebrating a brand's heritage, such as an early 20th-century craftsman carefully shaping an elegant piece of wood trim.
The Chinese premium car launches in Paris were different.
During Aito's unveiling of four electric SUVs, Seres Vice President Clifford Kang, representing the brand's parent company, highlighted its "intelligent technology". An accompanying video showed Aito vehicles automatically swerving to avoid obstacles or carrying a tower of full champagne glasses on the hood without spilling a drop.
Aito's philosophy, Kang said, is "intelligence redefining luxury".
Brad Kuntz, a partner at consultancy Grant Thornton Stax, said Chinese automakers are reshaping what luxury means for some consumers.
"You've got that old bespoke luxury of European cars of years ago," he said. "But in the EV world you've got more of the elegance being built in from a technology standpoint."
European premium brands are watching the newcomers closely.
"Audi is confidently embracing growing international competition, including from China," a spokesperson said. "It is the task of European policymakers to ensure fair competitive conditions in Europe."
Top-end brands such as Volkswagen's Bentley appear unfazed.
During the unveiling of Bentley's first EV last month, CEO Frank-Steffen Walliser told reporters that real luxury comes from the "heart of Europe" and is irreplaceable.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, an executive at a major Chinese automaker acknowledged the challenge. "Deep down in my heart, we still have a gap between us and those European luxury brands," he said.
But he added that Chinese automakers should be able to catch up "within a decade or two".
For now, Chinese premium sales remain a tiny share of Europe's market, though they are growing rapidly.
Zeekr's European sales more than tripled to 9,525 vehicles in the first nine months of 2026 from 3,025 a year earlier. Having entered 22 European markets, Zeekr plans to expand into another eight this year, European CEO Lothar Schupet said.
"Our starting point where we are now is very strong and we will keep on accelerating," he said.
Avatr's Li said the brand plans a gradual expansion across Europe, starting with Spain, Britain and Denmark in 2027, followed by Germany and a handful of other countries in 2028.
"We have only one chance to get this right," he said.

articles.title: GlobalData: UK offshore wind build-out to depend on grid connections and market reforms - Energy Global
articles.summary: GlobalData: UK offshore wind build-out to depend on grid connections and market reforms  Energy Global
articles.full_text:
The UK’s clean power transition is moving into an infrastructure-intensive phase, with offshore wind, solar photovoltaics (PV), and new nuclear capacity set to reshape the generation mix. Delivering this build-out will depend on faster grid connections, transmission reinforcement, and market reforms that preserve investor confidence while managing a more variable power system, according to GlobalData.
GlobalData’s latest report, UK Power Market Trends and Analysis by Capacity, Generation, Transmission, Distribution, Regulations, Key Players and Forecast to 2035, reveals that the country’s installed power capacity is projected to almost double between 2025 – 2035. Renewables are expected to account for 73% of the generation fleet by the end of the forecast period, led by offshore wind, solar PV, and onshore wind.
Attaurrahman Ojindaram Saibasan, Power Analyst at GlobalData, commented: “Offshore wind is central to the UK’s clean power strategy. The project pipeline includes large North Sea developments and the ScotWind leasing round, while annual Contracts for Difference (CfD) auctions continue to provide the principal route to market for large scale renewable projects. However, project awards alone will not ensure delivery. Developers require timely connections, supply-chain capacity, and a market framework that reflects the changing value of power by location and time of day.”
Electricity demand in the country is expected to recover and grow as transport, heating, and industrial processes electrify. Renewable generation will account for roughly two-thirds of gross power output by 2035, while gas-fired capacity continues to provide flexible balancing capacity and nuclear contributes firm low-carbon generation. The expected retirement of older nuclear stations before new projects enter operation will make the timing of replacement investment important for system security.
The grid is the main delivery constraint. A large share of the UK’s renewable pipeline is seeking access to networks that already face connection queues, while new offshore generation will require expanded transmission links from coastal landing points to demand centres. The National Energy System Operator, transmission owners, and Ofgem are pursuing reforms intended to accelerate strategic network investment and improve the connection process.
Saibasan added: “The UK has a strong foundation for a high-renewables system: a mature CfD mechanism, deep offshore wind resources, extensive interconnection, and a competitive retail market. Yet the next stage of the transition requires the network to become more anticipatory. Transmission, distribution capacity, storage, demand response, and digital flexibility must develop alongside generation rather than after it.”
The UK remains among Europe’s most interconnected power markets, with operating links to France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Norway, Denmark, and Ireland. Interconnectors can support security of supply and help balance renewable output across markets, although they also increase the importance of coordinated market arrangements and resilient cross-border infrastructure.
Investment through the end of the decade is expected to focus on offshore wind and nuclear, alongside solar PV, onshore wind, grid infrastructure, and flexibility assets. CfDs provides long-term revenue support for renewable generation, while the Regulated Asset Base model is designed to support financing for new nuclear projects. The Review of Electricity Market Arrangements will be influential in determining how investors manage locational constraints and periods of high renewable output.
Saibasan concluded: “The UK’s challenge is no longer setting clean-power ambitions; it is converting an extensive development pipeline into operating assets. Success will depend on synchronising renewable deployment with grid expansion, flexible capacity, and reforms that maintain the investment case for low-carbon generation.”

articles.title: EU Caps Chinese Hybrid Vehicle Imports at 350,000 Amid Trade Tensions - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: EU Caps Chinese Hybrid Vehicle Imports at 350,000 Amid Trade Tensions  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
The European Union has moved to cap imports of Chinese-made hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles at 350,000 units annually starting in December 2026, establishing a four-year safeguard measure to protect its domestic automotive sector from a rapidly shifting trade dynamic.
A Strategic Pivot and Surging Volumes
The quota represents a definitive escalation in Brussels' trade defenses following the bloc's 2024 anti-subsidy tariffs on battery-electric vehicles (BEVs). Those initial duties, designed to counteract state-sponsored manufacturing advantages, inadvertently accelerated a strategic pivot by Chinese automakers. Exempt from the earlier BEV levies, plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) became the primary conduit for Chinese manufacturers to maintain and expand their market share in Europe.
Data illustrates the sheer velocity of this market shift. EU imports of China-made hybrids surged from just 3,800 units in October 2024 to 50,000 units by July 2026, according to industry tracking. Furthermore, Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the bloc's 27 member states tripled to $7.5 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $2.5 billion during the same period a year earlier. This explosion in volume prompted European officials to seek immediate containment measures after Beijing rejected proposals for voluntary export limits.
Quota Mechanics and Legal Architecture
Under the newly agreed framework, the 350,000-vehicle ceiling applies strictly to the first 12 months of enforcement. The cap will then increase by 6 percent annually over the subsequent three years of the safeguard window. Trade legal experts note that the EU is utilizing a tariff-rate quota mechanism, a tool permitted under international trade rules when domestic industries face sudden import surges.
- Base Allocation: 350,000 vehicles permitted at standard tariff rates during the first year.
- Annual Escalation: The ceiling expands by 6 percent in each subsequent year of the four-year window.
- Overage Penalties: Shipments exceeding the allocation face prohibitively high duties or border blocks.
This legal architecture is designed to withstand challenges at the World Trade Organization, a crucial consideration for Brussels given the protracted disputes that followed previous industrial safeguards.
Impact on Chinese Conglomerates and European Legacy Brands
The policy directly targets major Chinese manufacturing conglomerates such as BYD, SAIC Motor, which owns the MG brand, and Geely. These companies have heavily invested in PHEV technology specifically to navigate European regulatory environments. The aggressive push into European markets is also a symptom of intense saturation within China's domestic automotive sector. A bruising multi-year price war among local electric vehicle manufacturers has severely compressed profit margins at home, forcing companies to seek higher returns in overseas markets. Europe, with its stringent emissions regulations and consumer appetite for transitional hybrid technologies, emerged as the most lucrative destination for these excess capacities.
European legacy automakers have aggressively lobbied for these protections. Industry representatives argue that heavily subsidized Chinese imports undermine billions of euros in local investments dedicated to the green transition. Manufacturers including Volkswagen and Stellantis have warned that without intervention, the European automotive supply chain faces existential threats from lower-cost, state-backed competition.
Internal Divisions and Economic Scrutiny
The quota also exposes lingering internal divisions within the European Union regarding trade policy toward Beijing. France has consistently championed aggressive defensive measures to protect domestic manufacturers like Renault and Stellantis from what it views as unfair competition. Conversely, Germany, home to Volkswagen, BMW, and Mercedes-Benz, has historically advocated for a more cautious approach. German automakers rely heavily on the Chinese market for their own global sales and remain deeply concerned that overly punitive measures from Brussels could trigger retaliatory tariffs on European luxury and internal combustion engine exports.
Furthermore, the reliance on quotas has drawn scrutiny from economic policy experts. Researchers at the Bruegel think tank have cautioned that the European Union's automotive sector ultimately requires a robust, forward-looking industrial plan rather than depending on undue protectionism. Critics of the quota system argue that shielding legacy automakers from price competition may reduce the incentive to innovate and streamline production costs, potentially leaving European consumers with fewer affordable options during a period of high inflation.
Geopolitical Fallout and Market Recalibration
The arrangement underscores the broader geopolitical friction between Brussels and Beijing regarding industrial overcapacity and clean-tech dominance. While the EU frames the quota as a necessary safeguard against market distortion, Chinese officials have consistently criticized such measures as protectionist barriers that disrupt established global supply chains. By reaching a negotiated quota rather than imposing unilateral punitive tariffs, both sides have managed to avert an immediate retaliatory trade war on hybrid vehicles.
As the December implementation date approaches, the European automotive market faces a significant recalibration. For European consumers, the immediate consequence of the quota is likely to be a stabilization or slight increase in the retail prices of popular hybrid models. The era of deeply discounted, mass-market Chinese PHEVs flooding European showrooms is effectively drawing to a close. While environmental advocates have expressed concern that limiting affordable low-emission vehicles could slow the continent's overall decarbonization efforts, EU policymakers maintain that preserving the domestic industrial base is a prerequisite for long-term economic sovereignty.
