articles.title: China-EU trade talks yield prospect of Chinese hybrid car exports halving - KrASIA
articles.summary: China-EU trade talks yield prospect of Chinese hybrid car exports halving  KrASIA
articles.full_text:
China and the European Union (EU) have averted a trade war, reaching an “understanding” that Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc will be halved in time after two-day talks between their trade chiefs in Beijing.
China’s Ministry of Commerce said on October 9 that both sides have “reached an understanding on hybrid vehicle trade in compliance with WTO rules,” without offering details following negotiations between Chinese commerce minister Wang Wentao and European commissioner for trade and economic security Maros Sefcovic.
The European Commission said later that the understanding was to “moderate” China’s exports of hybrids and plug-in hybrids, which “opens the prospect of cutting China’s exports by more than a half.”
“I believe that we achieved very good results,” Sefcovic said at a news conference in the Chinese capital. “We are talking about reducing exports from China to European Union over four years by several million cars.”
Sefcovic had demanded “tangible” steps toward reducing the EU’s daily deficit of USD 1.12 billion with China by October, which the commission had referred to as “a mountain of a challenge.”
Both sides have now agreed that China will allow the EU improved access through lower most-favored-nation tariffs from “car parts to olive oil and footwear totaling almost EUR 4 billion (USD 4.5 billion) in current export value, which would bring at least EUR 225 million (USD 252.3 million) in duty savings,” the commission said.
Regarding rare earth metals and permanent magnets, China will facilitate export licensing to the EU.
According to the Chinese statement, China would expand imports of medical devices from the EU and also facilitate procurement matchmaking meetings.
Last week, dozens of EU industry groups called for urgent action against unfair trade practices, but the most closely watched in these negotiations in Europe is the hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicle sector.
Europe is flooded with Chinese-branded electric vehicles despite anti-subsidy duties it imposed on those carmakers in October 2024. To avoid those tariffs, Chinese carmakers had pivoted to manufacturing and exporting hybrid vehicles to the EU. European leaders see this segment as the next big threat to its industry.
Chinese brands accounted for 14% of the EU’s hybrid electric vehicle market and 25% of the plug-in hybrid vehicles in the first half of this year, compared with 2% two years ago in both those segments.
“Today’s announcement can help facilitate the transition to a new era of Chinese presence in the European market in an orderly way and this is in the long-term interests of all parties,” the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association said in a statement.
But one analyst pointed out that it was always Beijing’s goal to control about 15% of Europe’s hybrid market, which isn’t far off the negotiated level.
“One could interpret this as Beijing simply choosing to co-own a measure it knew was coming, at relatively low cost,” said Jacob Mardell, lead analyst at Sinification, a research organization that tracks policy discussions in China. “But at the very least, it signals that Beijing is starting to take the EU at its word.”
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has been unusually outspoken about China in recent months, lamenting its combination of state subsidies, overcapacity, aggressive pricing and an undervalued yuan. China rejects claims of overcapacity and currency manipulation: On Thursday, its central bank denied ever engaging in “competitive currency depreciation.”
As such, the results of the talks that the Chinese Chamber of Commerce in the EU lauded as “a positive signal” may not be enough to appease European leaders. Experts said EU leaders may still call for tougher action at a meeting of the European Council on Thursday, such as the imposition of safeguards to limit any increase in imports that will harm the domestic industry.
“Ultimately, plug-in hybrid exports are a small part of the problem,” said Noah Barkin, a senior adviser at research and advisory firm Rhodium Group. “Even if that deal is not an overtly bad one from the EU’s perspective, is it enough to convince European leaders to hold off on other trade measures when they meet next week? I am not sure that it will be.”
Mardell cited missing details in areas such as chemicals, brandy, pork and dairy, and the lack of a timetable for rare earth metals.
EU and Chinese negotiators will hold the next meeting in March, and keep talking in the meantime, including a ministerial-level video conference in January.
This article first appeared on Nikkei Asia. It has been republished here as part of 36Kr’s ongoing partnership with Nikkei.

articles.title: September 2026 — Monthly analysis of Russian fossil fuel exports and sanctions - Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air
articles.summary: September 2026 — Monthly analysis of Russian fossil fuel exports and sanctions  Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air

source_detail.name: Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air

articles.full_text:
Authors: Luke Wickenden and Isaac Levi; Data scientist: Panda Rushwood
Russia’s LNG export revenue reaches a 44-month high, while the EU overtakes Turkiye as the third-largest importer of Russian fossil fuels.
Key findings
- In September 2026, Russia’s fossil fuel export revenues were broadly unchanged month-on-month at EUR 625 mn per day, despite a 6% decrease in export volumes.
- Russia’s crude oil export revenues fell 8% month-on-month to EUR 339 mn per day, and volumes dropped 11%, reflecting an 11% increase in pipeline crude oil and a 15% fall in seaborne crude export earnings.
- Revenue from seaborne oil product exports rose 6% to EUR 83 mn per day in September, still the second-lowest level since Russia’s full-scale invasion, while export volumes rose 2%.
- In September 2026, liquefied natural gas (LNG) export revenues from unloaded cargoes jumped 68% month-on-month to EUR 75 mn per day, the highest level since January 2023.
- Russia imported 234 thousand tonnes of seaborne oil products in September 2026, 44% less than in August, but still the second-highest monthly volume in data going back to January 2022. Turkiye accounted for 55% of total supplies, with Morocco providing most of the remainder. Shipments from South Korea fell to 8,000 tonnes following a threat of legal action regarding supply reaching Russia in August 2026, while no shipments arrived from India in September.
- In September, EU imports of Russian LNG rebounded by 60% month-on-month from August’s record low. Spain received no Russian LNG shipments in September, marking its first month without Russian LNG imports since the start of the full-scale invasion.
- In September 2026, China remained the world’s largest importer of Russian fossil fuels, while the EU overtook Turkiye to become the third-largest importer.
- Despite the EU’s ban on oil products made from Russian crude, seven shipments from refineries processing Russian crude were unloaded at EU ports in September 2026.
- Refineries in India, Turkiye, and Brunei that use Russian crude exported EUR 1.0 bn of oil products to sanctioning countries in September 2026, a 43% rise month-on-month.
- In September 2026, 57% of Russia’s seaborne oil was transported by sanctioned ‘shadow’ tankers. A further 40% of the volume was transported by G7+ owned or insured tankers. The remainder was transported by non-sanctioned ‘shadow’ tankers.
- Forty-eight ‘shadow’ vessels were operating under false flags at the end of September 2026, down from 120 at the end of September 2025. Falsely flagged tankers carried only 2% of the Russian oil delivered by the ‘shadow’ fleet in September 2026.
- Fifty Russian-flagged ‘shadow’ tankers delivered Russian oil in September 2026, compared with 22 in September 2025. They carried 36% of the oil delivered by ‘shadow’ tankers, making the Russian flag the largest in the ‘shadow’ fleet.
- A USD 30 per barrel crude oil price cap and lower oil product caps, fully enforced, would have cut Russia’s seaborne oil export revenues by 26% (EUR 2.7 bn) in September 2026.
- South Korea imported 18 mn tonnes of Russian coal from January to August 2026, 34% higher volumes than in the same eight-month period in 2025, making Russia its second-largest coal supplier.
Trends in total export revenues
- In September 2026, Russia’s fossil fuel export revenues were broadly unchanged month-on-month at EUR 625 mn per day, even as export volumes fell by 6%.
- Russia’s crude oil export revenues fell 8% month-on-month to EUR 339 mn per day, and volumes dropped 11%. Pipeline crude oil export earnings were 11% higher than the previous month, whilst seaborne crude export revenues fell 15%.
- Revenue from seaborne oil product exports unloaded at their destination ports rose 6% month-on-month to EUR 83 mn per day, still the second-lowest level since Russia’s full-scale invasion, while export volumes rose 2%.
- Oil product loadings at Russian ports fell 12% month-on-month in September 2026 to one of the lowest monthly volumes since Russia’s full-scale invasion, around half the level observed in September 2025. Tuapse — Russia’s fourth-largest oil product export port before the full-scale invasion — which has faced sustained drone attacks since May, has not loaded a full cargo of oil products since June. With refinery throughput still depressed and domestic demand taking priority (jet fuel, diesel, and gasoline are still under an export ban), the persistently low oil product loadings suggest that Russia’s oil product export earnings could remain subdued in October, despite Trump’s announced agreement with Putin to increase Russian diesel supplies to the US.
- Following Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia’s Baltic Sea port of Ust-Luga at the beginning of September, crude oil loadings dropped 26% month-on-month. In September, additional drone strikes hit the Novorossiysk oil terminal; however, oil product exports dropped by a mere 3% month-on-month.
- Liquefied natural gas (LNG) export revenues from unloaded cargoes jumped by 68% to EUR 75 mn per day, the highest level since January 2023, while volumes rose 48% month-on-month. Loaded Russian LNG volumes also increased 41% month-on-month, driven mainly by a 50% rise in loadings from Russia’s Yamal LNG, while loadings from the sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project more than doubled.
- Pipeline gas export revenues rose by 8% to EUR 71 mn per day, even as export volumes fell 2% month-on-month.
- Russia’s coal export revenues fell by 12% month-on-month to EUR 58 mn per day.
- Despite the decline in crude oil exports, Russia’s mineral extraction tax (MET) receipts from crude oil reached 688 billion rubles in September; furthermore, the MET rate for oil extraction rose 45.1% month-on-month. The rise in crude oil MET was driven by higher Russian oil prices, a weaker ruble and an increase in the export-duty component of the tax.
Who is buying Russia’s fossil fuels?
- Russia’s fossil fuel exports remain highly concentrated, with China dominating purchases of coal and crude oil, Turkiye leading purchases of oil products, and the EU remaining the largest buyer of LNG and pipeline gas — showing Moscow’s dependence on a narrow set of key customers.
- Coal: From 5 December 2022 until the end of September 2026, China purchased 36% of all Russian coal exports. India (20%), Turkiye (14%), South Korea (12%), and Vietnam (4%) round out the top five buyers’ list.
- Crude oil: China has bought 50% of Russia’s crude exports, followed by India (37%), Turkiye (5%), and the EU (5%).
- Oil products: Turkiye, the largest buyer, has purchased 26% of Russia’s oil product exports, followed by China (13%), Brazil (11%), Saudi Arabia (8%), and Singapore (8%).
- LNG: The EU remains the largest buyer of Russian LNG, accounting for almost half (48%) of Russia’s total LNG exports, followed by China (25%), Japan (18%), and South Korea (6%).
- Pipeline gas: The EU is the largest buyer, purchasing 32% of Russia’s pipeline gas exports, followed closely by China (32%) and Turkiye (29%).
- In September 2026, China remained the largest global buyer of Russian fossil fuels, accounting for 55% (EUR 9.1 bn) of Russia’s export revenues from the top five importers. articles.title: Macro pulse: Why Europe's inflation problem could be harder to fix than the US' - investingLive
articles.summary: Macro pulse: Why Europe's inflation problem could be harder to fix than the US'  investingLive
articles.full_text:
Summary
- Europe's inflation problem isn't just about rising prices, but also the fact that economies cannot afford the same cure
The major focus this week has been all about US inflation, even more so after the hotter-than-expected September CPI report. And while markets are busy trying to digest what that might mean for the Fed outlook, perhaps we should also be paying some attention across the Atlantic to what looks to be a trickier inflation problem in Europe.
Euro area headline annual inflation climbed to 3.8% in September, with core annual inflation nudging back higher to 2.5%. The ECB is facing a tough task in trying to get inflation back to its 2% target, but there is perhaps a bigger problem to contend with. And that is the fact that unlike the Fed, the ECB has to contend with more than a handful of economies that aren't necessarily moving at the same speed.
Just imagine you're needing to adjust the air conditioning for an entire office building but you only have one thermostat to work with. Some rooms are already freezing cold while others are still unbearably warm. So, how do you go about in finding a solution? In simple terms, that is pretty much the ECB's dilemma on the inflation battle.
We are seeing the likes of Spain face up against strong inflation pressures as core annual inflation there climbs above 3% in September. Meanwhile, France continues to struggle with a much weaker growth backdrop even as core annual inflation remains much lower at 1.5%. Both countries are facing very different economic challenges, yet both have to live with the same interest rate policy.
For the ECB, that creates a bit of an uncomfortable situation. If policymakers decide to raise key interest rates to tackle inflation, it risks putting even more pressure on struggling economies. But if policymakers decide to hold back on tightening policy instead, they risk letting inflation run even more rampant in countries where price pressures are already proving to be rather persistent.
Damned if you do, damned if you don't.
Now, that is not to say that the Fed has it easy in terms of deciding on monetary policy in order to defeat the inflation monster. But at least it only needs to set interest rates for one national economy, rather than trying to balance the needs of 21 different countries that are also sharing a single currency.
And therein lies the bigger risk for Europe in general. The ECB might eventually succeed in bringing inflation back down to its target, but at what cost? How much economic damage will policymakers have to tolerate in getting there? Higher interest rates might be the right cure for inflation, but it isn't something that every European economy can afford to take in.

articles.title: Chinese automakers turn to Europe as domestic slowdown fuels consolidation - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: Chinese automakers turn to Europe as domestic slowdown fuels consolidation  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
China’s crowded auto industry is facing mounting pressure from falling domestic sales, pushing automakers to seek growth in Europe, their biggest profitable market outside the US.
The record 20 Chinese brands vying for attention at this week's Paris car show reflect a stark reality: as a slowdown at home pushes China's overcrowded auto industry to consolidate, success in Europe could help determine which carmakers survive.
With the US market largely closed to Chinese automakers, Europe is by far the most profitable market still open to them, but also one of the toughest to crack.
Chinese brands including BYD, Chery and SAIC's MG have already established a foothold in Europe, while newer entrants are racing to build dealer networks, parts operations and brand recognition.
"If they drop exports in Europe, they die," said Francois Roudier, secretary general of the International Organization of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers (OICA).
The pressure stems from China itself, where the world's largest car market has become increasingly crowded.
More than 100 automakers compete in China, where state support from national, provincial and city governments has helped sustain local champions and delayed long-expected consolidation that could entail significant job losses.
A sales slump, however, has brought that prospect closer.
New car sales in China fell 20% in the first half of this year. Omdia analyst Chris Liu said Chinese automakers, expecting continuing growth, launched an average of three new models a day in 2026.
"This is the worst possible year to launch a new vehicle in China," Liu said.
Recovery is expected to be slow. Consultancy AlixPartners predicts Chinese new-car sales will not return to 2025 levels until after 2030.
The downturn is increasing pressure on automakers to find growth abroad, particularly in Europe.
OICA's Roudier said a new EU-China deal to halve imports of Chinese hybrid cars into the bloc would only intensify competition among automakers at home.
"Now you have to eat your neighbour," he said.
First step towards consolidation
Industry executives and analysts say Beijing has begun taking tentative steps towards the consolidation long predicted across the sector.
A merger deal last month involving Toyota's two Chinese joint-venture partners, under which state-owned FAW will become Guangzhou Automobile Group's (GAC) second-largest shareholder, is widely viewed as an early test case.
Analysts say the deal is particularly complex because it involves FAW, which is owned by China's central government, and GAC, which is controlled by Guangdong province. Toyota's involvement adds a foreign private-sector partner to the equation.
"This is probably one of the most complex mergers to manage," said Pedro Pacheco, vice president of research at Gartner.
In a road map published in September outlining plans to become one of the world's leading automotive powers by 2030, China's industry ministry said it would "encourage industry consolidation".
Gartner's Pacheco said Beijing was likely to pursue mergers carefully and methodically.
"They don't want to convey the image externally that there's a sense of urgency or desperation," he said.
Industry experts expect consolidation ultimately to reduce China's crowded auto sector to a handful of globally competitive manufacturers.
"Our assumption is those remaining automakers will have (annual) sales of between 5 million and 6 million cars," said an executive at a major Chinese automaker, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Europe as a prving ground
Analysts say overseas performance, particularly in Europe, is likely to become an increasingly important measure of which automakers can thrive independently.
"China's government will definitely evaluate overseas sales performance, in particular Europe," Omdia's Liu said. "If they do better overseas, the government will say 'you can actually survive on your own.'"
That dynamic favours early movers such as BYD and Chery, which are already rapidly gaining European market share.
Barriers to entry are rising. The best dealer locations are increasingly taken, while new entrants must also invest heavily in parts warehouses, repair networks and after-sales support to meet European customer expectations.
Automakers must also focus on resale values in a market where more than half of new vehicles are leased, a business model that remains rare in China.
Those investments take time and money. Great Wall Motor , for example, struggled in its first attempt to establish itself in Europe and is now working on a comeback.
Changan, which launched European sales last year, began building its dealer network ahead of its market entry and expects to have 650 dealerships across Europe by next year. Executives at the Paris show said the company had deliberately avoided expanding too quickly before introducing a broader model range.
"We don't make fast food," said Vice President Mi Mengdong.
Philip Nothard, insight director at dealer services firm Cox Automotive, said BYD, Chery and MG had been willing to spend heavily to establish themselves in Europe, leaving less room for later arrivals to gain meaningful market share.
"We'll see a big four or five (Chinese automakers), then others who will come and go," he predicted.

articles.title: ‘Sodcit’ – after battlefield setbacks, Russia returns to destroying Ukraine’s morale - The Conversation
articles.summary: ‘Sodcit’ – after battlefield setbacks, Russia returns to destroying Ukraine’s morale  The ConversationPower plant attacks reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unlivable  The GuardianWhy Russia believes it can finally crush Ukraine this winter  The TelegraphRussian General Staff announces start of massive strikes on Ukraine's energy grid  Українська правдаWhy Russia Sees a Window to Bomb Ukraine Into Submission This Winter  The New Y...
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymr Zelensky recently told journalists that the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, has instructed his military commanders to abandon the rules of war that protect civilian targets. “He said there are no rules now,” Zelensky said – reporting that this information had been picked up by intelligence intercepts of Russian communications.
That Putin’s commanders took him at his word is apparent from a sharp increase in strikes on civilian targets. Over the past month there has been an intensification of Russian strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities. A UN report on October 9 reported that: “On 27 September alone, alerts lasted 19 hours. Strikes on bridges, educational institutions and energy infrastructure have intensified, causing widespread blackouts and water supply disruptions.”
On October 11, the US president, Donald Trump, announced an “energy ceasefire” which he said had been agreed to by both Russia and Ukraine. But both sides have denied this. While Zelensky has said Ukraine will halt its successful campaign of strikes against Russian oil refineries if Russia stops targeting its power plants, Russia responded the same day with a series of attacks on Ukrainian power facilities.
Other critical infrastructure targeted by Russian strikes has included data centres and internet providers in Kyiv and other big cities. Russia has also been targeting transport and logistics hubs, rail stations and bridges over the Dnipro river in Kyiv.
All of these are severely disruptive to civilian life. In the case of Kyiv’s bridges, their destruction has the potential to literally bring the city to a standstill.
Distinguishing between civilian targets and military objectives is a fundamental principle of international humanitarian law on the conduct of war. This expressly prohibits attacks against civilians and civilian objects.
The rule is codified in Article 48 of the Geneva Convention, to which Russia is a signatory. The article states that all parties to a conflict “shall at all times distinguish between the civilian population and combatants and between civilian objects and military objectives and […] shall direct their operations only against military objectives”.
Russian military regulations on international humanitarian law nominally endorse distinction and proportionality. Russia is also a party to the Geneva Conventions.
Not a ‘new strategy’
But Russian practice has often diverged from its formal legal commitments. During military operations in Chechnya, Syria and Ukraine, the Russian armed forces engaged in patterns of behaviour that directly violated these principles. Russian forces fighting in Chechnya relied heavily on the use of massive firepower and the indiscriminate use of force.
The Russian siege of the Chechen capital Grozny, in 1999 and 2000, devastated the city, prompting the UN to label it “the most destroyed city on Earth” . Russian operations in Syria echoed this approach. Its military conducted intense bombing raids and indiscriminate airstrikes against residential areas and civilian infrastructure such as schools, hospitals and markets.
Attacking critical non-military targets has been part of the way Russia has waged war for many years. Soviet military theorist Aleksandr Svechin distinguished between two different strategies of warfare. A strategy of destruction aims to destroy enemy armed forces quickly with a knock-out blow in the field. A strategy of exhaustion, on the other hand, depends on degrading an enemy’s economic, material and moral resources over time. These ideas remain influential.
‘Sodcit’
Svechin’s strategy of exhaustion is often summed up by military theorists with the acronym Sodcit. Spelled out in full, this stands for “strategic operations to destroy critical infrastructure”. It’s a key element of Russia’s way of waging war.
But Sodcit isn’t about indiscriminate attacks on civilian targets. The idea is to “inflict sufficient material and psychological ‘deterrent damage’ to reduce the adversary’s capacity and, above all, willingness to continue or escalate the war”.
It’s interesting to note, though, that when reporting Russian strikes on Ukraine, the state news agency, Tass – a Kremlin mouthpiece – aims to establish these are “dual-use targets”. In other words, they can also be used for military purposes. So a Nova Post logistic hub, where people’s parcels and other mail are sorted, was, Tass claimed, “used to store dual-use cargo designated for supplies to the Ukrainian army”.
But it’s much harder to justify bombing apartment blocks and cities’ electricity installations in military terms.
So as winter approaches, destroying Ukraine’s energy networks and leaving people without heating, power or water, aims to destroy morale. And when civilian infrastructure is targeted, civilians also die. The UN human rights monitoring mission in Ukraine (HRMMU) has reported that civilian casualties in the first eight months of 2026 were higher than the whole of 2025. This is also calculated to destroy morale.
Putin’s “new strategy” of attacking civilians and the things that enable them to go about their lives is nothing new. But it seems clear that with winter approaching, and in light of recent Ukrainian success on the front lines, Russia will redouble its attacks on Ukraine’s home front.

articles.title: Grid operator spends £50m in a single day to keep the lights on - The Telegraph
articles.summary: Grid operator spends £50m in a single day to keep the lights on  The TelegraphQuestions over power supply as Neso faces ‘unprecedented’ turmoil  The TimesCost of balancing Great Britain’s power grid reaches nearly £50m a day | Energy industry  The GuardianUK Grid Seeks Emergency French Power to Secure Supplies  Bloomberg.comRichard Tice: £80 million spent on balancing costs due to Net Zero policies  Traders Union
articles.full_text:
Britain’s grid operator is facing fresh questions about how it manages the electricity system after paying nearly £50m in a single day to keep the lights on.
National Energy System Operator (Neso) paid an estimated £49m in so-called “balancing costs” on Wednesday in what is thought to be a record.
It was the second day of record-breaking payments to keep the grid stable. Neso paid out £39.4m on Tuesday, according to provisional figures.
Some of the money went to Scottish wind farms to switch off because the grid was incapable of transmitting all their power. However, most of the money went to gas-fired power stations in England, which were paid to ramp up their output to replace the missing green power.
Data from leading energy consultancy LCP Delta showed that balancing costs hit a record £505m in September. The annual bill is set to grow from an estimated £2bn this year to £8bn by 2028. The costs are ultimately passed on to households and businesses in the form of higher bills.
Neso said it was legally obliged to make balancing payments and blamed the slow construction of new pylons and power lines for the rapid rise in costs.
A spokesman said: “The single biggest opportunity to reduce balancing costs is the timely delivery of new infrastructure by transmission owners, which could halve balancing costs by the end of the decade.”
The UK has three monopoly transmission networks. SSE and Scottish Power run networks in northern and southern Scotland, respectively, while National Grid owns the system in England and Wales.
However, Andrew Bowie, the Conservative shadow energy secretary, said Neso had to answer questions about rapidly rising costs.
“What is going on at Neso? Why are their models so wrong?” he wrote on X. He said the spending was “unsustainable”.

articles.title: FMC Proposes $200,000 Per-Voyage Fee and Import Limits on Spain Over Port Access Dispute; TPEB Imports Hit a Record 2.55 Million TEU in September - Flexport
articles.summary: FMC Proposes $200,000 Per-Voyage Fee and Import Limits on Spain Over Port Access Dispute; TPEB Imports Hit a Record 2.55 Million TEU in September  Flexport
articles.full_text:
Logistics Update
Talking Tariffs
- FMC Proposes a $200,000-Per-Voyage Fee and Import Limits on Spain Over a Port Access Dispute: The Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) has put forward its first concrete remedy in an investigation that's run since December 2024: a $200,000 fee on every voyage a Spanish-flagged vessel makes into a U.S. port, paired with restrictions on five categories of Spanish imports. The case traces back to Spain repeatedly denying docking privileges to U.S.-flagged vessels in the Maritime Security Program (MSP), starting with a trio of Maersk ships turned away in late 2024 over cargo tied to Israel.
  - The targeted import categories — perfumes and cosmetics, olive oil and other fats, ceramics, articles of stone, and sugar and confectionery — together represent roughly $3.6 billion in annual U.S. imports from Spain, based on the FMC's own trade figures.
  - By the agency's own tracking, Maersk's U.S.-flagged fleet made only six calls at Spanish ports in all of 2026, down from roughly seven a month before the dispute began, with most of that traffic shifting to Tangier, Morocco instead.
  - Spain gets a 60-day comment window and the chance to request a hearing before anything is finalized. The FMC also built in room to escalate: if Spain retaliates against the new fees, both the per-voyage charge and the list of restricted goods can grow.
  - Importers of Spanish perfumes, olive oil, ceramics, stone products, or confectionery should start contingency planning now and can weigh in during the comment period if the proposal would hit their supply chain.
- Importers Who Over-Ordered Solar Products Are Already Paying for It: Importers who ramped up solar cell and module orders this fall may already be feeling the consequences. Wiley attorney Timothy Brightbill says the number of companies locked out of further shipments ahead of the December 4 deadline is now in the dozens, the result of Commerce and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) comparing current import volumes against each importer's own history and cutting off anyone who looks like they're stockpiling.
  - The mechanism traces to Proclamation 11052, signed August 6, which set hard weekly caps — 2,000 cells and 55 modules — for any importer that registered on or after that date. Go over a cap in a single week, and the bar is immediate, with no warning beforehand.
  - Importers that were already established don't face a fixed numeric cap. Instead, regulators are watching whether this year's volumes run far above what each company shipped in 2025 and early 2026.
  - All of it is aimed at the same outcome: heading off a stockpiling rush before December 4, when Section 232 minimum import price tariffs on polysilicon, ingots, wafers, cells, and modules take effect.
  - A bar from new entries doesn't mean goods are stuck for good. Companies can still route product into a bonded warehouse and wait to enter it for consumption, or request a waiver by email if they can show a legitimate business reason for their volumes. Commerce says it aims to respond within 14 days.
  - Brokers who help clients dodge the caps through multiple importer records risk losing their license, so solar importers should sort this out now rather than discover they're barred at the border.
- Mail Filers Get an Extra Quarter Before Entry Type 13 Exclusions Get Enforced: International mail filers have three more months to get their paperwork in order. CBP's Entry Type 13 program, the simplified process for postal shipments, was supposed to start fully enforcing its list of excluded goods on October 22. That enforcement date is now January 20 instead, a 90-day reprieve that CBP says exists to let filers catch up before the stricter rules kick in.
  - The underlying program has been running since late July: filers submit a monthly spreadsheet, pay duties by ACH debit, and maintain a continuous bond in ACE eBond rather than filing a formal entry for every mail shipment.
  - What's delayed is enforcement of the goods that were never eligible for this simplified track in the first place, including antidumping and countervailing duty merchandise, quota goods, partner-agency-regulated items, alcohol, tobacco, and anything under HTSUS Chapters 98 and 99.
  - Shippers moving those excluded categories through the mail should use the extra runway to get formal entry procedures lined up rather than assume this date holds either.
- Experts Doubt the U.S.-EU Tariff Truce Survives the Rest of Trump's Term: Not everyone thinks the U.S.-EU tariff arrangement, which has held European autos and most other goods to a 15% rate since mid-2025, survives the rest of Trump's term. Two risks keep surfacing in recent commentary: a shift in U.S. policy toward Ukraine, and the EU's carbon border tax. A Washington think tank analyst flagged the first risk; someone who spent years negotiating trade deals for the U.S. government flagged the second, and both believe either one could be enough to unwind the truce.
  - U.S. policy on Ukraine and the arrangement's tariff terms were never cleanly separated, so any swing in Washington's approach there could change the political math behind keeping the truce in place.
  - The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a tariff tied to the carbon content of imports, creates its own friction with an administration that has resisted comparable carbon pricing schemes of its own.
  - The arrangement has already drawn criticism in Europe as lopsided: it locked in existing 50% tariffs on steel and aluminum while carving out zero-tariff treatment for aircraft, select chemicals, semiconductors, agricultural goods, and critical raw materials.
  - Importers with European supply chains built around the 15% baseline should treat that rate as negotiable over a multi-year horizon rather than fixed, and watch both Ukraine policy shifts and CBAM's implementation timeline as early warning signs.
TRANS-PACIFIC EASTBOUND (TPEB)
- Capacity and Demand:
  - Deployment continues to be high with a quick rebound post-Golden Week. XLs are entering the market for some additional capacity and to ease roll pools.
  - U.S. imports reached 2.55MM TEU in September, a record for the month, with imports from China up 21.2% year over year.
  - The Port of Los Angeles handled more than 1MM TEU, its busiest month ever.
  - Asian schedule delays are adding uncertainty to arrival dates.
- Freight Rates:
  - Rate action has hit a bit of a lull with Golden Week; expect it to pick up as the month goes along.
  - Strong import demand is expected to support Trans-Pacific rates into the new year.
  - The faster return of capacity to Suez routing could bring additional capacity to the TPEB in 2-4 months before CNY.
  - Shippers should add buffer to delivery plans and secure space for late October and November cargo-ready dates.
FAR EAST WESTBOUND (FEWB)
- Capacity and Demand:
  - Capacity is deployed in full this week, with blank sailings at 0%.
  - Blank sailings are forecast to build to 3.6% the week of October 19 and 6.6% the week of November 2, then reach 13.9% the week of November 9. Forward schedules are still being finalized and these figures can move.
  - With Asia to North Europe SCFI going up after 13 straight weeks of decreases and capacity optimization, carriers are cutting sailings to support rate increases effective October 19, rather than responding to a demand squeeze.
- Suez Canal Return:
  - Capacity is also shifting back to standard Suez Canal routing gradually. Container ship transits through Suez reached 61 in the week ending October 4, up 154% year over year.
  - Carriers are moving at different speeds, and security risks in the Red Sea remain, including cargo insurance that can be hard to secure on short notice.
  - Shorter transit times are now an option on part of the network.
  - Shippers should confirm routing and insurance terms at booking and plan for the November blank sailings by booking early for those weeks. The situation will continue to be monitored.
TRANS-ATLANTIC WESTBOUND (TAWB)
- Capacity and Demand:
  - Capacity is largely deployed in full, with blank sailings at 4.3% this week.
  - Selective blanks persist on North Europe–U.S. East Coast/Gulf loops through weeks 42–43 (approximately 10–13% cancellations). The week of October 19 peaks at 19.4% of scheduled capacity, then falls to 1% or less through mid-November.
  - To secure space and equipment — especially for inland origins or Mediterranean ports — forwarder guidance recommends booking 3-4 weeks in advance during peak months. This lead time helps ensure timely shipments, avoids rollovers, and keeps surcharges manageable.
- Operations:
  - German port strikes were averted after dockworkers accepted a new contract.
  - Low water on the Rhine is still delaying barge cargo to major gateways; shippers with inland European origins should allow extra time.
- Freight Rates:
  - Rates are holding steady into late October.
INDIAN SUBCONTINENT TO NORTH AMERICA
- Capacity and Demand:
  - Available space to the U.S. East Coast is improving as carriers have upsized capacity on the trade before Diwali.
  - Asian port congestion and low schedule reliability continue to affect departure and arrival dates on this corridor, especially for cargo transshipping through Colombo.
  - Shippers should book the added November sailings early and keep delivery buffers in place.
- North China:
  - Demand to the U.S. picked up as Golden Week ended, with general cargo and e-commerce restocking ahead of Black Friday and Christmas. Rates rose 5-10% versus the holiday week.
  - Space is tight into ORD, DFW, and ATL, with rates elevated. The U.S. West Coast is tightening more slowly.
  - China-to-U.S. tonnage grew 17% year over year in September. Rates are expected to keep rising through October.
  - Europe-bound demand is recovering gradually, with rates up mildly week over week. Mainland China-to-Europe tonnage fell 2% year over year in Sep

articles.full_text:
EU Industrial Production Falls 0.3% in August 2026 as Eurozone Output Drops 0.5%
Seasonally adjusted industrial production across the European Union declined by 0.3% in August 2026 compared with the prior month, while the eurozone recorded a 0.5% decrease, according to preliminary Eurostat data cited by GMK Center. The monthly figures show divergent performances among Member States, with Sweden posting the strongest gain at 6.5%, followed by Estonia at 4.3% and the Netherlands at 2.6%. The steepest monthly contractions occurred in Belgium, which fell 5.1%, Ireland at 3.1% and Portugal at 2%.
On an annual basis, industrial production in the EU slipped 0.2% in August, while the eurozone registered a 1.1% decline. Compared with August 2025, Ireland recorded the largest year-on-year drop at 15%, followed by Belgium at 7.1% and Bulgaria at 5.4%. The strongest annual increases were seen in the Netherlands at 9.8%, Hungary at 8.8% and Denmark at 8.3%.
Energy Sector Output
Energy sector output in August fell 0.6% month on month in the eurozone and 0.5% in the EU. Year on year, energy production rose 3.1% in the eurozone and 2.4% in the EU.
Monetary Policy and Forecasts
On 10 September, the European Central Bank raised its three key interest rates for the second time this year, with an increase of 25 basis points. The ECB kept its inflation forecast for this year unchanged at 3%, while revising upward its projections for 2027 and 2028 to 2.5% and 2.1% respectively compared with its June outlook. The regulator also lifted its forecast for eurozone GDP growth in 2026 to 0.9%, up from 0.8% in the June review, reflecting greater-than-expected economic resilience in the region.

articles.title: EU Opens Probe Into OpenAI, Anthropic Over AI Agents That Escaped Tests and Hacked Systems - International Business Times, Singapore Edition
articles.summary: EU Opens Probe Into OpenAI, Anthropic Over AI Agents That Escaped Tests and Hacked Systems  International Business Times, Singapore Edition
articles.full_text:
The European Union is investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over AI agents that autonomously hacked outside organizations, opening a major test of whether the EU's AI Act can regulate rogue models that escape controlled testing environments and affect real-world systems.
The investigations come as governments, lawmakers and legal experts grapple with who should be held responsible when AI agents take unauthorized actions without direct human instructions.
The European Commission's AI Office has launched inquiries into incidents involving OpenAI and Anthropic after both companies disclosed cases in which AI agents gained unauthorized access to external systems.
The incidents occurred over the summer, and the Commission sought additional information after determining that documents voluntarily provided by the companies were insufficient.
EU Tests Limits of AI Act After Rogue Agents Escape
EU digital chief Henna Virkkunen said the Commission has begun enforcing the bloc's AI rules and is seeking information on security, external evaluations and monitoring of how AI models are used.
"Our AI Office has started enforcing these rules, and sent requests for information addressing issues such as security, external evaluation and monitoring how models are used," Commission Executive Vice-President for Technological Sovereignty Henna Virkkunen said at the International AI Summit in Dublin.
One investigation concerns an OpenAI agent that escaped its testing environment and hacked AI platform Hugging Face. Another involves an Anthropic model that gained unauthorized access to three outside organizations.
Because Hugging Face operates globally and serves customers in the EU, the Commission argues that the OpenAI incident had an impact on the European market.
The legal question is complicated by the AI Act's research and development exemption. Legal experts argue that because the incidents occurred during testing, before the models were placed on the EU market, the law may not apply.
"The AI Act very clearly doesn't apply to the development and testing activity. It never envisaged the problems we are now seeing with rogue agent escapes during testing. It's a bit of a stretch to say that an agent was put into service if it escapes its testing environment during development," Barry Scannell, a partner at William Fry, told Euronews.
A Commission official offered a different interpretation, saying the AI Act could become enforceable when a model escapes testing and affects the EU market.
AI Hacks Raise Questions About War, Criminal Liability
The broader incidents are also raising concerns far beyond regulatory compliance. Forbes reported that an experimental OpenAI agent, during a June 18 research task, accessed an Australian government Medicare statistics service, obtained internal files and credentials and read source code.
OpenAI said it had not authorized the actions and that no patient records were accessed. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the agent "didn't accept 'no' for an answer".
Reports also warn that a future AI agent could potentially target critical infrastructure, creating difficult questions about whether an attack constitutes an act of war and whom a government should retaliate against if the agent's origins are deliberately disguised.
Attackers using AI agents were also reported to have compromised 85 Taiwanese government accounts and reached at least seven energy companies. "The investigation found clear indications that the attacks originated overseas and involved a hybrid approach in which hackers combined conventional operations with AI agents such as OpenClaw," said Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs.
Meanwhile, it was also reported that existing criminal laws may struggle to address autonomous AI hacking because anti-hacking statutes generally require proof of human intent. The Hugging Face incident has prompted a lawsuit by the Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology, while experts argue traditional liability could still apply to developers, users and operators.
"We haven't created a new problem here. In other words, it's still analogous — from the perspective of the law — to a tool," University of Pittsburgh professor David Thaw said.
"And just like with any tool, the traditional theories of liability can apply to the person who purchased it and is the user, the manufacturer might potentially be liable, and then anybody involved as an operator," he added.
The EU's investigations could therefore establish an important precedent for how governments regulate AI agents that act beyond their intended boundaries and determine whether companies can be held responsible when their systems cross those lines.

articles.title: Nigeria’s Cocoa Exports Face EU Compliance Risk as Deforestation Rules Tighten - Investors King
articles.summary: Nigeria’s Cocoa Exports Face EU Compliance Risk as Deforestation Rules Tighten  Investors King
articles.full_text:
Nigeria’s cocoa export industry faces growing uncertainty ahead of new European Union deforestation requirements with the Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) warning that more than half of the country’s cocoa production could struggle to meet the documentation standards required to access the European market.
The warning raises concerns about Nigeria’s agricultural export earnings, particularly as cocoa remains one of the country’s most important sources of non-oil foreign exchange.
LCCI President Leye Kupoluyi disclosed the concern during the chamber’s fourth-quarter economic briefing in Lagos, citing industry estimates that more than 50% of Nigerian cocoa beans may not currently satisfy the traceability requirements under the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR).
The regulation is scheduled to apply from December 30, 2026, for large and medium-sized operators, while most micro and small operators have until June 30, 2027.
For Nigeria, the immediate challenge is ensuring that cocoa exporters can provide verifiable information about where their products originate and demonstrate that production complies with the EU’s environmental requirements.
The regulation requires companies placing covered commodities on the European market to establish that they were not produced on land deforested after December 31, 2020.
It also requires compliance with relevant laws in the producing country and supporting due diligence documentation.
These obligations create additional responsibilities for exporters purchasing cocoa from numerous smallholder farmers whose produce may pass through several intermediaries before reaching international buyers.
In many cases, cocoa from different farms is aggregated during purchasing, storage and transportation, making it difficult to connect individual export consignments to the specific plots where the beans were harvested.
Under the new requirements, such gaps in traceability could prevent European buyers from completing the necessary compliance checks, even where the cocoa itself was produced legally and without recent deforestation.
The commercial implications are significant.
According to figures cited by the LCCI, Nigeria generated N596.9 billion from cocoa exports in the first quarter of 2026, representing approximately 51% of the country’s agricultural export earnings during the period.
The scale of those receipts highlights the importance of preserving access to international markets at a time when Nigeria is seeking to increase non-oil exports and diversify foreign exchange earnings.
The Nigerian Export Promotion Council (NEPC) has also warned that the country could lose more than $1 billion in annual export earnings if affected exporters fail to meet the EU’s requirements.
The estimate represents a potential exposure rather than an actual loss, and the outcome will depend on how quickly exporters and producers improve compliance.
The NEPC identified cocoa as particularly vulnerable because of the importance of European buyers to Nigeria’s export market.
At an industry seminar in Lagos, the council disclosed that only about half of an estimated 350,000 smallholder cocoa plots had been geolocated.
This suggests that substantial work remains in identifying farms, collecting accurate geographic coordinates and connecting production records to the cocoa eventually shipped abroad.
For exporters, meeting the requirements could involve additional spending on farm mapping, digital recordkeeping, farmer registration, supply-chain monitoring and independent verification.
Larger exporters may be better positioned to finance these systems, while smaller operators could face difficulties absorbing the costs.
Smallholder farmers may also encounter challenges where they lack formal land records, reliable digital access or the technical support required to document their production activities.
These constraints could affect the ability of exporters to purchase cocoa from certain communities, potentially creating differences in market access between farmers whose production can be verified and those whose records remain incomplete.
However, the LCCI’s warning does not mean that more than half of Nigerian cocoa has already been rejected by European buyers.
It also does not establish that the affected cocoa was produced through deforestation.
The concern is that insufficient documentation could make otherwise eligible cocoa difficult to sell into a market with increasingly strict verification requirements.
The distinction matters because the industry’s immediate response must address both environmental compliance and the systems needed to demonstrate it.
The LCCI has called for coordinated intervention involving the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security, the NEPC and cocoa-producing state governments.
Its recommendations include accelerated mapping of cocoa farms and the development of a national traceability platform capable of connecting farmer identities, farm locations and commodity movements.
Such a system could reduce the burden on individual exporters by making verified production information more accessible across the supply chain.
Nevertheless, its effectiveness would depend on accurate data collection, regular updates and compatibility with the information required by European importers.
The European Commission has introduced measures intended to simplify aspects of the regulation and improve the digital systems used for submitting compliance information.
These adjustments have not removed cocoa from the commodities covered by the law.
For Nigeria, the approaching deadline presents both a regulatory challenge and an opportunity to modernise agricultural export infrastructure.
Reliable farm records and traceability systems could strengthen relationships with international buyers, improve supply-chain transparency and support access to markets that increasingly demand evidence of sustainable production.
Failure to close the existing documentation gaps, however, could expose exporters to shipment delays, additional compliance expenses and the possible loss of European contracts.
With cocoa accounting for a substantial share of Nigeria’s agricultural export earnings, the industry’s ability to meet the new requirements will be an important test of the country’s readiness to compete in international markets where environmental compliance is becoming a condition of trade.

articles.title: The Houthis are Europe’s problem - The Telegraph
articles.summary: The Houthis are Europe’s problem  The TelegraphWhat do the Houthis want?  Financial TimesHow the Houthis are helping Iran turn Saudi Arabia into a pressure point  ReutersIran cultivated Houthis for years before opening new war front, Yemeni insider says  Iran InternationalWhy not deal with the Houthis instead of fighting them?  アラブニュース
articles.full_text:
The level of sophistication demonstrated by the latest Houthi missile attacks against Saudi Arabia does not just signal a serious upgrade in the military capabilities of an organisation once regarded as a rag-tag terrorist group. It begs the question of why the West is not doing more to support its Saudi allies. The Houthi attacks threaten to cause even greater disruption to global energy supplies, with all the implications that could have for already hard-pressed Western economies – including the UK.
The latest Houthi attacks on the Saudis represent a major escalation in the threat they pose to regional stability. In the decade or so since the Iranian-backed Houthi rebels provoked Yemen’s disastrous civil war by attacking the country’s democratically elected government, the Houthis tended to rely more on basic weaponry, such as rocket-propelled grenades and the ubiquitous Soviet-era AK-47 assault rifles. That is now very much no longer the case.
Fourteen people have so far been killed in the Houthi missile strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, which succeeded despite the Saudis’ sophisticated anti-missile defences. The headquarters of the Saudi state oil giant Aramco in the eastern city of Dhahran were also hit. Several further Houthi missile strikes were intercepted, the Saudis confirmed.
The Houthis claim they launched the attacks in retaliation for what they call “brutal Saudi aggression” in western Yemen, where the Kingdom’s forces are fighting to reclaim territory recently captured by the terrorists in their bid to seize control of the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which is the southern entrance to the Red Sea. But the Saudis, together with their Gulf allies, are under no illusions that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is behind the attacks as they seek to increase their stranglehold over global energy supplies.
Having succeeded in causing severe disruption to the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf, which in normal times carries around one fifth of the world’s energy needs, the IRGC believes it can increase the pressure on global economies if it can use its Houthi allies to simultaneously disrupt shipping heading for the Suez Canal.
There is no doubt that the IRGC is deeply involved in supporting the Houthi attacks. Missile fragments recovered by the Saudis from previous Houthi attacks have carried unmistakable Iranian markings. Yet, rather than scrambling to support their Saudi allies, Western leaders appear strangely reluctant to provide Riyadh with effective military backing, an oversight that seems all the more unfathomable given that the upsurge in Houthi attacks is ultimately as disruptive for the West as the Saudis.
Donald Trump’s preoccupation with next month’s midterm elections means that he is unlikely to approve any meaningful military response to the Houthis’ aggression, despite reprimanding the group for “behaving very badly”. Nor are there any indications that other Western leaders are willing to come to the Saudis’ aid.
Andy Burnham was happy to utter his predictable platitudes in the Commons earlier this week, declaring that “we will continue to stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis”. But that support amounts to little more than the temporary loan of a single air refuelling tanker, as well as some air defence assistance.
Other European countries are similarly proving reluctant to deploy military assets, with only the Netherlands and Belgium responding to appeals from Brussels to strengthen the EU’s Red Sea Naval mission. This force still does not have enough warships to fulfil its stated mission objective of safeguarding the Bab el-Mandeb.
The West’s underwhelming response bears little comparison to the robust action mounted in 2024, when the Houthis first attempted to disrupt merchant shipping in the Red Sea, claiming they were acting in support of Hamas terrorists in Gaza. While the US deployed a naval battlegroup, the UK dispatched a destroyer and launched air strikes against Houthi positions from the UK’s Akrotiri base in Cyprus.
The Israelis too, proved to be effective allies in that campaign, regularly launching airstrikes against Houthi positions. After Ed Miliband’s pointless diplomatic spat with the Israelis over imposing sanctions against Israeli settlements, any future UK cooperation with Israel on tackling the Houthis is out of the question.
The West’s reluctance to provide the Saudis with tangible support is short-sighted, especially for the European leaders who need to understand that the Houthis’ decision to escalate their attacks against the kingdom is as much a problem for Europe as it is the Saudis themselves.
With European countries – including the UK – already anticipating an energy crisis this winter, the prospect of rising bills and power shortages will become ever greater the longer the Houthis and their Iranian-backers are allowed to implement their plan to disrupt global shipping.
Burnham and his fellow European leaders need to understand that, by failing to confront foes who threaten their countries’ interests, they are demonstrating a level of weakness that their enemies will be only too eager to exploit.

articles.title: Trump waives US sanctions, tariffs on Russian oil & gas - what it means for India - The Times of India
articles.summary: Trump waives US sanctions, tariffs on Russian oil & gas - what it means for India  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
In what is being seen as a big relief for India and China, US President Donald Trump has waived sanctions, restrictions and duties provided for under the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, citing the national interest of the United States.
The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 gave Trump the authority to impose broad sanctions on Russia and levy steep tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India.
The legislation, principally backed in Congress by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, provided for tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on goods entering the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas. It also covered countries that knowingly purchased Russian oil or gas 30 days after the law's enactment, as well as those among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.
Also Read | 
The return of Middle East oil: Has Iran lost control of Strait of Hormuz & why are crude prices still up?
What Trump announced
Trump announced the waiver just days before several provisions of the legislation were due to take effect. He had signed the bill into law in mid-September.
“I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act,” Trump said in an executive order issued on Friday evening.
In the order, Trump said he had submitted a certification to Congress stating that granting the waiver at this stage was in the US national interest.
The executive order comes as Trump has adopted a warmer stance towards Russia while publicly criticising Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. He has even suggested that Ukraine needs a new leader.
The proposed Russia sanctions had also raised concerns among countries that rely heavily on Russian oil imports. India, one of the largest buyers of Russian crude, was among the countries that expressed concerns about the legislation.
What it means for India
Russia continues to be the single largest supplier of oil for India. A waiver of tariffs of up to 100% which may have come into place in the coming days means that India can continue importing oil in large numbers from Moscow without any economic fallout.
If 100% tariffs had been imposed by the Trump administration, then it would have hit exporters as the US is the largest trading partner for India. At the same time, any sanctions may have rendered Russian crude economically unviable which would have added to the supply crunch at a time when Middle East tensions continue.
The Middle East is a big supplier of energy needs for India - crude oil, LPG and LNG. Shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have been hit, leading India to diversify its energy basket more aggressively.
Russian oil has played a big role in India’s crude oil imports at this time, with numbers hitting record highs a few months ago.
In fact, Russia gradually became India’s largest crude supplier since the start of Moscow’s war with Ukraine, when European sanctions prompted Russia to sell oil to India and China at deep discounts.
Last year, Donald Trump imposed 25% penal tariffs on India for its crude oil purchases from Russia, taking the total tariff figure to 50%. India did not stop buying crude from Russia, but after the US imposed sanctions on two Russian oil majors, the imports started coming down.
In February this year, announcing while lowering tariffs on India to 18% and removing the 25% penal tariffs, Trump claimed that India would stop buying oil from Russia. India never made any such statement, and before a clear trend on its crude purchases from Russia could emerge, the Middle East conflict erupted.
In between, the US waived sanctions on Russian crude to lower global crude oil prices, but even with those waivers lapsing, India continued to procure from Russia to meet its energy needs.
The Trump administration’s move to sign the sanctions bill last month was also hinted to have been weighing on the India-US trade deal talks. With sanctions now being waived off, some movement may also be seen on that front, especially with Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal recently hinting that a draft is almost ready.
Competing for oil with China
But even as the threat of tariffs related to Russian oil recedes, India may still have to compete aggressively with China for crude from Moscow.
Indian refiners expect Russian crude supplies to become even tighter in October and November as exports decline and competition from China intensifies, reports suggest.
Also Read | 
Beijing’s billion-barrel weapon: Why India must prepare for China-driven oil prices
The shortfall is likely to push the world's third-largest crude importer towards more expensive alternatives for the remainder of the year.
In recent months, China, the world's largest crude importer, has increased its purchases as the Iran war disrupted supplies from the Middle East.
"Demand from China has been really high. They were willing to book cargoes in advance and to pay firmer prices compared to Indian refiners," a source involved in the sale of Russian crude told Reuters recently.
Though Kpler data from October suggests that oil supplies are recovering and for now are averaging above 2 million barrels per day.

articles.title: Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC - BBC
articles.summary: Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC  BBC
articles.full_text:
Italy's defence minister has said it is a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks.
In a BBC interview, Guido Crosetto warned that any such move by US President Donald Trump's administration "makes absolutely no sense" and risked prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to bring peace.
US officials have said Trump has not asked for the slowdown of internet speeds the US provides to Ukraine and which are vital for its war effort. Trump has also denied that the US has stopped sharing early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks with Ukraine.
Crosetto's comments continue Italy's sharpening criticism of the US.
Earlier this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia a "very risky choice", and said it would "grant Russia legitimacy" as it bombed cities in Ukraine.
Trump agreed the deal with Vladimir Putin, blaming Kyiv's own attacks on Russian refineries for rising fuel prices.
Meloni, once considered so close to the US president she was dubbed a "Trump whisperer", said the move ran counter to efforts to bring Putin to the negotiating table.
"Peace will come when Putin is convinced there is a stalemate, that he cannot advance any further," her defence minister told the BBC at his ministry building in Rome.
Crosetto was a co-founder of Meloni's hard-right Fratelli d'Italia party, which has led a right-wing government coalition since 2022, shortly after the start of Russia's full-scale war.
"If [Putin] sees weakness on the Ukrainian side – and if the US deprives Ukraine of resources, that creates weakness – then he will believe he can win. So he will continue the war," Crosetto warned.
"I think that is completely wrong."
Despite widespread public scepticism, Meloni's Italian government has been a strong ally of Ukraine from the start, sending both military and humanitarian aid.
The specifics of those deliveries have always been classified.
In our interview, the defence minister vowed that Italian military support would continue "for as long as this government is in place", though he warned that getting parliament to approve further deliveries would be "more difficult" as elections approached.
The vote has to take place by the end of 2027 and opinion polls currently put a new far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, ahead of all Meloni's coalition partners.
That party's leader, former general Roberto Vannacci, is openly sympathetic to Russia and opposes aiding Ukraine, arguing that Europe is wasting its money as Russia's military "continues to advance" on the ground.
At a recent event in Tuscany, he described himself as "neither pro-Putin nor pro-Russian" but "pro-Italian".
Crosetto brushed off questions about Vannacci, including on whether his views reflected those of many Italians, saying he had more "serious matters to deal with".
But, perhaps to underline the difference, he was unequivocal on Russia.
"When one state crosses another state's border with tanks, when it bombs hospitals and schools, kills civilians and bombs power plants, and has been doing so for four years, I can only describe that as evil," he said.
But Italians, like many Europeans, are seeing prices go up, driven by the high cost of energy.
During street protests in Rome on Friday, where firecrackers were thrown, secondary school students complained that resources were being diverted to arms, instead of education.
Some chanted: "We want more classroom, not more bombs."
In southern Italy, truckers have begun blocking roads complaining at the hike in fuel prices.
Polls here regularly show that a majority of Italians want an end to military aid for Ukraine. One, conducted for the Ixè institute in September, put support for continuing to supply arms at just 18%.
There are many factors behind that, from a long-standing pacifist tradition to a history of strong business ties to Moscow. Unlike Poland or the Baltic states, Italy feels physically distant from the danger, too.
But the defence minister also blamed an active campaign of disinformation by Moscow – targeting, he said, "certain political figures... and narratives to weaken the political climate against Russia".
"In some way they shift public opinion," the minister argued.
"It's very hard to explain to a citizen who's having trouble at the petrol pump that we can't give any concessions to Russia right now. But that's the only way to defend the future of that very citizen who's complaining."
Italy has not been targeted for major acts of sabotage, unlike other allies of Ukraine in Europe.
The minister said a fire at an arms depot outside Rome in August was not arson, but "human stupidity".
A report last month that Russia was planning to launch drone attacks at Italy, France and Spain from the container ships in the Mediterranean was not proven, Crosetto also told us.
But cyber-attacks, which he linked to Russia, were now routine - "there are hundreds every day" - and he believed Europe had been too weak in its response.
"You can't win a war... if you don't fight back," the minister said.
With additional reporting from Rome by Davide Ghiglione.

articles.title: Rich make millions by flipping private jets - Financial Times
articles.summary: Rich make millions by flipping private jets  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Rich people are making millions of dollars by reselling desirable models of private jets shortly after they receive them, in the latest sign of the boom in the industry.
Strong demand for private air travel, combined with production delays driven by supply chain constraints, has boosted prices and led to original buyers flipping the jets as soon as they arrive, industry experts said.
“Anyone taking delivery of a new heavy jet is likely to find a ready resale market,” said Oliver Tebbit, a partner in the aerospace team at law firm HFW.
“We are aware people are selling jets once they have taken delivery,” said one industry executive familiar with the situation. “Demand is very strong and it’s most apparent in the secondary market.”
The AI boom has helped drive demand in the private jet market, as a new class of super-wealthy people who have made money in the tech sector emerges. At the same time, companies are grappling with industry-wide logistical issues including a shortage of castings and forgings and labour.
As a result, order backlogs at the large business jet manufacturers have grown faster than the companies are able to build aeroplanes.
Tebbit said that someone ordering a jet today might have to wait until 2029 or 2030 for delivery, driving customers into the second-hand market. A new Gulfstream G700, which charter experts said typically costs about $80mn before customisation, could be sold at an uplift of 10 per cent, he said.
Barbara Pansadoro, a partner at Addleshaw Goddard, said: “Depending on the model, on the type of aircraft, the price can go quite high, it could be several million” above the original purchase price.
Industry figures say another reason behind the boom in private jet demand is US President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed into law in 2025.
Pansadoro said the “bonus depreciation” element of the act, which allows a company to offset the entire cost of the aircraft against its tax bill in the first year of ownership, had spurred demand.
Previously, original buyers had flipped their purchase agreements before delivery to other buyers for a profit, but manufacturers had clamped down on this, said Mike Francis, head of aviation finance at Citi, “because it affected their ability to have control over pricing in the market”. Now, original buyers — both individuals and companies — tended to sell the aeroplane on or soon after delivery, he said.
One adviser said a public company had ordered a private jet three years ago for $77mn and sold it, when it was delivered six months ago, for $84mn. The aeroplane is now being offered off-market in the mid-$90mns, they added.
Contracts can vary depending on the individual customer. Standard contracts, said the industry executive, usually contain a clause prohibiting a buyer from selling a plane until it has been delivered.
Buyers who opt to turn a chunky profit on what is normally a depreciating asset are turning instead to private aviation businesses such as NetJets, which offer fractional ownership or a guaranteed number of flying hours, advisers said.
“If you have a chance to make 10mn bucks but [are] putting zero effort into it, why wouldn’t you?” said Francis.
General Dynamics, the US defence group which owns Gulfstream, and Bombardier, the owner of Challenger jets, declined to comment.
