articles.title: Miracle on the Vistula 2.0: How Poland became an economic powerhouse shaking up Europe - i24NEWS
articles.summary: Miracle on the Vistula 2.0: How Poland became an economic powerhouse shaking up Europe  i24NEWS
articles.full_text:
- International
- Europe
- Miracle on the Vistula 2.0: How Poland became an economic powerhouse
Miracle on the Vistula 2.0: How Poland became an economic powerhouse
Market reforms and EU membership have helped Poland build a trillion-dollar economy, but an aging population, coal dependence and rising defense spending put future growth to the test
Poland’s GDP crossed the $1 trillion mark this year, placing it alongside Western Europe’s wealthy nations. Its success offers a lesson in managing the transition from central planning to a thriving free market.
When the Berlin Wall fell and the Iron Curtain lifted over Eastern Europe in 1989, they revealed battered, impoverished countries. Poland was a country of endless bread lines, rampant inflation and gray apartment blocks that bore witness to decades of failed central planning. Few imagined that, within three and a half decades, it would become a European success story and one of the world’s most dynamic economies.
This year, Poland reached a major milestone: its gross domestic product surpassed $1 trillion for the first time. That makes it the world’s 21st-largest economy, close to wealthy Switzerland, and fundamentally changes the balance of power within the European Union. Poland is no longer the “poor neighbor to the east,” but an economic engine whose voice carries weight in Brussels, Berlin and Paris. The journey was far from easy. This is how Poland went from Europe’s backyard to an important and growing economic center at the continent’s heart.
**The shock therapy that transformed the country**
Modern Poland’s story began with a bold gamble. While other post-communist countries hesitated and pursued gradual reforms, Poland chose “shock therapy.” In 1990, then-Finance Minister Leszek Balcerowicz introduced a radical program of rapid price liberalization, large-scale privatization and a full opening of the economy to foreign trade.
The initial pain was considerable. Unemployment soared, outdated state-owned factories closed and inflation eroded household incomes. Yet that fiscal discipline laid the foundations for what we see today: a competitive market economy built on private enterprise. Poland was the first country in the former communist bloc to return to growth, in 1992, and has scarcely looked back since. Polish society’s ability to absorb the initial disruption became a strategic advantage, allowing the country to build modern legal and banking systems well ahead of its neighbors.
**The European engine and the German connection**
Poland’s accession to the European Union in 2004 gave fresh momentum to an economy already on the move. For Poland, the EU offered more than grants: it provided market access and an opportunity to join global supply chains.
Over the past two decades, Poland has become a production base for German industry. Its integration into the German economy began with cheap labor, as Polish workers moved to Germany to take manufacturing jobs. Over time, Poland became more than a source of workers. Many German companies relocated factories there, primarily to reduce production costs. Today, Polish factories produce everything from cars and spare parts to household appliances and processed food.
Warsaw made effective use of the billions of euros it received from EU cohesion funds, amounting to €161 billion in each budget cycle, to build highways, railways and digital infrastructure that rival those of Western Europe.
In 2024, following a period of political friction with Brussels, around €137 billion in additional recovery funds was unlocked. That money is now intended to finance the next task: the transition to green energy and comprehensive digitalization, ensuring Poland remains competitive in a low-carbon economy.
**Europe’s “green island”**
One of the Polish economy’s most striking characteristics is its resilience. In 2008, as the global financial crisis shook the world, Poland was the only EU country to avoid recession, earning it the nickname the “green island.”
The explanation lies in a combination of a large domestic market, with around 38 million consumers sustaining demand, and an independent currency, the zloty, which provides monetary flexibility unavailable to eurozone countries. Today’s Poland is more than an exporter. It is a vibrant consumer economy with a growing middle class that drives growth even when conditions abroad are difficult.
Poland has also succeeded in reinventing its image. Once seen as a source of manual labor, it is now a global hub for information technology services, advanced logistics, and research and development. Cities such as Warsaw, Wrocław and Kraków host development centers for international technology giants drawn by the country’s skilled, educated workforce.
Poland also hopes to strengthen its standing within the EU through an ambitious transport project in the center of the country. The plan would connect a new airport with high-speed rail, roads and logistics networks, reinforcing Poland’s role as a gateway between Western and Eastern Europe.
**Geopolitics as an economic catalyst**
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 changed Europe’s economic dynamics as well as its security landscape. Poland went from a peripheral transit route to a critical logistical and strategic hub. That position is attracting major investment in defense industries and energy infrastructure as Europe seeks to end its dependence on Russia.
As the EU’s center of gravity shifts eastward, Poland is demanding, and securing, a more prominent seat at the decision-making table, particularly given its position on the eastern flank of both the EU and NATO. It no longer simply implements rules set in Paris. It helps shape policy on security, EU enlargement and border protection.
**The challenges ahead: Can growth continue?**
Despite the celebrations over the trillion-dollar milestone, Poland’s path to lasting prosperity is lined with obstacles. The first is demographic: like much of Europe, Poland is aging. Its workforce is shrinking, threatening labor shortages and mounting pressure on pension and health care systems.
Poland’s restrictive immigration policies do little to ease the looming demographic crisis. To sustain growth, it will need to move from an economy built on efficient production to one driven by breakthrough innovation, a task requiring substantial investment in education and research.
The second challenge is energy. Poland remains heavily dependent on coal, making its energy supply polluting and expensive under the EU’s stringent climate regulations. The transition to nuclear power and renewable energy is an enormous infrastructure undertaking that will cost billions and require years of political stability.
Finally, there is the fiscal challenge. Poland has significantly increased defense spending, now around 4% of GDP, while maintaining generous social programs. The government deficit is expected to reach 6.5% of GDP in 2026, forcing Warsaw to strike a delicate balance between security and fiscal responsibility in the near future.
Poland’s achievement over the past 36 years has been nothing short of remarkable. From a country on the brink of bankruptcy and collective despair, it has become a force that cannot be ignored. Crossing the trillion-dollar threshold provides definitive confirmation that its transformation is complete.
The next chapter in Poland’s story will be its most demanding. Poland is no longer chasing the West; it must begin to lead it. If it can overcome its demographic and energy challenges, a decade from now it may be regarded as more than an economic success story: it could become one of the central pillars of 21st-century Europe.

articles.title: FX Summary: Warsh Drags DXY to 101.65, BoE Hike Bets Rise - FinanceFeeds
articles.summary: FX Summary: Warsh Drags DXY to 101.65, BoE Hike Bets Rise  FinanceFeeds
articles.full_text:
Fed Chair Warsh’s non-committal stance weakened the US Dollar, boosted foreign currencies, and left inflation and rate expectations in focus.
Fed Chair Warsh Adopts a Non-Committal Stance and Shifts Away From Forward Guidance
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh signaled a notable shift in communication strategy during his remarks in Bangkok, stating explicitly that he does not prejudge upcoming meetings and emphasizing that the Fed is actively moving away from previewing its policy decisions. By offering no explicit forward guidance on the future trajectory of interest rates, Warsh’s non-committal commentary immediately impacted market sentiment. Consequently, market pricing for a potential rate hike at the October 27–28 meeting plummeted from roughly 28% down to about 15% or 16%, though a December rate increase remained heavily priced in near 90%. This dovish-by-omission approach introduced immediate selling pressure on the greenback, driving the Dollar Index (DXY) down toward 101.65—its lowest level since October 1—as it headed toward its first weekly decline in five weeks.
Divergent Global Central Bank Expectations and Currency Responses
The shift in US monetary policy expectations rippled across global foreign exchange markets, amplifying divergences between major central banks. In the United Kingdom, resilient economic data and subdued signs of second-round inflation drove a Reuters survey to show that 54 of 63 economists expect the Bank of England (BoE) to implement a 25-basis-point rate hike in November. This hawkish outlook pushed the British Pound (GBP/USD) above 1.3350, registering gains of over 0.61%. Simultaneously, modest narrowing in front-end Eurozone-US yield spreads, catalyzed by Warsh’s remarks, provided upward momentum for the Euro (EUR/USD) and positioned the currency for a potential bullish weekly reversal. Broadly speaking, Warsh welcomed a synchronized global tightening cycle with no free riders, allowing key interest rate differentials—such as the gap between US rates and the European Central Bank’s 2.5% rate—to remain stable.
Persistent Inflation Risks, Geopolitical Pressures, and Cautious Safe-Haven Sentiment
Underpinning these currency and interest rate movements are stubborn macroeconomic and geopolitical headwinds. Hotter-than-expected US Consumer Price Index (CPI) readings and a stronger-than-forecast 0.7% expansion in September industrial production underscore that underlying price pressures remain sticky and above the Fed’s 2% target. These domestic inflation risks are further aggravated by elevated Middle East supply concerns, highlighted by deadlocked US-Iran negotiations and escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis. Meanwhile, concerns over debt-funded AI investments triggered a sharp flight to safety, pulling the benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield below 5.10% and supporting safe-haven assets. Despite lower yields and a softer US dollar, gold (XAU/USD) struggled to secure a robust recovery, trading below $4,200 as market participants continuously weighed safe-haven demand against the lingering prospect of future Fed tightening.

articles.title: EUR/USD Price Forecast — Euro Rises as U.S. Yields Fall From 5.33% — 1.1350 Target Above 1.1293 - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: EUR/USD Price Forecast — Euro Rises as U.S. Yields Fall From 5.33% — 1.1350 Target Above 1.1293  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- EUR/USD rose 0.34% to 1.1259, up 146 pips from its 1.1113 low as the 10-year Treasury yield fell to 5.09%.
- Eurozone inflation was confirmed at 3.8% in September, the highest since 2023, with energy prices up 18.9%.
- The French OAT-Bund spread sits at 135.2 basis points, after briefly topping 150 basis points on October 2.
EUR/USD is trading at 1.1259, up 38 pips, or 0.34%, on the day. Friday’s range runs from 1.1212 to 1.1273. The pair opened at 1.1222, just above Thursday’s close of 1.1221. The session high of 1.1273 is the strongest level since the start of October.
This is the second day of a sharp rebound. On Wednesday, October 14, EUR/USD fell to 1.1113, its lowest level in 17 months, after the U.S. September CPI report pushed Treasury yields higher and drove the dollar index to an 18-month high near 103. Since then, the pair has gained 160 pips at the high, or 1.44%, and is now 146 pips above the low.
The pair is on track for its first weekly gain in more than a month. Over five sessions, EUR/USD is up 0.48%. That ends a stretch in which the euro fell for five straight weeks through October 9 and lost 2% from late September.
The longer-term numbers are still weak. EUR/USD is down 2.42% over a month, 4.66% over six months, 4.16% year to date and 3.33% over 12 months. The 52-week range is 1.1114 to 1.2024. At 1.1259 the pair is 1.3% above the 52-week low and 6.4% below the 52-week high.
The move is mainly a dollar story. The dollar index is down 0.35% at 101.69, after testing 101.80 earlier in the morning. GBP/USD is up 0.69% to 1.3366, outperforming the euro. EUR/GBP has dropped 0.34% to 0.8421. AUD/USD is up 0.52% to 0.6959, and USD/JPY has slipped to 157.79. The dollar is weaker against every major currency, and the euro is gaining less than sterling or the Australian dollar.
That relative weakness is the central point of this forecast. The euro is rising because the dollar is falling, not because investors are buying euro-area assets. French sovereign risk, an ECB that is reluctant to commit to more hikes, and an energy shock hitting Europe harder than the U.S. are all holding the euro back.
The level that matters now is 1.1293, the 21-day moving average. EUR/USD has not closed above that line since early October. Friday’s 1.1273 high stalled 20 pips short of it. The 20-day exponential moving average sits close by at 1.1287. These two averages form the first real ceiling for the rebound.
The setup is clear: a rebound off a 17-month low driven by U.S. yields, now testing short-term resistance, with European risks still in place. The next sections lay out what could push EUR/USD through 1.1293 and what could send it back toward 1.1113.
U.S. Yields Drove the Bounce: 10-Year From 5.33% to 5.09%
U.S. Treasury yields are the main driver of EUR/USD this week. Higher U.S. yields pull money into dollar assets, and lower yields push it back out. The euro’s slide to 1.1113 and its recovery since then track the 10-year yield closely.
After Wednesday’s CPI report, the 10-year Treasury yield jumped to 5.33%. September consumer prices rose 0.6% in the month and 3.7% over 12 months, above the 3.6% forecast. Core CPI rose 0.3%, against a 0.2% forecast. Markets raised the odds of another Fed rate hike, and the dollar hit an 18-month high. That was the day EUR/USD fell to 1.1113.
The reversal came Thursday. The September producer price index rose 1.3% month over month and 6.3% year over year, but yields fell anyway. Investors moved into Treasuries as AI-related debt fears spread through equity and credit markets. CoreWeave’s 2031 bonds yielded 15.78% on more than $50 billion of debt, and the selloff in AI-linked stocks pushed money into government bonds. The 10-year yield fell 10 basis points to 5.09%, a three-week low.
On Friday the 10-year is at 5.09%, after touching 5.125% following today’s data. September U.S. import prices rose 1.1% for the month, above the 0.8% forecast, and are up 8.1% over a year. Export prices jumped 2.2%, against a 1.0% forecast, and are up 11.6% over a year. Industrial production rose 0.7%, above the 0.4% forecast, and capacity utilization reached 76.9%, against a 76.5% forecast. The data is hot, but yields barely moved. The bond market has absorbed the inflation news for now.
The yield gap between the U.S. and Germany shows why EUR/USD remains under pressure. The German 10-year Bund yields 3.39%. With the U.S. 10-year at 5.09%, the spread is 170 basis points in favor of the dollar. As long as that gap stays this wide, investors earn significantly more holding dollar assets, and the euro struggles to rally far.
Short-term rates tell the same story. The Fed’s target range is 3.75% to 4.00% after its September hike. The ECB’s deposit rate is 2.50%. That leaves a gap of 125 to 150 basis points at the policy-rate level.
The key point for the forecast is that EUR/USD now depends on whether U.S. yields keep falling. A move in the 10-year toward 5.00% would give the euro more room to rise. A return toward 5.20% to 5.33% would send the pair back toward its lows. The euro has little ability to rally on its own while U.S. rates remain this high.
Warsh’s Neutral Stance Removed the Fed Premium
The Federal Reserve’s tone on Friday was the second reason for the dollar’s slide. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh appeared at a fireside chat with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva at the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok. He gave no signal on the October decision.
Warsh said economic conditions since the September meeting had “broadly conformed to our expectations.” On the October meeting, he said: “I don’t prejudge meetings.” On forward guidance, he went further: “We’re not in that business anymore.”
Markets had been bracing for a hawkish message after the hot CPI and PPI reports. Warsh did not provide one. The dollar index fell to its lowest level in almost two weeks, and EUR/USD climbed toward 1.1250 in the European morning. Markets now price an 85% probability that the Fed will leave rates unchanged on October 28.
That marks a sharp shift from Wednesday. The CPI data had roughly doubled bets on an October hike. After PPI, Warsh’s comments and Thursday’s yield drop, those bets have largely disappeared. Other Fed officials had already pointed toward a hold. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson, New York Fed President John Williams and Governor Christopher Waller all signaled patience. Waller noted that rate increases do not have to come at consecutive meetings.
Warsh’s remarks came just before the Fed’s pre-meeting blackout period. No more official guidance will come before the decision on October 28. That leaves markets reacting to data and yields for the next 12 days.
The Fed’s hold expectation helps EUR/USD in the short run, but it does not change the larger picture. The Fed raised rates in September, its first hike since 2023, and December remains a live option. With inflation at 3.7% on CPI and 6.3% on PPI, the risk of a December hike keeps a floor under the dollar.
Warsh also called the AI investment boom “probably the most important thing that’s happening in the global economy on the upside.” He has linked part of the rise in long-term yields to large technology firms competing for capital. That matters for EUR/USD. If AI firms keep borrowing heavily, U.S. yields stay elevated and support the dollar. If AI credit stress pushes money into Treasuries, as it did Thursday, yields fall and the euro benefits.
The market is now pricing a Fed on hold through October. That removed the dollar’s short-term premium and gave EUR/USD room to bounce. The next move depends on whether the Fed signals a December hike and whether European risks ease or worsen.
Eurozone Inflation Confirmed at 3.8%: The Highest Since September 2023
Final eurozone inflation data released Friday confirmed the energy shock hitting Europe. Annual HICP inflation was 3.8% in September, up from 3.2% in August and matching the flash estimate published on October 2. It is the highest rate since September 2023. A year earlier, in September 2025, eurozone inflation stood at 2.2%.
Month over month, prices rose 0.6%. Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, rose to 2.5% from 2.4%. Energy prices jumped 18.9% year over year, the largest increase of any component. Food, alcohol and tobacco inflation rose to 1.3% from 1.1%.
Energy contributed 1.71 percentage points to the annual inflation rate. Services added 1.52 points. Industrial goods excluding energy added 0.29 points, and food, alcohol and tobacco added 0.25 points.
The country breakdown shows how widespread the increase is. Germany’s rate rose to 3.3% from 2.9%. France climbed to 3.4% from 2.6%. Italy jumped to 4.2% from 3.2%. Spain reached 5.0% from 4.6%. The Netherlands rose to 3.0% from 2.8%. Greece hit 5.1%, 1.3 points above the eurozone average. Inflation rose in 23 EU member states, held steady in three and fell only in Slovakia.
For EUR/USD, the inflation data creates a policy dilemma. Inflation at 3.8% is far above the ECB’s 2% target and argues for more rate hikes. But the shock is driven by energy, which Europe imports. Higher energy prices act as a tax on European consumers and businesses. They push inflation up while slowing growth. That combination makes the ECB cautious about raising rates too far.
The U.S. faces a smaller version of the same shock. U.S. CPI is at 3.7%, close to the eurozone’s 3.8%. But the U.S. is a net energy exporter. Higher oil prices boost U.S. producers’ income and export values, as today’s 11.6% annual rise in export prices shows. Europe pays the higher bill. That difference in exposure is one reason the dollar has outperformed the euro since the Middle East conflict escalated.
Brent crude is at $105.36, down 56 cents, and WTI is at $95.63, down 87 cents. The International Energy Agency is releasing the last 100 million barrels from its March emergency agreement. The U.S. is considering easing sanctions on shadow-fleet tanker

articles.title: French police accused over war-like injuries to teenagers in school protests | France - The Guardian
articles.summary: French police accused over war-like injuries to teenagers in school protests | France  The GuardianAre student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?  BBCFrance’s student uprising and young people’s mental health – what are the common causes?  The ConversationYellow Vests and high school students rally online ahead of October 17 protest  Le Monde.frFrance to witness a 'crossroads of anger' as mass protests expected on Saturday ...
articles.full_text:
French lawyers and rights groups have said that several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons used during school protests, and an unprecedented number of children have been held in police custody, some of whom reported being hit or racially insulted.
France is in the fourth week of its biggest youth protest movement in decades, during which hundreds of high schools across the country have been blockaded as students demand the replacement of absent teachers and repairs to decrepit buildings.
Police have opened internal investigations into 36 allegations of officer violence against demonstrators, including four children allegedly being “mutilated” by explosive weapons, and six sustaining “significant injuries”, as well as other complaints over physical blows, insults or alleged sexual assault, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, told the senate.
Evan, a 15-year-old studying carpentry at a vocational high school, had a hand blown off in the explosion of a police stun grenade outside a school protest in Lens, northern France, on 5 October. His lawyer, Bertrand Wattez, said: “His injuries resemble war injuries.”
Wattez said Evan had gone to school to attend class and discovered a protest under way. He said Evan had not taken part in violence and denied the Béthune state prosecutor’s assertion that the grenade had been picked up from the ground. When the grenade exploded, Evan lost his left hand, several fingers from his right hand and suffered injuries to other parts of his body. He remained in hospital “in a very difficult condition” and his family had filed a criminal complaint, Wattez said.
Another boy, Eden, 14 – who had been near a school protest in Saint-Ouen-l’Aumône, north-west of Paris – suffered extensive facial injuries, including two fractures to his jaw, the loss of his bottom teeth and all his top teeth broken after he was allegedly hit by a shot from a grenade launcher.
His lawyer, Elsa Marcel, said the shot from a grenade launcher was fired at close range, from a distance of 1.5 metres. “This is the equivalent of war weaponry,” she said. The family has filed a legal complaint for attempted murder.
Eden’s parents said he had gone to school but found it blockaded and had wanted to go home. Video footage appeared to show him facing three riot police officers. One officer hit out in his direction with a truncheon and Eden kicked in the direction of the police before a grenade shot was fired. An officer has been suspended and placed under official investigation.
This week, a police officer in the western city of Tours was charged with aggravated battery after Maël, a 16-year-old at a vocational high school, lost the use of his eye allegedly after a shot from a form of rubber-bullet launcher. The officer denies the charges. The family’s lawyer said Maël had not been involved in any violent confrontation with police but had simply been present at a school protest, and that the family felt a sense of “injustice”.
For several years, France has faced scrutiny over police use of explosive weapons, particularly after serious injuries were reported during the 2018-2019 gilets jaunes (yellow vests) street demonstrations, including allegations that people had lost eyes and had their hands and feet mutilated.
The current wave of protests has also led to lawyers raising concerns that an unprecedented number of children have been arrested and placed in police custody, with some lawyers reporting that teenagers said they were hit, humiliated or verbally abused during arrests.
Since the school protests began in mid-September, a total of 6,773 under-18s have been taken into police custody after they were arrested, the justice ministry said. For more than 1,000 of those children, no charges were brought; 2,190 are facing legal action and almost 2,000 were handed an alternative to further legal action, such as a citizenship course, without their case being heard at trial and without a conviction.
Lawyers said accusations against children included gathering with violent intent, violence against police and damage to property.
Nathalie Tehio, a lawyer and the president of the French Human Rights League, said the fact that only a minority of children’s cases would end up before a judge raised concerns that arrests could be unfounded. She said: “There are a record number of arrests … Often, the legal dossiers are empty. In reality, this is more about stopping people from demonstrating. I think there is a sense of hitting hard to try to dissuade people and scare them.”
Tehio said: “We have received accounts of racist comments made. Lawyers have told us that their clients say they have been humiliated or treated violently or pushed.”
Romain Boulet, a co-president of France’s Association of Criminal Lawyers, said: “Criminal lawyers are worried and raising concerns about the potential misuse of police powers to dissuade citizens aged under 18 from demonstrating.”
Mohamed Jaite, the president of the Paris branch of the leftwing union Syndicat des Avocats de France, has represented several teenagers stopped in Paris and its suburbs. “I have seen one youth limping in a police station,” he said. “Some have reported being humiliated or receiving racist and sexist insults.”
Prisca Ancion, a lawyer from the leftwing lawyers’ group Collectif d’Action Judiciaire, which demonstrated this week in front of a high school in Saint-Denis, in the northern suburbs of Paris, said: “There have been racist insults during arrests, as well as homophobic, sexist comments or sexual touching. We encourage families to file complaints.”
Another lawyer from the collective, Romane Bartoli, who assisted several teenagers after their arrest, said: “Youngsters told us they were slapped, kicked or punched.”
One 16-year-old from a high school in a suburb north of Paris described being arrested 100 metres from his school on the day of a blockade in late September. He plans to study medicine at university and said he had intended to go to class before he saw there was a protest.
Answering questions from the Guardian with his lawyer, he said he had been held in police custody for more than 12 hours, mostly with two others in a police cell with two mattresses.
“It was hard psychologically because I felt I hadn’t done anything wrong,” he said. “I was hit with a truncheon and punched.”
He said a police officer told him to “shut his mouth” and said: “It’s always you lot,” which he understood to be a racist insult. He was released after a state prosecutor instructed him to carry out a citizenship course as an alternative to facing legal action.
The justice ministry and the interior ministry, which oversees policing, did not comment on allegations of insults or violence in police custody.
In parliament, Nuñez denied any form of excessive policing or police repression. He suspended the use of stun grenades at school demonstrations.
Audrey Bailleul, a magistrate and national representative of the Union Syndicale des Magistrats, said it was hard to have a clear view of events at this stage. She said: “There is nothing to show that there has voluntarily been a massive intention to not respect [legal] procedure.”

articles.title: Bus driver's farts were so bad colleague 'needed to take a shower' - Metro.co.uk
articles.summary: Bus driver's farts were so bad colleague 'needed to take a shower'  Metro.co.ukBus driver 'farted so badly' it led to sacking as colleagues 'needed a shower'  Daily Star'Flatulent' bus driver loses discrimination case after colleague complains of smell  The IndependentFoot On The Gas: UK Bus Driver Fired For Cutting Rancid Farts  BroBibleSacked bus driver 'farted so badly' colleague 'washed uniform and needed shower'  LADbible
articles.full_text:
A bus driver tried to sue her employer after being accused of a fart that smelt so foul it meant a colleague had to wash her uniform.
Stephanie Bryan was behind the wheel for electric bus company The Big Lemon when she allegedly produced ‘significant flatulence’.
An ‘episode’ ensued, a tribunal heard, with co-worker Samantha Bingham noticing the lingering odour when she started her shift and sat in the same seat, concluding that Ms Bryan had soiled herself.
Upon returning home, Ms Bingham’s partner also sensed a nasty stench and asked if she had defecated.
Ms Bingham then felt compelled to wash her uniform and ‘immediately’ take a shower to remove the smell.
When her colleague confronted her, Ms Bryan said in her defence, ‘Everyone needs to fart and let out gases.’
The tribunal heard that Ms Bryan reacted ‘negatively’ to the accusations and displayed ‘personal hostility’, despite Ms Bingham being ‘genuinely and reasonably concerned by the situation she found herself in’.
Ms Bingham reported the matter to her line manager, with personal hygiene concerns raised during Ms Bryan’s employment review, which was conducted ‘sensitively and appropriately in private’.
Ultimately, Ms Bryan was dismissed. She was on a three-month probation from September 2024, extended to January 2025 due to ‘concerns regarding her performance’, but she failed.
Consequently, she took legal action against the bus operator for disability discrimination and harassment.
She argued her employer had discriminated against her for having bladder issues.
However, the Bristol Employment Tribunal rejected her claims.
An employment judge ruled that Ms Bryan’s complaints were not related to her health.
It was also found that Ms Bryan did not inform The Big Lemon bosses of her depression or borderline personality disorder diagnoses, nor her existing bladder weakness.
As such, management had no idea these could contribute to hygiene problems.
Judge Jonathan Walters said: ‘The odour was consistent with faecal matter potentially caused by significant flatulence which had led to soiling and was not associated with urine or urinary incontinence.’
It was ruled that Ms Bingham had raised ‘a genuine workplace concern’, and there was ‘absolutely no evidence before the tribunal that [she] had any knowledge of the claimed disabilities nor ought she reasonably to have known about them’.
‘The actions of [Ms Bingham] were unrelated to disability and were not motivated by disability,’ said Judge Walters.
‘She had attempted to address [her concerns] with [Ms Bryan], whose reaction was not conducive to resolution, and, therefore, she had no option but to raise the matter with management, as the situation which occurred was indeed detrimental both to her and to the business itself.’
He added: ‘The tribunal does not find that the dismissal arose because of any consequence of [Ms Bryan’s] depression, borderline personality disorder or bladder weakness.’
Instead, she was fired because of her poor driving standards, which led to her failing to ‘satisfactorily complete her probationary period’.
The Big Lemon said in a statement: ‘We do not comment on individual members of staff but would like to thank Ms Bingham for her professionalism throughout this case, and thanks are also due to Judge Walters for the consideration he gave to what was quite a sensitive situation.’

articles.title: '‘It’s easier dealing with Trump than Putin,’ Zelenskyy tells Euronews amid US tensions - Euronews
articles.summary: '‘It’s easier dealing with Trump than Putin,’ Zelenskyy tells Euronews amid US tensions  EuronewsZelensky: My people are dying after Trump’s Starlink betrayal  The TimesThe new unequivocal Zelenskyy  Financial TimesZelensky’s despair as Trump turns towards Russia  The IndependentZelenskyy on Trump saying Putin is easier to negotiate with: I find him easier than Putin  Українська правда
articles.full_text:
After a week of tensions between Washington and Kyiv, Zelenskyy said Trump was still easier to deal with than Putin, despite the US president’s calls for new leadership in Ukraine and criticism of the Ukrainian leader.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has rejected Donald Trump's claim that he is more difficult to deal with than Vladimir Putin, telling Euronews that negotiating with the US president is easier than dealing with the Russian leader.
Speaking to Euronews on Friday at an EU summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy was asked about Trump's criticism and whether European leaders supported Ukraine's continued strikes on Russian oil refineries despite pressure from Washington to halt them.
"Well, it's easier dealing with him than with Putin. I'm talking about Trump," Zelenskyy said.
"I've had several meetings with the President of the United States of America, and we always find topics for discussion and decision-making."
The remarks come amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington over Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil infrastructure and Trump's decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel. The US president has criticised the strikes, blaming them for contributing to rising global fuel prices.
Zelenskyy said his priority was to defend Ukraine's national interests, regardless of external pressure.
"I defend the interests of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people exclusively. We were attacked, occupied, and our people were killed. It is only logical that we have the right to defend ourselves," he said.
"This is entirely lawful, and so we will do just that. We will stand firm."
He did not directly address whether European leaders had backed further strikes on Russian refineries, instead reiterating Ukraine's right to defend itself.
Zelenskyy accuses Putin of blocking peace efforts
The Ukrainian president said Ukraine remained committed to ending the war through negotiations but accused Putin of having no genuine interest in a peace agreement.
"Putin does not want negotiations right now, in any format," he said, describing Moscow's rhetoric as "a parody of a genuine desire to end the war".
"He does not want the war to end. I am convinced that this is why even the Donbas is too small for him."
Zelenskyy warns against easing sanctions on Russia
Zelenskyy also warned that easing restrictions on Russian diesel could lead to further concessions, undermining Western efforts to limit Moscow's ability to finance its war against Ukraine.
"In my view, we cannot accept these diesel deals, these agreements, because gas deals will follow. I am absolutely certain of this. After gas, sanctions will be lifted on other things as well," he said.
"It will all come down to the banking system, individuals, and the chemical industry."
He also voiced concern over the future of frozen Russian assets, suggesting they could be at risk if Western countries continued to make concessions to Moscow.
"If I do not defend this, who will do it for us? I mean diplomatically," Zelenskyy said.
European leaders have meanwhile sought to maintain pressure on Moscow despite Washington's decision to ease some sanctions.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Friday that the EU would not lift its sanctions until Russia ended the war. European Council President António Costa called for increased pressure on Moscow rather than further concessions.

articles.title: Could Tesla’s flying car send sales and shares soaring? - Euronews
articles.summary: Could Tesla’s flying car send sales and shares soaring?  EuronewsElon Musk reveals ‘world’s first flying car’ at Tesla event  The GuardianTesla's new Roadster turns in air with SpaceX thrusters, won't land until 2028  ReutersThe Tesla Roadster has finally landed: thrusters, 0-60mph in 0.59s… and *flight*  Top GearOf course the new Tesla Roadster can fly  PistonHeads
articles.full_text:
Tesla revealed its next-generation Roadster on Thursday in Texas, with one of the three new versions performing a jaw-dropping kickflip and demonstrating flying capabilities. However, analysts contacted by Euronews Business do not expect the model to generate significant revenue.
Elon Musk, Tesla’s CEO and co-founder of SpaceX, recreated a “Knight Rider” moment, showing off his companies’ engineering capabilities with a supercar equipped with cold-gas thrusters developed using SpaceX technology.
Tesla's share price increased on Friday, largely due to the hype, but while the demonstration impressed, analysts see limited commercial value in the new model.
Mamta Valechha, consumer discretionary analyst at Quilter Cheviot, described it as a “headline-grabbing engineering moment” designed “to generate excitement around the brand”.
Rico Luman, senior sector economist, transport and logistics, at ING, called the presentation “a publicity stunt which emphasises Tesla’s image as an innovative company, which offers brand value”, adding that cars are still about emotion and lifestyle, so the demonstration makes an impression.
Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, called the demonstration on X “an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers”.
Valechha noted that even Elon Musk had previously played down the Roadster’s likely financial impact. “The commercial value is likely to be strengthening Tesla's innovation narrative rather than generating meaningful profits.”
Musk said production is expected to start in 2028. Tesla has opened reservations, although the flying Rocket version is available by invitation only. The company has not announced final selling prices.
The Roadster was unveiled in 2017, and a year later Musk suggested that thrusters might allow it to fly. This was followed by repeated delays, as the production was originally promised for 2020. "Credibility and execution risks remain high,” summarised Valechha.
Could flying cars reach a wider market?
The flying features of the Roadster are not approved for public road use, adding another hurdle to any ambitions of a wider roll out of the technology, on top of the high production costs.
Luman said the flying car has been designed as a niche sports vehicle, but “larger scale flying car activity won’t be realistic in the foreseeable future as the same airspace rules apply as for aircraft and certification as aircraft by EASA (in Europe) is then required”.
Whether the Roadster falls within aviation regulations depends on its design, capabilities and intended operation, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) told Euronews Business.
The agency said it does not comment on “specific certification applications or activities involving individual manufacturers”.
However, “any vehicle intended to operate as an aircraft would need to meet the applicable aviation safety requirements”, the agency said. These could include pilot qualifications for the driver.
Luman added that, on top of the complex rules that apply, airspace is already rather full, particularly with increasing drone activity.
“Large numbers of uncontrolled flying cars won’t likely be allowed by authorities for safety reasons.”
Valechha also sees limits to how widely the technology could be used.
“Some technologies could filter into other vehicles over time, but flying or thruster-assisted features are unlikely to be economically viable for higher-volume cars in the foreseeable future due to cost, complexity and regulatory hurdles.”
Luman agreed, adding that some space technology could be useful in high-end cars.
“Flying cars in general may be a cheaper alternative for private jets, but not in this concept”.
Pressure to turn technology into profits
Like many big tech companies, Tesla is growing, but faces pressure to turn expensive technology projects into stronger profits.
The company is investing heavily in new technology, while profit growth is failing to keep pace with sales.
Second-quarter revenue rose 26% year on year to $28.24bn (€25.20bn), but net profit attributable to shareholders fell about 5% to $1.11bn (€990m).
First-half capital spending more than doubled to $8.28bn (€7.39bn). Tesla expects capital spending above $25bn (€22.31bn) in 2026, driven by AI and manufacturing investments.
Investors have been pricing the company's value gradually lower than at the beginning of the year, when Tesla shares traded at $438, whereas on Thursday they cost more than $362, amounting to a 14.6% fall in 2026 so far.
Other analysts also mentioned that Tesla valuation is largely based on its self-driving ambitions, the Optimus model, and SpaceX merger hopes.
Merging SpaceX and Tesla?
The technology in Tesla's Roadster, borrowed from SpaceX, fuelled expectations that the two companies are going to be merged in the future.
Barclays analyst Dan Levy has suggested an announcement could come before Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting, according to Barron’s. However, a deal remains speculative, with no certainty about whether or when it would happen.
For now, the Roadster’s clearest appeal may be to wealthy enthusiasts.
“This new futuristic model is great for fans and lovers of gadgets who have the ability to spend the money on it. And I’m sure there are quite some around,” added Luman.

articles.title: Germany's “Invest in Germany” Summit: Chips, AI and Deep Tech - Freshfields
articles.summary: Germany's “Invest in Germany” Summit: Chips, AI and Deep Tech  Freshfields
articles.full_text:
Following our first post, in which we introduced the Invest in Germany Summit in mid-October 2026 and its seven thematic deep dives, we now take on the two sessions at the Summit next week (20 October) framing the government's technology agenda: Industrial AI & Semiconductors, hosted by Federal Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy, Katherina Reiche, as well as Innovation, Deep tech & Space, hosted by Federal Minister of Research, Technology and Space, Dorothee Bär. They are a natural pair: Both rest on the same policy foundation, and both have quietly become as much about economic and national security as about growth.
One agenda behind two sessions
Industrial AI, chips, quantum computing, biotech and space cover a broad spectrum of – not always directly connected – topics. In the German government, they are promoted in one joint strategy: the Hightech Agenda Deutschland, adopted by the cabinet in July 2025 with around EUR 18 billion earmarked until 2029. Rather than spreading money thinly, the government has selected six key technologies, ranging from AI to quantum technologies and climate-neutral energy generation.
That choice matters for investors. The government is focusing on specific fields it believes Germany can lead in, and it is prepared to co-invest to prove it. The coalition agreement of spring 2025 already pointed the way: support for at least one European AI Gigafactory on German soil, two quantum computers at European top level by 2030, and a stronger national space programme.
Industrial AI and semiconductors
The two deep dives at the Invest in Germany Summit are where those promises to turn into pitches to investors. There is a lot to talk about: Since the coalition agreement early last year, the follow-through has been steady. The government adopted a Microelectronics Strategy in October 2025, followed by a National Data Centre Strategy in March 2026, which aims to double overall data centre capacity and quadruple AI and high-performance computing capacity by 2030. In July 2026, it also submitted 14 projects under the IPCEI for Advanced Semiconductor Technologies, backed by up to EUR 3.8 billion in combined federal and state funding.
Deeptech and space: closing the growth-capital gap
Germany has a strong research base in deep technology, but access to later-stage financing remains a challenge in several fields. As companies scale, their capital requirements can rise substantially. But large growth rounds are frequently led by non-European investors, and some companies relocate or list abroad as they scale, making it more difficult to retain investment and growth in Germany.
The space sector faces similar conditions, including high technical risks, long development cycles and significant funding needs, while public procurement is becoming an increasingly relevant source of demand.
The government's answer combines public co-investment with dedicated funding instruments. The Zukunftsfonds, with around EUR 10 billion in public capital, includes a EUR 1 billion DeepTech & Climate Fund. Alongside it, the WIN initiative aims to mobilise roughly EUR 12 billion in private venture capital by 2030.
On space, Germany's first-ever Space Security Strategy (November 2025) commits around EUR 35 billion to military space capabilities by 2030. At the November 2025 ministerial conference of the European Space Agency, Germany pledged EUR 5.4 billion and is its largest contributor. And it has now moved to close one notable gap: a draft bill for a national space law (Weltraumgesetz) has been circulated at ministerial level. The draft would give companies a domestic framework for licensing, registration, supervision and liability, including a cap on recourse claims against operators. Industry associations have nonetheless warned of added red tape and legal uncertainty, and the national rules will have to fit with the EU's own Space Act, which is still being negotiated in Brussels.
Where the two stories meet: economic security
Taken together, the two sessions suggest that technology policy is increasingly being considered alongside economic and national security concerns in Berlin. Recent developments have highlighted the importance of resilient semiconductor supply chains for German industry, including for established legacy components. Similar considerations apply to AI and space, where secure access to key technologies, infrastructure and service providers is increasingly shaping policy discussions. The government’s approach therefore places greater emphasis on strengthening European capabilities, safeguarding digital sovereignty and diversifying supply relationships.
The two sessions illustrate how Germany’s proposition to investors is evolving. The offer is no longer based solely on research excellence or the size of its industrial base. It increasingly combines public co-investment, procurement, infrastructure policy and a clearer focus on strategically important technologies. This may entail additional regulatory considerations, particularly in dual-use and critical sectors (see ourblogpost on the draft Investment Screening Actin Germany) but it also reflects the government’s intention to provide more active support to technologies considered important for future competitiveness.
The timing is no coincidence. With the economy only slowly emerging from stagnation, the government is using the fiscal room created by the 2025 reform of the debt brake, including the EUR 500 billion infrastructure special budget and higher defence budgets, to back strategic technologies with public money and procurement. Investors will look for accessible funding instruments, faster administrative procedures, regulatory certainty and a reliable pipeline of projects. Germany does not yet have all these elements in place, and some initiatives remain at an early stage. Nevertheless, the direction of travel is becoming clear.

articles.title: UK Defence Secretary Warns of Funding Gap Amid Escalating Russian Threat - https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.summary: UK Defence Secretary Warns of Funding Gap Amid Escalating Russian Threat  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Defence Secretary John Healey is facing mounting pressure to urgently divert spending from across Whitehall to plug a £4.7 billion shortfall in the government’s Defence Investment Plan, as military insiders warn that "the gloves are now off" regarding Russia's hostile activity against the UK.
With the Chancellor preparing to deliver the Budget on 28 October, the armed forces are demanding a significant injection of capital to fund critical next-generation drones and missile systems. However, the proposed funding maneuvers have sparked concerns about the sustainability of domestic public services and the long-term viability of the UK’s commitment to NATO spending targets.
The £4.7 Billion Black Hole
The Defence Investment Plan, originally touted as a comprehensive roadmap to modernize the British military, has been marred by a persistent £4.7 billion funding gap. According to defence analysts and former military ministers, this shortfall was inherited by the current administration and left unaddressed in previous fiscal projections. The gap threatens to delay or cancel several high-profile procurement programs, including upgrades to the Royal Navy's fleet and the acquisition of advanced air defence systems. Military insiders argue that the current geopolitical climate, characterized by escalating Russian aggression and hybrid warfare tactics across Europe, renders the existing budget wholly inadequate. The Ministry of Defence has been instructed to identify "efficiency savings" in areas such as infrastructure and workforce management, but experts warn that such measures cannot bridge a multi-billion-pound deficit without compromising operational readiness.
The Demand for Drones and Missiles
At the heart of the military’s urgent request is the need to rapidly scale up the UK’s stockpiles of loitering munitions, long-range precision missiles, and autonomous drone swarms. The conflict in Ukraine has fundamentally altered modern warfare, demonstrating that mass-produced, relatively low-cost unmanned systems can neutralize heavily armored traditional assets. The British Army and Royal Air Force are seeking funds to accelerate the procurement of systems like the Sky Sabre air defence network and new variants of loitering munitions capable of striking targets deep behind enemy lines. Furthermore, there is a pressing need to replenish the stockpiles of Storm Shadow cruise missiles and Brimstone anti-armor missiles, which have been depleted through international aid commitments. Without immediate capital investment, the UK risks falling behind its European allies in the emerging drone arms race. The integration of artificial intelligence into these systems is also a priority, requiring substantial investment in software development and secure data links. Defence experts note that the UK’s current industrial capacity is strained, necessitating long-term contract guarantees to encourage private sector investment in manufacturing facilities.
Political Fallout and Budgetary Raids
To address the £4.7 billion gap, the Chancellor is reportedly considering raiding capital budgets from other government departments, a move that has alarmed ministers overseeing health, education, and local government. The political risk for the ruling party is significant; diverting funds from domestic priorities to fund defence could alienate core voters who are already feeling the squeeze of the cost-of-living crisis. Moreover, the government has deferred its commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP until after a comprehensive spending review next spring. This delay has drawn criticism from NATO allies and opposition defence spokespersons, who argue that the UK is failing to meet its obligations as a leading European military power. The upcoming Budget will be a critical test of the government's ability to balance fiscal responsibility with the imperatives of national security.
Secondary Domestic Pressures
While defence spending dominates the political agenda, the government is also grappling with complex domestic regulatory challenges. Reports indicate that boiler manufacturers could face significantly increased targets for selling heat pumps by 2030, even as ministers consider scaling back the grants that help households afford the transition to green energy. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has reportedly been asked to identify hundreds of millions in savings within the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, potentially impacting the Boiler Upgrade Scheme. Simultaneously, the government is navigating the legal and diplomatic fallout from international incidents, including the sentencing of a British man in Cyprus following the tragic death of his son. These intersecting pressures highlight the immense difficulty of managing a sprawling domestic agenda while simultaneously responding to an increasingly volatile global security environment.

articles.title: Irish farmers need clarity on EU deforestation rules - Agriland
articles.summary: Irish farmers need clarity on EU deforestation rules  Agriland
articles.full_text:
TDs and senators have this week raised concerns around EU deforestation rules.
The Oireachtas Joint Committee on Agriculture and Food held a meeting for pre-legislative scrutiny of the general scheme of the Deforestation and Forest Degradation Bill 2026.
The main purpose of the bill is to give effect to the EU Deforestation Regulation in Ireland by providing for its regulatory and enforcement requirements, particularly its specified penalties.
'Complex'
Senator Victor Boyhan raised how "complex" the regulation is, saying "if there was ever a need for simplification - this is one".
He added: "We need to prepare the stakeholders for this huge piece of bureaucracy".
He asked for clearer guidance for farmers on what the EU law will mean for them.
Damien Flynn, assistant secretary general in the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, outlined the key timeline of the EU Deforestation Regulation's implementation.
"The EU Deforestation Regulation aims to minimise the EU's contribution to deforestation and forest degradation worldwide," Flynn said.
The regulation will take effect from December 30, 2026.
It requires these commodities and products may only be placed or made available on the EU market, or exported, if:
They are deforestation-free,
Have been produced in accordance with the relevant legislation of the country of production;
Are covered by a due diligence statement or a simplified declaration.
Flynn continued: "However, for individual operators or micro or small enterprises, established by December 31, 2024, the regulation will take not effect until June 30, 2027.
"However, this exception does not extend to timber products already covered by the EU Timber Regulation, for which the date remains December 30, 2026."
Amendment
He said the regulation has been amended since it was adopted in 2023.
"The most significant amendment for Ireland was agreed in December 2025," he said.
"It deferred application by a further year, from December 2025 to December 2026, and introduced a simplified regime for small primary producers, such as farmers and forest owners, in countries classified as low risk.
"In May, the commission completed the simplification review that the amendment required.
"This review did not propose any change to the regulation, and the application dates are unchanged."
Low risk category
In July, the European Commission adopted a delegated actadjusting the list of products covered and an implementing act on the EU information system.
Ireland, like all EU member states, is classified in the low risk category, Flynn said.
"This means Irish farmers and forest owners who are individuals or micro or small enterprises, and who place their own produce on the market or export it, will not need to submit due diligencestatements," he said.
"Instead, they will submit a single, one-time simplified declaration.
"Where all of the required information is already held in a database that exists under EU or national law, the producer does not need to submit the declaration, and the member state makes the information available in the EU information system instead."

articles.title: Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed - The Guardian
articles.summary: Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed  The GuardianCrew searching for Amelia Earhart plane lands at remote island infested with carnivorous crabs  BBCRare 1938 Nikumaroro Island Aerial Photos Released as Amelia Earhart Search Escalates  cristinaiglesias.comEarhart expedition update: Underwater survey of Taraia Object begins  Purdue UniversityGiant Crabs Complicate New Amelia Earhart Search  Explorersweb...
articles.full_text:
A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.
The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues.
While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and had released the full set of 47 images in digital high-resolution format on its website.
The negatives were found more than a decade ago by Matthew O’Sullivan, the keeper of photographs at the museum in Christchurch.
Earhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” in his blog, saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations.
What happened to Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan when they disappeared on 2 July 1937 during an attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator has been a stop-and-start search over eight decades, filled with false leads.
A leading theory is that the aviator, who broke several records including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.
The hypothesis is that she survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating fish and turtles, based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and artefacts, including glass from a jar that is thought to have contained cosmetic cream.
This week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, are searching a part of the island for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image. Other longtime Earhart explorers, including Gillespie, are not convinced, saying it is probably a fallen tree and not the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. The small atoll has been visited dozens of times.
In their latest update on Nikumaroro, which is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, the expedition said severe weather had hampered their metal-detecting but that they would release an update within 48 hours.
“Despite Thursday’s weather delay, the expedition remains on schedule, with two more days of field operations planned – and an update on the identification of the Taraia Object expected,” Purdue University said.
Rick Pettigrew, the expedition lead and executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute, said: “We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s patience. This is a complex scientific process. You don’t simply arrive at a site and immediately identify what’s there. We have to carefully collect the data, analyse it and reach sound conclusions.”
The New Zealand military images are some of the earliest photographic evidence of the island. There is no immediate sign of an object in the Taraia area.

articles.title: The drones and missiles the UK needs to defend itself – and the cuts to pay for them - The i Paper
articles.summary: The drones and missiles the UK needs to defend itself – and the cuts to pay for them  The i Paper
articles.full_text:
John Healey must urgently divert spending from other Whitehall departments to fund defence because “the gloves are now off” when it comes to Russia’s hostile activity, military insiders say.
The Chancellor is expected to use his Budget on 28 October to fund the £4.7bn gap in the Defence Investment Plan left by Sir Keir Starmer, and is set to raid capital budgets across the Government to find the money.
But Labour and Conservative former defence ministers and military experts say Healey needs to go further and find more money for the Armed Forces to prepare for the escalating threat from Vladimir Putin.
Shorts
Moscow’s heightened “grey-zone” activity and recent drone strikes on merchant shipping in the Black Sea in the past fortnight, killing a number of civilian crewmen, have alarmed defence industry insiders, who believe that a major hybrid warfare attack on the UK by Russia could be imminent.
It has even led to Defence Secretary Wes Streeting toughening the UK Government’s rhetoric against Russia, by labelling its grey-zone activity as “state-backed terrorism”.
But the Chancellor is likely to hold off from major decisions on funding the Armed Forces and kit until next year’s spending review, which could be as late as autumn 2027.
How the scale of the threat is growing
The messages from the UK Government’s own ministers and senior officials about the dangers posed by Moscow could not be clearer.
Streeting told the House of Commons Defence Committee this week that while the British public should be “alert but not alarmed” to the growing threat, “every single day Russia is testing us”.
And on Wednesday, UK politico-military counsellor Arron Newble warned fellow European states that the levels of spending on defence by Moscow – 44 per cent of federal budget outlays in the first half of 2026 – showed Russian “society is being reorganised around war”.
Former Labour defence secretary Lord Hutton told The i Paper that Streeting had “called it right” when describing Russia’s activities as “state-backed terrorism”.
The Kremlin’s involvement in the killing of Alexander Litvinenko with radioactive material in London in 2006 and the Salisbury poisonings of 2018 pass the “terrorist threshold”, Hutton said.
He added: “We’ve got to understand that the gloves are off, and [that] this is a very serious situation we’re facing.
“I think it would be better if we heard more from Government about the nature of these Russian threats and operations against the UK and our allies, because only then I think will the public really genuinely come to understand the seriousness of the situation and why so many people are saying now that we really have to invest significantly in our Armed Forces.”
What is needed immediately
When he stands to deliver his first Budget on 28 October, Healey is expected to outline how he will fund the £4.7bn shortfall in the Defence Investment Plan – the blueprint for boosting the UK’s military industrial base unveiled by the Starmer government in July.
Gen Sir Richard Barrons, co-author of the Strategic Defence Review, told The i Paper: “I think the die is cast for the Budget. The first challenge to overcome is making sure that the £4.7bn for the DIP that still needs to be identified has been found and allocated.
“Other than that, I think the current DIP settlement will be as good as it gets for this Budget.”
Barrons urged the Ministry of Defence to advance talks with the City and private sector about how private capital and expertise can be brought in to augment the public sector.
“This is very likely to be a much more promising way of funding defence better and sooner than trying to squeeze more public money in the short term.”
Britain has some air defence from drones and missiles, but this is not comprehensive and the only protection from ballistic missiles is from interceptors on board Type 45 Destroyers, which have to be in UK waters at the time.
The UK also has depleted ammunition stocks, with missiles being supplied to Ukraine for the past three years, and shortages of operational heavy armour. It also lacks ground-based air defence systems.
Last year’s Strategic Defence Review also said more early-warning aircraft and radar “would enable
the UK to maintain round-the-clock airborne surveillance”. 
It added that the “the uncrewed aircraft Reaper and its successor Protector have been highly successful. Protector should be enhanced with maritime surveillance.” It called for new fast jet trainers, an upgrade of RAF Brize Norton and more RAF transport aircraft.
Military insiders want the Chancellor to go further
Defence spending as a share of GDP is set to rise to 2.7 per cent next year, but the UK has to meet a Nato commitment to spend 3.5 per cent by 2035.
Healey is under pressure to pledge reaching 3 per cent by 2030 as a “waymarker” to reassure Nato allies and the defence industry – particularly because intelligence suggests Russia could launch a military strike on the alliance by the end of this decade.
It was the Chancellor himself who, when he resigned as defence secretary in June, complained that the government was not committing to the 2030 date.
His Labour predecessor Lord Hutton said the Chancellor had to go faster on ramping up defence spending.
Hutton added: “I don’t dispute it’s difficult for him. He’s in a very tight straitjacket when it comes to public spending, but how many times have we heard people say it’s the government’s number one priority?
“But somehow that never seems to translate into additional resources being available. I think there’s a very high level of concern about that. I’ve made the case that we need right now a national rearmament programme, and it should start now.
“The thing about putting the extra spending off into the spending review, that doesn’t start to change departmental budgets until 2028. That’s too late.”
The Conservatives have pledged to increase spending to 3 per cent by cutting the welfare bill – which would allocate an extra £10bn a year for defence, £1bn of which would go towards their plan for a “Britannia Shield” to protect the UK from missile attacks.
Shadow Defence Secretary James Cartlidge said: “Instead of prioritising social security over national security, Labour urgently needs to set out a clear plan to get to 3 per cent, as we have done.
“John Healey resigned as defence secretary over the need to get to 3 per cent. Now that he is Chancellor he has nowhere to hide. Instead of yet more dither and delay, he must use the Budget later this month to set out his plan for 3 per cent.”
Barrons said: “The clock for confronting Nato and therefore the UK is owned firstly by Russia and what it decides to do in and around its struggling war in Ukraine and later with China as it advances beyond everybody else in many forms of military-relevant technology.
“So the current predicament whereby the Government plans to get defence to a better, more transformed place over 10 years remains firmly at odds with a darker world which could present serious risk of confrontation and conflict much sooner, maybe even next year.
“It is becoming supremely important that the public and private sector accept that the chances of being bounced by events is now very high and very dangerous.”
What should be cut to pay for it?
The UK spends about 10.9 per cent of GDP on welfare – which includes pensions as well as benefits – or around £334bn, and military experts have long called for this budget to be cut to fund defence.
But insiders say there are other areas that could also be targeted, including capital spending across Whitehall departments and even making the case for an increase in income tax.
Former defence minister Tobias Ellwood said: “Welfare is the obvious starting point. But given it’s our economy in the crosshairs – and if hit would be far more costly in the long run, we may need to consider a 1p increase in income tax.
“Where Government is failing is explaining the scale and imminence of the threat. If the British people were better informed about what’s coming over the hill [grey-zone attacks on the UK mainland] there would be more support for limited, ring-fenced tax rises.
“[For] example, the taxpayer cost on the [cyber attack] hit to Jaguar Land Rover was over £1bn. This type of attack will increase, along with sabotage and drone attacks unless we upgrade our resilience.”
Hutton said capital spending had to be prioritised “because primarily it’s a capital problem about getting new equipment, and investing in new kit”.
He cited the case of the government’s walking and cycling strategy, which is costing the state £4.5bn over the next four years, as something that could be cut to pay for defence.
The ex-Labour minister said that this expenditure “really sticks in my throat”, adding: “I think we should stop that and transfer that money. That’s a billion pounds a year extra for the MoD straight away.
“I think welfare spending needs to come down, but I’m not in favour of doing what the Conservatives suggested, which is to just slash benefit levels. That’s absolutely looking at the problem through the wrong lens.
“We’ve got to get more people into work. We’ve got to be tougher, I think, with particularly some benefit claimants about actively seeking work. We’ve certainly got to sort out the shambles of the sickness and incapacity benefit system, which is just leeching money and actually not doing its job at all in helping people get back into work.”

articles.title: Morning Coffee: The 41-year-old ex-gas trader and the “unlimited” money. Private equity firm cuts jobs - eFinancialCareers
articles.summary: Morning Coffee: The 41-year-old ex-gas trader and the “unlimited” money. Private equity firm cuts jobs  eFinancialCareersCoreWeave Stock Wipeout Exposes Divide Between AI Fear and Greed  Bloomberg.comSizing CoreWeave’s ‘unlimited’ insurance capital  Financial TimesCoreWeave Shares Plummet 11% After Jensen Huang’s Endorsement  ForbesWhy CoreWeave is in the crosshairs of the AI scare  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Brannin McBee is a billionaire. But as of his interview with the Financial Times on Wednesday, he is probably worth less than before. McBee is among the founders of CoreWeave, the $39bn "neocloud" provider beloved of places like Jane Street. His comments to the FT came during a week when CoreWeave's stock at one point declined 28% amidst a surge in the cost of insuring against a default on the $35bn of debt that CoreWeave carries on its balance sheet alone. Following this, the WSJ noted that one of CoreWeave's bonds was trading at distressed levels.
What did McBee say exactly? Several things. Speaking to the FT while wearing trainers (sneakers), bangles and what appeared to be a Patek Philippe perpetual calendar chronograph, McBee said CoreWeave wants its debt to have an investment grade rating so that it can borrow money from insurers whose pockets are immeasurably deep. Their capital, “is unlimited. Like, that’s all the money in the world that sits in the insurance tranche,” he pondered.
This appears to have freaked out investors, who were already wondering when the borrowing might stop. The implication is maybe never.
The FT's interview with McBee also suggests that Coreweave is, at heart, a kind of project financing firm. The FT didn't quote him directly, but noted that CoreWeave is a 'financing machine.' CoreWeave owns hundreds of thousands of NVIDIA AI chips and it uses them as security for loans in so-called 'offtake' contracts, under which clients pay to rent GPU clusters that haven't been built yet. “You say, here’s an idea, and then you forward-sell contracts associated with that idea, and you use those contracts with that collateral to go finance it,” declared McBee.
While this happens, the chips sit in subsidiaries. McBee informed the FT that each dollar they earn first pays interest, principal and running costs, with the remaining 20 cents going to the parent. That parent is CoreWeave.
CoreWeave's leveraged project finance vibes have been noted before. Offtake structures are usually used to finance power plants and McBee is not afraid to point this out. McBee himself helped pioneer the method for financing GPUs, with the help of bankers at Morgan Stanley and MUFG.
McBee knows a few things about energy and power plants because before he found himself a billionaire wearing an apparent Patek Philippe watch, he was a project manager in the energy industry and a prop trader working in the energy sector. Early in his career, he completed a one year internship at McBee Oil Corp in Dallas, suggesting his family might know about the energy industry too.
What now? McBee might not be giving unfettered FT interviews in the future. CoreWeave shares recovered yesterday after Jensen Huang at NVIDIA helpfully declared “CoreWeave’s strength is improving every day.” But doubts remain over CoreWeave's debt. What happens, for example, if the NVIDIA chips become outdated and worthless by the end of the contracts? What happens if CoreWeave's customers on short term contracts decide they want to use someone else's data centres instead? What happens if CoreWeave's borrowing costs keep rising?
McBee is untroubled by these questions. Or at least he was, when he spoke to the FT. CoreWeave's debt structure is not "scary debt at all. I look at that as accelerating debt and great debt,” he said.
McBee also observed that he has no intention of riding into the sunset. “We could go off to a ranch and retire,” he told the FT of himself and his CoreWeave cofounders. “But you’re watching us show up every single day and put our time into this business.” It probably helps that the co-founders have already sold $3.3bn of CoreWeave shares and so are helpfully insulated from what happens hereafter.
Separately, private equity jobs have historically been nice steady seats leading to nice steady carried interest payments, but this is no longer so.
Carried interest is harder to get now. And at least one private equity firm is cutting jobs.
Bloomberg reports that Partners Group, a Swiss-based firm with an unfortunate array of deals cut in 2021 and 2022, has been cutting or 'reassigning' dozens of jobs in its private equity division.
In a comment to Bloomberg, Partners Group declared that the size of its private equity team, "remains consistent with its long-term average, while we have significantly strengthened our senior operational capabilities over the past year.” It also said: “This reflects a buyout environment in which creating long-term value and driving distributions require greater operational intensity.”
Operationally intense times require operationally intense hires. Junior bankers maybe less so.
Meanwhile...
CoreWeave debt is priced for a 60% chance of default in five years. (Bloomberg)
Deutsche Bank likes CoreWeave. “A confluence of factors appear to have led to a sharp selloff in CoreWeave’s public equity and debt over the past week...we struggle to find company specific factors that justify the recent move.” (Bloomberg)
Telecom bonds began cracking six months before the dot-com crash. In 2007, subprime mortgage bonds peaked eight months before the S&P 500 did. Equity investors get paid to be dreamers. Lenders get paid not to lose money. (Semafor)
Shares in Société Générale have dropped more than 20 per cent since the start of August, and BNP Paribas has tumbled 19 per cent. (FT)
The British government is preparing to increase the tax on banks from 3% to 8%. The TUC wants a 16% tax and is saying: “Britain’s big four banks are making a billion pounds a week, while bonuses have hit a post-crash record. These are bumper profits – driven by high interest rates and households’ mortgage misery. It’s time to make sure banks pay their fair share.” (Guardian)
Credit Suisse bankers lost their bid to get their bonuses back. The Swiss finance ministry cut bonuses for about 1,000 senior bankers at Credit Suisse. The executive team lost their bonuses entirely. Bonuses for managers one level below the executive board were cut 50%. while employees two levels below had their bonuses cut by 25%. The Swiss Supreme Court said this was fair. (FT)
How it is when you work in AI. 'To seduce a U.S. diplomat in Russia, a foreign espionage operation first sent a blond woman to his hotel room with Champagne. When he declined, the spies sent a redheaded woman, and then next a young man.' (WSJ)
