articles.title: Europe’s Carmakers Under Pressure from Chinese Imports - Universul.net
articles.summary: Europe’s Carmakers Under Pressure from Chinese Imports  Universul.net
articles.full_text:
Europe’s automotive industry is facing a widening gap between recovering demand and weakening manufacturing performance. New car registrations in the European Union rose 5.7% in the first half of 2026. Despite this, production edged lower and the bloc’s passenger-car trade surplus shrank by more than a third as imports accelerated, especially from China.
Meanwhile, exports lost ground, according to ACEA’s October Economic and Market Report. Romania’s production fell the most in percentage terms among all European countries, etoro analyst for Romania, Bogdan Maioreanu writes.
Right now, stronger car sales in Europe are not translating into higher output at European factories. Imports, particularly from China, are capturing a growing share of demand, while manufacturers face weaker overseas sales, rising costs and a deteriorating economic outlook. EU passenger-car registrations reached almost 5.9 million units in the first six months of 2026. ACEA attributes the recovery to demand incentives, competitive pricing and a broader offering of electrified vehicles. Italy recorded growth of 9.5%, Poland 9.4%, Spain 6.2% and Germany 5.8%, while France returned to modest growth of 1.8%. This improvement contrasted with a weaker global market. Worldwide car registrations fell 4.9% to 35.7 million units, largely reflecting a 23.2% contraction in China and declining demand in the United States, Middle East and Africa. South America moved in the opposite direction, with registrations rising 16.9%, driven primarily by Brazil.

articles.title: Trump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Trump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters  Al JazeeraExclusive: US considering using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran, sources say  CNNTrump says US may need to strike Iran's Pickaxe Mountain  ReutersWashington eyeing MOAB deployment against Iran's underground nuclear facilities  Fox NewsTrump's 'Mother Of All Bombs' Threat Would Miss Iran's Buried Nuclear Sites  Bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
United States President Donald Trump has for the first time explicitly ruled out the use of a nuclear weapon against Iran, but has not denied US media reports that his administration is considering deploying the US’s most lethal non-nuclear munition, nicknamed the “mother of all bombs” in the near future.
In an interview published on Thursday by right-wing American news site Newsmax, Trump suggested he does not plan to use nuclear weapons, but also clarified that the devastating aerial weapon, the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB – ‘mother of all bombs ) “is not nuclear”.
“I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he told Newsmax.
The comments marked Trump’s first definitive statement on the nuclear topic following speculation about a possible atomic conflict earlier in the US and Israel’s war on Iran. They also appeared to confirm speculation that another phase of the war is imminent, likely after the US midterm elections on November 3.
Here’s what we know:
What did Trump say?
Trump told Newsmax that the US might indeed launch another strike on Iran’s nuclear sites, particularly on Pickaxe Mountain, where Tehran is believed to be hiding a nuclear facility deep under layers of granite.
He ruled out using a nuclear weapon or a tactical nuclear weapon.
“I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he said.
He also clarified that the MOAB, which CNN reported the US government is considering using, “is not nuclear”.
Responding to a question about whether the MOAB is “tactical nuclear” – meaning smaller nuclear munitions – Trump reiterated that it is not.
“Well, the mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” Trump said. “It’s not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb.”
Trump declined to say whether he had authorised its use in Iran.
Trump also suggested renewed attacks are likely in the near future. The US cannot end the war now because it has to ensure Iran cannot produce a nuclear weapon, he argued, saying he believes that “if they had it, they would use it, in my opinion, instantaneously”.
Trump also reiterated that the war would end “very soon” whether by force or diplomacy and that oil prices would then drop.
When asked if he would put “troops on the ground”, Trump said: “No, I don’t see that, I don’t see it.” Earlier in the war, Trump had made comments regarding sending in troops, a move analysts said would be devastating for US soldiers because of Iran’s mountainous territory.
What is the ‘mother of all bombs’?
The MOAB carries a massive payload of about 8,500kg (18,000 pounds or 8.5 tonnes) of high explosives. It weighs 9,800kg (21,605 pounds or nearly 10 tonnes) – about the same as four cars – and is just over nine metres (about 30 feet) long. Stealth bombers are too small to carry it, so it has to be deployed by larger, Lockheed C-130 Hercules transporters.
It is designed to explode a few metres above the ground, sending out intense fireballs that can blast buildings and other hard-surface structures within a 1km radius, experts have told Al Jazeera. It is so powerful that a mushroom cloud from its blast has been seen 32km (20 miles) away in tests, the US Air Force has said.
“Its large explosive charge can produce devastating blast effects against exposed personnel, equipment and vulnerable structures,” Brussels-based military and weapons analyst Elijah Magnier said. “Its purpose is to generate an exceptionally powerful blast across a surface area.”
However, Magnier said there is doubt about whether using the massive surface explosive would be effective against deeply buried nuclear installations in Iran. He added that the terrain in Iran could be difficult for larger cargo aircraft to access.
What has Trump previously said about nuclear weapons?
Trump has never explicitly mentioned using a nuclear weapon, but he has also never ruled it out.
Speculation regarding whether Washington might use nuclear weapons was rife in the early days of the conflict, largely because of the extreme nature of Trump’s numerous threats against Tehran.
In April, for example, as Iran enforced a blockade on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, Trump posted on his Truth Social site that “…a whole civilisation will die tonight, never to be brought back again”, if Iran did not agree to a peace deal and reopen the strait.
He also threatened to destroy Iran’s infrastructure, saying a bombing campaign “will be Power Plant Day and Bridge Day, all wrapped up in one”, in Iran.
Experts widely interpreted his statements as a threat of nuclear destruction, but one that still failed to force Iran to the table.
Although Trump largely moved away from his sabre-rattling rhetoric in the following weeks, he reiterated at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month that he could “annihilate” Iran. He also told the assembly that he believed a deal would emerge after the midterms.
What is a ‘tactical’ nuclear weapon?
“Tactical” nuclear weapons (TNW) are smaller nuclear munitions designed for the battlefield as opposed to strategic nuclear munitions designed for mass destruction.
Some perceive TNWs as having a lesser impact than an atomic bomb, but experts warn that their names are misleading and they can nevertheless be devastating. Their explosive yield, between 0.3 and 50 kilotons, can impact areas within a 500-600km radius.
The US dropped a 15-kiloton nuclear bomb on Hiroshima, meaning that weapon would today be considered a TNW. The US, North Korea and Russia have TNWs in their arsenals, although no country has ever used them. TNWs are not subject to any international treaties and are largely unregulated.
What might another US attack on Iran look like?
With Trump failing to rule out dropping the MOAB, analysts speculate that the US might launch another – perhaps final – intensive bombing campaign targeting Iran’s nuclear and defence sites, particularly Pickaxe Mountain.
The US could also continue its naval blockade on Iranian ports, while providing escorts for commercial ships through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has vowed to respond to escalatory strikes by targeting oil and digital infrastructure in neighbouring Gulf states.
Senior defence officials have also warned that Iran will invade its neighbours if the US launches a ground operation, although Trump appears to have ruled that out.
Earlier in the war, he hinted at the possibility of sending ground forces to retrieve some 400kg of highly enriched uranium that Washington and Israel claim Tehran has hidden underground.
Trump’s phone calls in March to Kurdish militia groups fighting Iran provoked speculation that Washington could coordinate with them for an invasion, although that did not happen.

articles.title: Open Source Summit Europe shifts sovereignty talk to practical compliance plans - news.lavx.hu
articles.summary: Open Source Summit Europe shifts sovereignty talk to practical compliance plans  news.lavx.hu
articles.full_text:
Attendees at Open Source Summit Europe heard less about AI and more about how to meet EU security rules and measure open source value. Speakers from Dell, Microsoft, SUSE and government agencies presented concrete plans for digital sovereignty.
Speakers at Open Source Summit Europe shifted from sovereignty rhetoric to practical plans. They detailed how to meet EU security rules and measure open source value.
Nithya Ruff of the Linux Foundation and Johan Linaker of Research Institutes of Sweden opened the event with a keynote on geopolitics and the fight to stay open. Ruff said digital sovereignty extends beyond Europe.
Companies must report vulnerabilities under active exploitation and severe security incidents under the EU Cyber Resilience Act. Reporting obligations began last month. Main requirements take effect in December 2027.
Dell and Microsoft discussed OpenSSF's CRABFOSC catalog, which helps manufacturers build lists of open source components to meet CRA compliance. The EU Open Source Observatory released its 2026 report, with Éléonore Daxhelet highlighting Ukraine's Diaa initiative and Switzerland's EMBAG legislation.
Kazuki Imamura from Japan's Innovation Platform Agency presented the Japan-Type OSS Model. His team studied hundreds of companies across seven countries and more than 30,000 GitHub repositories. They found many organizations talk about open source but few use it.
Dawn Foster of Fast Wonder presented guidance from the CHAOSS Project, which stands for Community Health Analytics in Open Source Software. Foster's deck included links to practitioner guides on viability metrics and demonstrating value to executives.
Officials in Schleswig-Holstein plan to move away from US cloud services. Berlin officials work with PwC on the city's digital sovereignty strategy and target 70 percent open source on administrative workstations by 2032.
Emiel Brok from SUSE discussed the Cloud and AI Development Act and the EU Cloud Sovereignty Framework. The framework sets eight Sovereignty Objectives and a SEAL scale from SEAL-0 to SEAL-4. SEAL-4 means complete EU control with no critical non-EU dependencies.
SUSE offers a Cloud Sovereignty Framework Self Assessment that rates an organization in 10 minutes. These plans and targets show organizations treat open source as infrastructure rather than an experiment.

articles.title: Why is France Burning? - Time Magazine
articles.summary: Why is France Burning?  Time Magazine
articles.full_text:
The French like to take to the streets, and they do it often.
On Sept. 17, students at Lycée Saint-Exupéry, a rather underprivileged high school in the Paris suburb of Créteil, erupted in protest over the abysmal conditions of their institution: chronic shortfall of teachers, poor facilities, long declining quality of education. Two weeks later, a wave of protests had swept cities across France. Students from hundreds of schools and scores of universities joined the protests, backed by their parents, teachers, and trade unions. More than 160,000 students and trade unionists protested across France on Tuesday in the third week of demonstrations.
France has never seen so many violent incidents in a movement made up largely of high school students. So far, over 200 students, 85 school staff, and 700 police officers have been injured in clashes across the country. Protesters have broken into schools and, in some cases, set fire to occupied or blockaded buildings. On Oct. 5, a 15-year-old boy had his hand blown off by a police grenade during a protest in Lens in northern France, an incident that crystallized the heavy-handed response authorities had adopted from the earliest days of the protest. More than 6,000 protesters have been arrested, most of them minors, and later released without charge.
The protests erupted after nearly a decade of Macronisme, the right-of-center, top-down governing style that President Emmanuel Macron of France incarnates. And they express a broader discontent: anger over disparities in school quality, university admissions decisions, and latent racial discrimination, and a sense among young people that those in power were not listening to them, that the country offered them little hope for the future.
The protests are also occurring amid a wider crisis of political confidence in the country. France is holding its presidential elections in April 2027, and the far-right and far-left are leading the opinion polls. The frontrunner is Marine Le Pen, who has worked for years to make her far-right party, the National Rally, more electable while campaigning on immigration, crime, and denunciation of an out-of-touch political class. Her party is already the largest opposition party in parliament, and a snap legislative election following the presidential vote could entrench it further.
On the other side is Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of France Unbowed, a far-left party, who is promising a sweeping redistribution of power and resources toward the working class. Both have built much of their appeal on opposition to the political establishment, the promise to wish away budget constraints, and deep hostility toward the European Union.
If France today feels like it is at a crossroads, it is because it is. The postwar model of a large welfare and regulatory state, run by a class of civil servants charged with modernizing the economy, tempering market forces and defining the common good, has run its course.
The collapse of postwar France
France now runs one of Europe’s largest budget deficits: its public debt stands at 119.3 % of GDP and is expected to rise next year. Fears of a crippling financial crisis are growing. Borrowing costs have risen so high that France is drawing comparisons with Greece, whose debt crisis in 2010 threatened the survival of the Eurozone. And with economic growth stagnating, there is no easy way out.
If anything, France would need to spend more: on defense, as Russia grows more threatening, the war in Ukraine continues, and the United States retreats from its traditional role as Europe’s security guarantor; on new technologies, as the country that once produced Concorde and high-speed trains now trails in high-tech innovation and AI; on strained public services, from schools to hospitals to neglected neighborhoods; and on infrastructure capable of withstanding the growing effects of climate change.
Successive French governments have promised to turn things around and allow for these badly needed investments in the country’s future, but none has succeeded.
The French malaise goes deeper. Inequality has been one of the students’ central grievances. They are not wrong. As in many countries, economic inequalities in France have widened over the past two decades under the combined effects of globalization, industrial decline, and the growing concentration of inherited wealth.
In Capital in the Twenty-First Century, the French economist Thomas Piketty showed how wealth perpetuates across generations and widens the divide between those who own capital and everyone else. This concentration of wealth and power remains deeply resented: for many, President Macron’s original sin is still his brief stint at the Rothschild investment bank before entering politics.
But the most injurious form of inequality lies elsewhere: in the power of France’s national meritocratic myth, which holds that people broadly owe their social position largely to their academic performance. At the top of that system sit the highly competitive grandes écoles, the elite institutions of higher education that have produced leaders in politics, culture, and business.
What makes the myth so corrosive is not that academic achievement goes unrewarded but that it remains a pretty reliable path to better jobs, higher status, and positions of power. In such a system, students from underfunded public schools face a profound disadvantage compared with peers who attend better-resourced schools and whose better-educated parents know how to navigate the system.
Private schools offer another route, but are still frowned upon as a way to buy an advantage. It is no surprise that the protests broke out in Créteil, a working-class suburb just outside Paris, where schools are chronically under-resourced.
We shall always have Paris
Racial and geographic discrimination also contribute to the crisis of France. The collection of ethno-racial statistics is prohibited by French law; it is a laudable restriction in principle but problematic in practice. Visible minorities remain vastly underrepresented among France’s political and business elites.
Families with immigrant backgrounds, many with roots in African and Asian countries once colonized by France, are disproportionately concentrated on urban peripheries, where jobs are scarce and residents often face discrimination from employers elsewhere.
Islamophobia has also grown over the last decade amid conflicts in the Middle East and a string of Islamist-inspired terrorist attacks. Rhetoric once largely confined to the far right has seeped into the mainstream right, where calls for “order” and “security” often carry an anti-immigrant charge. Macron’s references to the “decivilization” of some young people and former Interior Minister Bruno Retailleau’s description of immigrants’ participation in the protests that followed the police killing of a teenager in 2023 as a “regression towards ethnic origins” are emblematic of that shift.
There is another problem with France’s meritocratic ideal: Paris. Political power, economic opportunity, cultural prestige, and elite education remain extraordinarily concentrated in the capital. The result is a deep economic divide between Paris and the rest of the country and an elite that lives largely among its own, surrounded by people with similar educations, careers, and assumptions, and cut off from much of the country.
The Yellow Vest revolt of 2018 to 2019 was an earlier social explosion of precisely that resentment. It is hardly surprising that students are denouncing the unequal distribution of resources between Paris and the rest of the country, or that the protests began in Créteil, close enough to the capital for the contrast to be impossible to miss.
When students from my own former school, the elite Lycée Henri-IV, where I was a rather poor student, joined the movement in its third week, I noticed how carefully they described themselves as protesting “in solidarity” with less privileged schools. They knew which side of the divide they were on. So much for meritocracy.
Racing to the Elysée
Where does this leave France? With the presidential elections approaching next April, political parties are scrambling to position themselves in relation to a protest movement that has shown no sign of abating. On Oct. 6, more than a quarter-million people took to the streets as high school students were joined by university students, teachers, parents and trade unions. An even wider “national day of protest” is planned for Oct. 17.
Both familiar and new dynamics will shape the election. The familiar one is the runoff dilemma: voters may once again be asked to support a candidate from the opposite political camp simply to prevent Le Pen from reaching the Élysée. Le Pen made the runoff in both 2017 and 2022 and is leading the polls by a large margin. This time, however, the field trailing her is unusually fragmented. Two former prime ministers under Macron, Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, are in the race; Philippe is competing with Mélenchon for second place, while Attal trails both.
Whatever the outcome, the presidential vote may resolve little. A president from the far-right National Rally could find herself governing without a stable parliamentary majority or broad support among the public or within the civil service. A compromise candidate from the center or left could face the same fractured parliament that has bedeviled the final years of Macron’s presidency, during which France has had five prime ministers in two years.
What is new is the extent to which France is being reshaped by forces now familiar across the globe: a crisis of confidence in democracy, conservative billionaires building media empires and financing ideological movements, polarizing social media, foreign interference in elections, and growing voter distrust of supranational institutions, including the European Union.

articles.title: Advantech Partners with DEKRA, Signing MOU to Strengthen Global Industrial Cybersecurity Compliance in Response to EU CRA - TradingView
articles.summary: Advantech Partners with DEKRA, Signing MOU to Strengthen Global Industrial Cybersecurity Compliance in Response to EU CRA  TradingView
articles.full_text:
TAIPEI, Oct. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As the European Union's Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) enters its implementation phase, cybersecurity compliance is becoming an increasingly important requirement for industrial equipment and Edge AI products entering global markets. Advantech (2395), a global leader in IoT intelligent systems and embedded platforms, announced the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with DEKRA, a trusted global expert in testing, inspection, and certification with more than 100 years of expertise. By combining the expertise in industrial computing, cybersecurity testing, and global certification, the partnership aims to help end customers and system integrators address cybersecurity requirements from the product design stage, accelerate compliance with EU CRA requirements and international standards such as IEC 62443, reduce compliance risks, and shorten time to market.
Miller Chang, President of Advantech's Embedded Sector, said at the MOU signing ceremony: "As Edge AI continues to advance rapidly, compliance is evolving from a certification procedure before product launch into a critical consideration that customers need to address from the early stages of product design. By combining Advantech's expertise in industrial computing and Edge AI with DEKRA's global certification expertise, we aim to enable customers identify regulatory requirements earlier, reduce compliance risks, and shorten time to market, enabling trusted Edge AI innovations to reach global markets more efficiently."
Stan Zurkiewicz, CEO of DEKRA, said: "Digital trust is essential for industrial innovation to succeed in global markets. As AI and connected technologies become integral to manufacturing, energy and transportation, companies need verifiable evidence of safety and cybersecurity to build confidence in new technologies. Our collaboration with Advantech combines its industry experience with DEKRA's third-party independent testing and certification expertise. DEKRA's role is to provide independent assurance, helping companies navigate evolving international requirements and build trust in new technologies."
Addressing Cybersecurity Compliance from the Design Stage to Reduce Development Costs and Market Access Risks
Advantech and DEKRA are bringing testing and compliance expertise into the early stages of product development, helping customers identify regulatory and technical requirements across different markets from the design stage, plan certification pathways in advance, and identify and address potential cybersecurity gaps throughout development. The collaboration covers technical and feasibility assessments, documentation review, certification preparation, vulnerability management, and secure development support. This approach helps customers reduce the time and costs associated with late-stage design changes while establishing a comprehensive compliance process from product concept and design development to testing, certification, and market deployment.
First Milestone: Industrial Edge System Meet IEC 62443-4-2 SL2 Requirements
As an initial outcome of the collaboration, Advantech's AFE-E630 industrial edge system has passed an independent assessment by DEKRA and received an Attestation of Conformity (AoC). Designed for commercial and industrial energy storage management applications, the AFE-E630 security functions meet IEC 62443-4-2 SL2 requirements within the assessed scope. This provides a verified basis for product cybersecurity in these applications and a reference for customers' subsequent product integration and system-level compliance assessments.
Extending Collaboration to Edge AI, Semiconductors, Robotics, Energy, and Transportation to Strengthen Cyber Resilience and Expand into Global Markets
Beyond established industrial applications, Advantech and DEKRA plan to extend the collaboration to emerging technology areas, including AI-enabled industrial systems, semiconductor manufacturing, robotics, drones, other mission-critical unmanned systems, as well as energy site equipment and transportation management, to accelerate global market access. As Edge AI becomes increasingly integrated with physical devices, product safety, functional safety, and cybersecurity requirements are becoming increasingly interconnected. Advantech and DEKRA will combine Advantech's edge computing platforms and industry application knowledge with DEKRA's expertise in cybersecurity, testing, and functional safety to enhance the safety and trustworthiness of next-generation intelligent devices.
As cybersecurity regulations continue to evolve across global markets, Advantech and DEKRA will continue to combine their respective expertise to help customers address compliance requirements across different markets more efficiently, reduce risks associated with global deployment, and accelerate time to market, further supporting the expansion of Edge AI and intelligent industrial applications into global markets.
Click to learn more:
- Advantech Compliance Solutions
- Advantech Industrial Edge System AFE-E630
About Advantech
Advantech is a global leader in IoT intelligent systems and embedded platforms, with the corporate vision of "Enabling an Intelligent Planet." To embrace the trends of edge computing and artificial intelligence, Advantech fully deploys its sector-driven strategy and focus on Edge Computing and Edge AI, targeting five key markets: Edge Intelligence Systems, Manufacturing, Energy and Utilities, iHealthcare, and iCity Services & iRetail. In the meantime, Advantech is enhancing its global presence and core competitiveness by integrating its Edge Computing hardware platform, the WISE-IoT software platform, and sector-specific Edge AI solutions with domain expertise. The integration will form an "Orchestration" model for seamless industrial chain connections, benefiting both our partners and clients. Advantech is also working with business partners to co-create business ecosystems that accelerate the goal of industrial intelligence.
About DEKRA
For more than 100 years, DEKRA has been a trusted name in safety. Founded in 1925 with the original goal of improving road safety through vehicle inspections, DEKRA has grown to become the world's largest independent, non-listed expert organization in the field of testing, inspection, and certification. Today, as a global partner, the company supports its customers with comprehensive services and solutions to drive safety and sustainability forward. In 2025, DEKRA generated revenue of 4.4 billion euros. More than 48,000 employees are providing qualified and independent expert services in approximately 60 countries across five continents. DEKRA holds a Platinum rating from EcoVadis, placing it among the top 1% of the world's most sustainable companies.

articles.title: [不同来源] Euro gains as US Dollar weakens following Fed Warsh’s comments at IMF chat - www.tmgm.com
articles.summary: Euro gains as US Dollar weakens following Fed Warsh’s comments at IMF chat  www.tmgm.com
articles.full_text:
EUR/USD remains stronger after posting modest gains the previous day, trading around 1.1230 during Asian hours on Friday. The currency pair inches higher as the US Dollar (USD) declines following recent comments from key financial leaders.
Speaking at a fireside chat with International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva in Bangkok, US Federal Reserve (Fed) Chairman Kevin Warsh reiterated the Fed’s commitment to price stability while refusing to prejudge upcoming policy meetings. Warsh highlighted that an investment surge is currently the most significant upside force in the global economy.
Meanwhile, US Treasury Undersecretary for International Affairs, Erin Browne, called on the IMF to take a more assertive approach to identifying global imbalances and urged a balanced outlook considering positive US-led economic shocks. She further cautioned that sharp, disorderly currency moves could trigger volatility across broader financial markets.
However, the Greenback gained support from stronger-than-expected inflation data released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics on Thursday. The US Producer Price Index (PPI) surged 6.3% year-over-year in September, its largest gain since 2022, easily topping the market consensus of 5.3% and following a revised 5.6% increase in August. On a monthly basis, the PPI rose 1.3%, significantly outpacing the 0.5% analyst estimate. Core PPI, which excludes food and energy, also came in hotter than expected, rising 0.7% month-over-month and 5.0% year-over-year.
Despite the elevated inflation figures, market expectations regarding Federal Reserve interest rate decisions remained largely unchanged. According to the CME FedWatch Tool, traders are pricing in a 72% probability that the central bank will keep rates steady. However, expectations for a rate increase in December have climbed to 92%.
On the European front, upside momentum for the EUR/USD pair remains constrained due to political uncertainty in Europe, particularly in France. European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde emphasized that France must address its national debt challenges through fiscal consolidation, dampening speculation that the ECB might intervene by purchasing French bonds to contain rising yields.
While Lagarde noted that energy-driven inflation has not yet spread to the broader euro-area economy, supporting a cautious policy stance, ECB policymaker Gediminas Šimkus asserted that a rate hike this month remains an option if necessary. Markets continue to price in another ECB rate increase in December.
The Euro is the currency for the 20 European Union countries that belong to the Eurozone. It is the second most heavily traded currency in the world behind the US Dollar. In 2022, it accounted for 31% of all foreign exchange transactions, with an average daily turnover of over $2.2 trillion a day. EUR/USD is the most heavily traded currency pair in the world, accounting for an estimated 30% off all transactions, followed by EUR/JPY (4%), EUR/GBP (3%) and EUR/AUD (2%).
The European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt, Germany, is the reserve bank for the Eurozone. The ECB sets interest rates and manages monetary policy. The ECB’s primary mandate is to maintain price stability, which means either controlling inflation or stimulating growth. Its primary tool is the raising or lowering of interest rates. Relatively high interest rates – or the expectation of higher rates – will usually benefit the Euro and vice versa. The ECB Governing Council makes monetary policy decisions at meetings held eight times a year. Decisions are made by heads of the Eurozone national banks and six permanent members, including the President of the ECB, Christine Lagarde.
Eurozone inflation data, measured by the Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), is an important econometric for the Euro. If inflation rises more than expected, especially if above the ECB’s 2% target, it obliges the ECB to raise interest rates to bring it back under control. Relatively high interest rates compared to its counterparts will usually benefit the Euro, as it makes the region more attractive as a place for global investors to park their money.
Data releases gauge the health of the economy and can impact on the Euro. Indicators such as GDP, Manufacturing and Services PMIs, employment, and consumer sentiment surveys can all influence the direction of the single currency. A strong economy is good for the Euro. Not only does it attract more foreign investment but it may encourage the ECB to put up interest rates, which will directly strengthen the Euro. Otherwise, if economic data is weak, the Euro is likely to fall. Economic data for the four largest economies in the euro area (Germany, France, Italy and Spain) are especially significant, as they account for 75% of the Eurozone’s economy.
Another significant data release for the Euro is the Trade Balance. This indicator measures the difference between what a country earns from its exports and what it spends on imports over a given period. If a country produces highly sought after exports then its currency will gain in value purely from the extra demand created from foreign buyers seeking to purchase these goods. Therefore, a positive net Trade Balance strengthens a currency and vice versa for a negative balance.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones reportedly strike Yandex data center, warehouses in overnight attack on Russia - The Kyiv Independent
articles.summary: Ukrainian drones reportedly strike Yandex data center, warehouses in overnight attack on Russia  The Kyiv IndependentIs Zelensky right to say data centre strikes have taken down Russian bots?  BBCDid Ukrainian strikes on Russian datacentres reduce online disinformation?  The GuardianYandex outage: Data shows that instead of going dark, malicious bots went on the move  Cloudflare BlogHow Ukraine’s data centre strikes have thrown Russia into turmoil &nb...
articles.full_text:
Editor's Note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Ukrainian forces appeared to strike multiple targets across Russia's Moscow, Rostov, and Vladimir regions in a widespread drone attack overnight on Oct. 16.
The Kyiv Independent can not independently verify attack targets or damage at this time.
According to monitoring channels ExileNova+ and SuperNova+, Russian technology giant Yandex's data center in Vladimir Oblast, around 500 kilometers (310 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was targeted in the overnight operation.
Footage from residents at the scene shows large explosions and air defense systems operating around residential buildings.
Following strikes on the same Yandex site on Oct. 11, the company announced operations at the data center had been completely shut down. That strike marked the third near-consecutive day of attacks on Yandex data centers in Russia, following confirmed strikes in Ryazan and Kaluga oblasts on Oct. 8 and 9.
The string of attacks on Russian data centers follows President Volodymyr Zelensky's statement that Ukraine would retaliate in kind to Russian strikes on Ukrainian internet infrastructure.
Earlier in the night around Moscow, Ukrainian drones shut down airspace above multiple airports. According to Russian opposition news channel Astra, plane departures and arrivals to the Vnukovo, Domodedovo, Zhukovsky, and Sheremetyevo airports were canceled overnight.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that over 59 Ukrainian drones were destroyed by the capital's air defense system throughout the night.
The closure of Moscow's airspace partially realizes threats made by Zelensky in September when he promised that Russian skies would soon be "de facto closed."
"There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," said Zelensky.
It is currently unclear what, if any, targets were hit around Moscow. Eyewitness footage from city residents shows what appears to be flames illuminating the night sky, accompanied by the sounds of drones overhead and loud explosions.
Previously, several Moscow airports temporarily suspended flights on Oct. 9, as suspected Ukrainian drones and balloons entered airspace around the Russian capital.
Over 950 kilometers (590 miles) southeast of Moscow, Ukrainian drones attacked targets in the Rostov Oblast.
According to regional Governor Yuri Slusar, production and storage facilities were damaged, and a fire broke out as a result of the drone attack in the town of Aksay. The Chertkovsky district and the city of Bataysk in the region were also targeted, Slusar said.
